questions.e: A = [(x − 3) + (x + 5)]/2 = (2x + 2)/2 = x + 1. The expression 2x + 2 is the sum before halving.

questions.s: The sum 3 + 3² + 3³ + … + 3⁸ equals
questions.e: This GP has a = 3, r = 3 and 8 terms, so S = 3(3⁸ − 1)/2 = 3 × 6560/2 = 9840. The value 3280 = (3⁸ − 1)/2 forgets the first term a = 3.

questions.s: The nth term of a sequence is 2ⁿ + 3. The sum of its first 5 terms is
questions.e: Σ2ᵏ for k = 1 to 5 is 2 + 4 + 8 + 16 + 32 = 62, and the constant 3 added five times gives 15, so the sum is 77. The value 65 adds 3 only once.

questions.s: The sum to infinity of a GP is 15 and the sum to infinity of the squares of its terms is 45. The first term of the GP is
questions.e: a/(1 − r) = 15 and a²/(1 − r²) = 45. Dividing the second by the first gives a/(1 + r) = 3. So 15(1 − r) = 3(1 + r), giving r = 2/3 and a = 5. The value 3 is a/(1 + r), not a.

questions.s: The arithmetic mean of two positive numbers a and b (a > b) is twice their geometric mean. Then a : b =
questions.e: (a + b)/2 = 2√(ab). Put s = √(a/b): s² − 4s + 1 = 0, so s = 2 + √3 and a/b = (2 + √3)² = 7 + 4√3 = (2 + √3)/(2 − √3). The ratio 4 : 1 gives A = 5/2 and G = 2, so A is only 1.25 times G.

questions.s: The sum of all three-digit numbers that leave remainder 1 when divided by 4 is
questions.e: The numbers are 101, 105, …, 997, an AP with d = 4 and n = (997 − 101)/4 + 1 = 225 terms. S = (225/2)(101 + 997) = 225 × 549 = 123525. Counting 224 terms gives 122528, and 247050 forgets the factor ½.

questions.s: In an arithmetic progression the sum of the first 7 terms equals the sum of the first 11 terms. The sum of the first 18 terms is
questions.e: (7/2)(2a + 6d) = (11/2)(2a + 10d) gives 14a + 42d = 22a + 110d, so 2a + 17d = 0. Then S₁₈ = 9(2a + 17d) = 0, since T₁ + T₁₈ = 2a + 17d = 0 and the terms cancel in pairs. The value 2S₇ would need the extra terms to repeat the first seven.

questions.s: The sum of the first n terms of a geometric progression is 3ⁿ − 1. Its common ratio is
questions.e: T₁ = S₁ = 2 and S₂ = 8, so T₂ = 6 and r = 6/2 = 3. The value 2 is the first term, not the ratio.

questions.s: If a, b and c (all non-zero) are in arithmetic progression, then 1/(bc), 1/(ca) and 1/(ab) are in
questions.e: Multiplying each of 1/(bc), 1/(ca), 1/(ab) by abc gives a, b, c, which are in AP; multiplying an AP by a constant keeps it an AP. Choosing HP confuses this with the reciprocals 1/a, 1/b, 1/c.

questions.s: The arithmetic mean of two positive numbers exceeds their geometric mean by 2, and the geometric mean exceeds their harmonic mean by 8/5. The numbers are
questions.e: With A = G + 2 and H = G − 8/5, the relation G² = AH gives G² = G² + 2G/5 − 16/5, so G = 8, A = 10 and H = 32/5. Numbers with sum 20 and product 64 are 4 and 16. The pair 2 and 32 has G = 8 but A = 17.

questions.s: The sum of the first n even natural numbers, 2 + 4 + 6 + … + 2n, is
questions.e: 2 + 4 + … + 2n = 2(1 + 2 + … + n) = 2 × n(n + 1)/2 = n(n + 1); for n = 3, 2 + 4 + 6 = 12 = 3 × 4. The value n² is the sum of the first n odd numbers.

questions.s: The 12th term of the arithmetic progression 9, 6, 3, … is
questions.e: a = 9 and d = −3, so T₁₂ = 9 + 11(−3) = 9 − 33 = −24. Using 12 steps of d gives −27, the 13th term.

questions.s: The common ratio of the geometric progression 2/3, 1/3, 1/6, … is
questions.e: r = (1/3)/(2/3) = 1/2, and (1/6)/(1/3) = 1/2 confirms it. The value −1/3 is the difference of the first two terms, as if it were an AP.

questions.s: The 6th term of the harmonic progression 1, 1/4, 1/7, … is
questions.e: The reciprocals 1, 4, 7, … form an AP with d = 3, whose 6th term is 1 + 5(3) = 16. So the 6th term of the HP is 1/16. The value 16 forgets to take the reciprocal.

questions.s: The value of 1 + 2 + 3 + … + 30 is
questions.e: n(n + 1)/2 = 30 × 31/2 = 465. Forgetting the division by 2 gives 930.

questions.s: The positive geometric mean between 3 and 27 is
questions.e: G = √(3 × 27) = √81 = 9, and 3, 9, 27 is a GP with r = 3. The value 15 is the arithmetic mean, and 81 is G² before taking the root.

questions.s: The sum of the first 15 terms of the AP 2, 4, 6, … is
questions.e: S₁₅ = (15/2)[2(2) + 14(2)] = (15/2)(32) = 240, which also equals n(n + 1) for the first n even numbers. The value 225 = 15² is the sum of the first 15 odd numbers.

questions.s: Three arithmetic means are inserted between 6 and 26. The sum of these three means is
questions.e: 5 terms in all, so 26 = 6 + 4d and d = 5; the means are 11, 16, 21, with sum 48. In general the sum of n means is n times (a + b)/2 = 3 × 16. The value 32 is the sum of the two given numbers.

questions.s: Which term of the AP 64, 60, 56, … is its first negative term?
questions.e: Tₙ = 64 − 4(n − 1) < 0 needs n − 1 > 16, so n = 18 and T₁₈ = −4. The 17th term is exactly 0, which is not negative.

questions.s: The sum of the first 5 terms of the GP 16, 8, 4, … is
questions.e: S₅ = a(1 − r⁵)/(1 − r) = 16(1 − 1/32)/(1/2) = 32 × 31/32 = 31; directly 16 + 8 + 4 + 2 + 1 = 31. The value 32 is the sum to infinity.

questions.s: The sum of the infinite series 4 − 2 + 1 − 1/2 + … is
questions.e: a = 4 and r = −1/2, so S∞ = 4/(1 + 1/2) = 8/3. Ignoring the alternating signs (r = +1/2) gives 8.

questions.s: The harmonic mean between 6 and 12 is
questions.e: H = 2ab/(a + b) = 2(72)/18 = 8. Check: 1/6, 1/8, 1/12 have common difference −1/24. The value 9 is the arithmetic mean and 6√2 the geometric mean.

questions.s: The arithmetic mean of two positive numbers is 5 and their geometric mean is 3. Their harmonic mean is
questions.e: G² = AH gives H = 9/5 (the numbers are 1 and 9, and 2 × 9/10 = 9/5). The value 1 continues 5, 3, 1 as if A, G, H were in AP; 5/9 is 1/H, not H.

questions.s: The value of 1² + 2² + 3² + 4² + 5² + 6² is
questions.e: n(n + 1)(2n + 1)/6 = 6 × 7 × 13/6 = 91; directly 1 + 4 + 9 + 16 + 25 + 36 = 91. The value 441 = 21² is the sum of the first six cubes.

questions.s: The value of 1³ + 2³ + 3³ + … + 8³ is
questions.e: Σk³ = [n(n + 1)/2]² = 36² = 1296. The value 36 is 1 + 2 + … + 8 before squaring, and 204 is the sum of the first eight squares.

questions.s: Usman invests Rs 50 000 and its value grows by 20% of the current value each year. Its value after 2 years is
questions.e: The yearly values form a GP with ratio 1.2, so after 2 years the value is 50 000 × 1.44 = Rs 72 000. Adding Rs 10 000 each year gives Rs 70 000, which treats the growth as an AP.

questions.s: A shop in Peshawar sells 40 items on the first day and 5 more items each day than the day before. The total number of items sold in 8 days is
The sum of the first n terms of an AP is 2n² + 3n. Its 10th term is
questions.e: T₁₀ = S₁₀ − S₉ = 230 − 189 = 41; in general Tₙ = 4n + 1. The value 230 is S₁₀, the sum rather than the term, and 43 comes from wrongly differentiating Sₙ to get 4n + 3.

questions.s: The first term of a geometric progression with positive ratio is 1, and the sum of its 3rd and 5th terms is 90. The common ratio is
questions.e: r² + r⁴ = 90. Putting u = r² gives u² + u − 90 = 0, so u = 9 (u = −10 is rejected) and r = 3. The value 9 is r², not r.

questions.s: If H is the harmonic mean between two positive numbers a and b, then H/a + H/b equals
questions.e: H = 2ab/(a + b), so H/a = 2b/(a + b) and H/b = 2a/(a + b). Their sum is 2(a + b)/(a + b) = 2. Check with 3 and 6: H = 4 and 4/3 + 4/6 = 2.

questions.s: The sum of the first n terms of the series 1 + 11 + 111 + 1111 + … is
The value of 6!/4! is
questions.e: 6! = 6 × 5 × 4!, so 6!/4! = 6 × 5 = 30. The option 24 is just 4!, and 120 is 5!; neither is the quotient.

questions.s: By definition, 0! is equal to
questions.e: 0! is defined as 1, so that formulas such as n!/(n − r)! and ⁿCₙ = n!/(n! 0!) = 1 stay valid. Taking 0! = 0 would make ⁿCₙ undefined (division by zero).

questions.s: If n!/(n − 2)! = 56, then n is
questions.e: n!/(n − 2)! = n(n − 1) = 56 = 8 × 7, so n = 8. Choosing 7 picks the smaller factor, and 28 comes from wrongly halving 56 as if it were ⁿC₂.

questions.s: For a positive integer n, (n + 1)!/(n − 1)! simplifies to
questions.e: (n + 1)! = (n + 1) n (n − 1)!, so the quotient is (n + 1)n = n² + n. The form n² − n is n(n − 1), which would be n!/(n − 2)!.

questions.s: The value of 5! − 4! is
questions.e: 5! − 4! = 4!(5 − 1) = 24 × 4 = 96. Factorials do not subtract like ordinary numbers, so 5! − 4! is not 1! = 1.

questions.s: The number of zeros at the end of 50! is
questions.e: Zeros come from factors of 5 (factors of 2 are plentiful): ⌊50/5⌋ + ⌊50/25⌋ = 10 + 2 = 12. The answer 10 forgets that 25 and 50 each contain 5 twice.

questions.s: The value of 8!/(6! × 2!) is
questions.e: 8!/6! = 8 × 7 = 56, and dividing by 2! = 2 gives 28. The option 56 forgets to divide by 2!.
Since k·k! = (k + 1)! − k!, the sum telescopes to 5! − 1! = 120 − 1 = 119. Directly: 1 + 4 + 18 + 96 = 119. The option 120 forgets to subtract 1!.

questions.s: The highest power of 2 that divides 10! is
questions.e: Count factors of 2: ⌊10/2⌋ + ⌊10/4⌋ + ⌊10/8⌋ = 5 + 2 + 1 = 8, so 2⁸ divides 10!. The option 2⁵ counts only the even numbers and ignores that 4 and 8 contain extra 2s.

questions.s: Ayesha has 4 shirts and 3 trousers. In how many ways can she choose one shirt and one pair of trousers?
questions.e: By the fundamental counting principle the choices multiply: 4 × 3 = 12. Adding them (7) would be correct only if she chose a shirt or trousers, not both.

questions.s: How many 3-digit numbers can be formed from the digits 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 if digits may be repeated?
questions.e: Each of the three places can take any of the 5 digits: 5 × 5 × 5 = 125. The option 60 = 5 × 4 × 3 is the count without repetition, and 243 = 3⁵ reverses base and power.

questions.s: How many 3-digit numbers (100 to 999) have all three digits different?
questions.e: The hundreds digit cannot be 0: 9 choices; the tens digit can be 0 but not the first digit: 9 choices; the units digit: 8 choices. 9 × 9 × 8 = 648. The option 720 = 10 × 9 × 8 wrongly allows 0 in the first place.

questions.s: A vehicle number plate has 2 letters (A to Z) followed by 3 digits (0 to 9). If repetition is allowed, how many different plates are possible?
questions.e: Letters: 26 × 26 = 676; digits: 10 × 10 × 10 = 1000; total 676 × 1000 = 676000. The option 650000 = 26 × 25 × 1000 forbids a repeated letter, which the question allows.

questions.s: A coin is tossed 4 times and the sequence of heads and tails is recorded. The number of possible sequences is
questions.e: Each toss has 2 outcomes, so there are 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 2⁴ = 16 sequences. The option 8 = 2³ counts only three tosses.

questions.s: How many even 3-digit numbers can be formed from the digits 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 without repetition?
questions.e: Fill the units place first: it must be 2, 4 or 6 (3 ways). Then the hundreds and tens places take 5 × 4 = 20 ways. Total 3 × 20 = 60. The option 120 = 6 × 5 × 4 ignores the even condition, and 108 = 6 × 6 × 3 allows repetition.

questions.s: How many odd 4-digit numbers (1000 to 9999) have all four digits different?
questions.e: Units digit: one of 1, 3, 5, 7, 9 (5 ways). Thousands digit: not 0 and not the units digit (8 ways). Then 8 and 7 ways for the middle places. 5 × 8 × 8 × 7 = 2240. The option 2520 = 5 × 9 × 8 × 7 forgets that the first digit cannot be 0.

questions.s: The number of positive divisors of 72 is
questions.e: 72 = 2³ × 3². A divisor is 2ᵃ3ᵇ with a = 0 to 3 (4 choices) and b = 0 to 2 (3 choices), giving 4 × 3 = 12 divisors. The option 6 = 3 × 2 uses the exponents themselves instead of exponent + 1.

questions.s: A restaurant in Lahore offers 3 starters, 5 main dishes and 2 desserts. How many different three-course meals (one of each course) are possible?
questions.e: Multiply the independent choices: 3 × 5 × 2 = 30. The option 10 adds the choices, which counts picking just one dish.

questions.s: In how many ways can 3 different letters be posted into 4 letter boxes if a box may receive any number of letters?
questions.e: Each letter independently goes into one of 4 boxes: 4 × 4 × 4 = 4³ = 64. The option 81 = 3⁴ wrongly lets each box choose a letter.

questions.s: How many 4-digit numbers (1000 to 9999) have at least one digit repeated?
questions.e: There are 9000 four-digit numbers. Those with all digits different number 9 × 9 × 8 × 7 = 4536. So 9000 − 4536 = 4464 have a repeat. The option 3960 subtracts 5040 = 10 × 9 × 8 × 7, which wrongly allows a leading 0.

questions.s: The value of ⁵P₂ is
questions.e: ⁿPᵣ = n!/(n − r)!, so ⁵P₂ = 5 × 4 = 20. The option 10 is ⁵C₂, which ignores order.

questions.s: The number of different arrangements of all the letters of the word NUST is
questions.e: NUST has 4 different letters, so they can be arranged in 4! = 24 ways. The option 16 = 4² is not a permutation count.

questions.s: If ⁿP₂ = 90, then n is equal to
questions.e: ⁿP₂ = n(n − 1) = 90 = 10 × 9, so n = 10. The option 9 is the smaller factor, and 45 is 90/2 as if ⁿC₂ were meant.

questions.s: Five students sit in a row. In how many ways can they sit if two particular students, Ali and Bilal, must sit next to each other?
questions.e: Treat Ali and Bilal as one block: 4 units can be arranged in 4! = 24 ways, and the two can swap inside the block in 2! ways, giving 48. The option 24 forgets the swap inside the block.

questions.s: Five students sit in a row. In how many ways can they sit if Hamza and Usman must not sit next to each other?
questions.e: Total arrangements 5! = 120; arrangements with the two together = 4! × 2! = 48. So 120 − 48 = 72 keep them apart. The option 48 is the together count, not the apart count.

questions.s: In how many ways can 4 books, chosen from 7 different books, be arranged in a row on a shelf?
questions.e: Order on the shelf matters, so the count is ⁷P₄ = 7 × 6 × 5 × 4 = 840. The option 35 = ⁷C₄ only chooses the books without arranging them, and 2401 = 7⁴ allows the same book to be used twice.

questions.s: In how many ways can the letters of the word LAHORE be arranged so that the three vowels are always together?
questions.e: The vowels A, O, E form one block; with L, H, R there are 4 units, arranged in 4! = 24 ways. The vowels can be ordered inside the block in 3! = 6 ways, giving 24 × 6 = 144. The option 24 forgets the arrangements inside the block.

questions.s: The letters of SIALKOT are all different. How many arrangements of all its letters begin with S and end with T?
questions.e: With S fixed first and T fixed last, the remaining 5 letters fill the middle in 5! = 120 ways. The option 5040 = 7! ignores the fixed positions.

questions.s: The value of ⁶P₆ is
questions.e: ⁿPₙ = n!/0! = n!, so ⁶P₆ = 6! = 720. The option 1 is ⁶C₆, which counts selections, not arrangements.

questions.s: For 0 ≤ r ≤ n, the ratio ⁿPᵣ/ⁿCᵣ equals
questions.e: ⁿPᵣ = n!/(n − r)! and ⁿCᵣ = n!/(r!(n − r)!), so their ratio is r!. This makes sense: each selection of r objects can be ordered in r! ways. The option (n − r)! inverts the roles of the two factorials in the denominator.

questions.s: If ⁿP₄ = 20 × ⁿP₂, then n is equal to
questions.e: n(n − 1)(n − 2)(n − 3) = 20 n(n − 1), so (n − 2)(n − 3) = 20 = 5 × 4. Hence n − 2 = 5 and n = 7. The option 5 stops at n − 2 = 5 without solving for n.

questions.s: How many 4-digit numbers can be formed from the digits 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 if no digit is repeated?
questions.e: The first digit cannot be 0: 4 choices. The remaining three places take 4 × 3 × 2 = 24 ways from the other digits (0 now allowed). Total 4 × 24 = 96. The option 120 = ⁵P₄ counts strings that start with 0.

questions.s: How many even 4-digit numbers can be formed from the digits 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 with no digit repeated?
questions.e: Last digit 0: the first three places take 4 × 3 × 2 = 24 ways. Last digit 2 or 4: the first digit has 3 choices (not 0, not the last digit), then 3 × 2, giving 18 for each, so 36. Total 24 + 36 = 60. The option 36 forgets the case ending in 0.

questions.s: The number of different arrangements of the letters of the word BANANA is
questions.e: BANANA has 6 letters with A three times and N twice: 6!/(3! × 2!) = 720/12 = 60. The option 720 treats all letters as different.

questions.s: The number of different arrangements of all the letters of the word ISLAMABAD is
questions.e: ISLAMABAD has 9 letters, with A appearing 3 times and the rest different. Arrangements = 9!/3! = 362880/6 = 60480. The option 181440 = 9!/2 divides by 2 instead of 3!.

questions.s: How many arrangements of all the letters of the word PESHAWAR begin with P?
questions.e: Fix P first; the other 7 letters E, S, H, A, W, A, R contain A twice, so they can be arranged in 7!/2! = 5040/2 = 2520 ways. The option 5040 forgets that the two A's are identical.

questions.s: In how many ways can the letters of the word QUETTA be arranged so that the vowels U, E, A are always together?
questions.e: Make the vowels one block; with Q, T, T there are 4 units with T repeated, giving 4!/2! = 12 arrangements. The block itself can be ordered in 3! = 6 ways, so 12 × 6 = 72. The option 12 forgets to arrange the vowels inside the block.

questions.s: In how many ways can 5 identical red balls and 3 identical blue balls be arranged in a row?
questions.e: This is an arrangement of 8 objects with 5 alike of one kind and 3 alike of another: 8!/(5! × 3!) = 56, which also equals ⁸C₃ (choose the blue positions). The option 28 = ⁸C₂ chooses the wrong number of positions.

questions.s: On a square grid, a token moves from the point (0, 0) to (4, 3) using only unit steps to the right or upwards. The number of different paths is
questions.e: Every path uses 4 right steps (R) and 3 up steps (U) in some order: 7!/(4! × 3!) = 35. The option 128 = 2⁷ lets each step go either way without the fixed totals, and 5040 = 7! treats all steps as different.

questions.s: In how many ways can 5 people be seated around a round table?
questions.e: For circular arrangements, fix one person and arrange the rest: (5 − 1)! = 4! = 24. The option 120 = 5! counts rotations of the same seating as different.

questions.s: In how many ways can 8 different beads be strung on a necklace (which can be turned over)?
questions.e: Circular arrangements of 8 objects: (8 − 1)! = 5040. A necklace can be flipped, so clockwise and anticlockwise orders are the same: 5040/2 = 2520. The option 5040 forgets the flip.

questions.s: Six friends sit around a round table. In how many ways can they sit if Sana and Zainab must sit next to each other?
questions.e: Treat Sana and Zainab as one unit: 5 units round a table give (5 − 1)! = 24 arrangements, and the pair can swap in 2 ways: 24 × 2 = 48. The option 240 = 5! × 2 is the count for a straight row, not a circle.

questions.s: In how many ways can 4 men and 4 women sit around a round table so that men and women alternate?
questions.e: Seat the men first round the table: (4 − 1)! = 6 ways. This fixes 4 gaps, which the women fill in 4! = 24 ways. Total 6 × 24 = 144. The option 576 = 4! × 4! uses linear counting for the men.

questions.s: In how many ways can 3 boys and 3 girls stand in a row so that boys and girls alternate?
questions.e: The row can start with a boy (BGBGBG) or a girl (GBGBGB): 2 patterns. In each, the boys take their places in 3! ways and the girls in 3! ways: 2 × 6 × 6 = 72. The option 36 forgets the second pattern.

questions.s: How many 3-letter arrangements can be made from 5 different letters if no letter is repeated?
questions.e: ⁵P₃ = 5 × 4 × 3 = 60. The option 10 = ⁵C₃ ignores order, and 125 = 5³ allows repetition.

questions.s: Four different mathematics books and three different physics books are placed on a shelf so that the books of each subject stay together. The number of possible arrangements is
questions.e: Arrange the two subject blocks: 2! ways. Inside, the mathematics books: 4! = 24, the physics books: 3! = 6. Total 2 × 24 × 6 = 288. The option 144 forgets that the two blocks can swap places.

questions.s: The number of different arrangements of the letters of the word ZAINAB is
questions.e: ZAINAB has 6 letters with A twice: 6!/2! = 720/2 = 360. The option 180 divides by 2 twice, as if two letters were each repeated.

questions.s: For n ≥ 1, ⁿP₁ is equal to
questions.e: ⁿP₁ = n!/(n − 1)! = n: one object can be placed in a single position in n ways. The option 1 confuses it with ⁿP₀ or ⁿCₙ.

questions.s: In how many ways can a first, second and third prize be awarded among 10 students if no student gets more than one prize?
questions.e: The prizes are different, so order matters: ¹⁰P₃ = 10 × 9 × 8 = 720. The option 120 = ¹⁰C₃ treats the prizes as identical, and 1000 = 10³ lets one student win more than once.

questions.s: In how many arrangements of all the letters of the word FATIMA are the two A's not next to each other?
questions.e: Total arrangements: 6!/2! = 360. With the two A's together (one block AA), 5 units give 5! = 120. So 360 − 120 = 240 keep the A's apart. The option 120 is the count with the A's together.

questions.s: The value of ⁸C₃ is
questions.e: ⁸C₃ = (8 × 7 × 6)/(3 × 2 × 1) = 336/6 = 56. The option 336 is ⁸P₃, which forgets to divide by 3!.

questions.s: The value of ¹⁰C₈ is
questions.e: ⁿCᵣ = ⁿCₙ₋ᵣ, so ¹⁰C₈ = ¹⁰C₂ = (10 × 9)/2 = 45. The option 90 = ¹⁰P₂ forgets to divide by 2!.

questions.s: If ⁿC₇ = ⁿC₅, then n is equal to
questions.e: ⁿCᵣ = ⁿCₛ with r ≠ s means r + s = n, so n = 7 + 5 = 12. The option 2 subtracts the indices instead of adding them.

questions.s: In how many ways can a committee of 3 members be chosen from 9 people?
questions.e: A committee is a selection, so order does not matter: ⁹C₃ = (9 × 8 × 7)/6 = 84. The option 504 = ⁹P₃ counts ordered choices.

questions.s: A committee of 2 men and 3 women is to be formed from 5 men and 6 women. The number of ways is
questions.e: Choose the men: ⁵C₂ = 10; choose the women: ⁶C₃ = 20. Multiply: 10 × 20 = 200. The option 462 = ¹¹C₅ ignores the required split between men and women.

questions.s: The number of diagonals of a polygon with 10 sides is
questions.e: Any 2 of the 10 vertices give a segment: ¹⁰C₂ = 45. Of these, 10 are sides, so diagonals = 45 − 10 = 35. The option 45 forgets to remove the sides.

questions.s: At a meeting, each of 8 people shakes hands exactly once with every other person. The total number of handshakes is
questions.e: A handshake is a pair of people: ⁸C₂ = (8 × 7)/2 = 28. The option 56 = 8 × 7 counts each handshake twice (once from each person).

questions.s: How many triangles can be formed by joining 10 points in a plane, no three of which are collinear?
questions.e: Each triangle is a choice of 3 vertices: ¹⁰C₃ = (10 × 9 × 8)/6 = 120. The option 45 = ¹⁰C₂ counts lines, not triangles.

questions.s: There are 12 points in a plane. Exactly 5 of them lie on one straight line, and apart from these no three are collinear. How many triangles have their vertices among these points?
questions.e: All choices of 3 points: ¹²C₃ = 220. Choices of 3 from the 5 collinear points give no triangle: ⁵C₃ = 10. So 220 − 10 = 210. The option 220 forgets the collinear points.

questions.s: There are 12 points in a plane. Exactly 5 of them lie on one straight line, and apart from these no three are collinear. How many different straight lines pass through at least two of these points?
questions.e: Pairs of points: ¹²C₂ = 66. The ⁵C₂ = 10 pairs from the collinear points all give the same single line, so subtract 10 and add 1: 66 − 10 + 1 = 57. The option 56 forgets to count that common line once.

questions.s: A cricket squad has 14 players. In how many ways can a team of 11 be chosen?
questions.e: ¹⁴C₁₁ = ¹⁴C₃ = (14 × 13 × 12)/6 = 364. Choosing the 3 players left out is easier than choosing the 11. The option 2184 = ¹⁴P₃ forgets to divide by 3!.

questions.s: From a squad of 14 players, a team of 11 is chosen so that the captain, Usman, is always included. The number of possible teams is
questions.e: With Usman fixed, choose the other 10 from the remaining 13: ¹³C₁₀ = ¹³C₃ = (13 × 12 × 11)/6 = 286. The option 364 = ¹⁴C₁₁ ignores the condition.

questions.s: For any positive integer n, ⁿC₀ + ⁿCₙ is equal to
questions.e: ⁿC₀ = 1 (choose nothing) and ⁿCₙ = 1 (choose everything), so the sum is 2. The option 1 treats ⁿC₀ as 0.

questions.s: The value of ⁷C₀ + ⁷C₁ + ⁷C₂ + … + ⁷C₇ is
questions.e: The sum of all ⁿCᵣ for r = 0 to n is 2ⁿ (each of n objects is either chosen or not), so the sum is 2⁷ = 128. The option 127 leaves out ⁷C₀ = 1.

questions.s: For 1 ≤ r ≤ n, ⁿCᵣ + ⁿCᵣ₋₁ is equal to
questions.e: Pascal's rule: ⁿCᵣ + ⁿCᵣ₋₁ = ⁿ⁺¹Cᵣ. Check with n = 4, r = 2: 6 + 4 = 10 = ⁵C₂, while ⁵C₁ = 5. So ⁿ⁺¹Cᵣ₋₁ is wrong.

questions.s: If ⁿC₂ = 45, then ⁿP₂ is equal to
questions.e: n(n − 1)/2 = 45 gives n(n − 1) = 90, so n = 10. Then ⁿP₂ = n(n − 1) = 90, which is also 2! × ⁿC₂. The option 180 multiplies by 4 instead of 2!.

questions.s: If ²ⁿC₃ = 11 × ⁿC₃, then n is equal to
In how many ways can a person choose one or more fruits from 5 different fruits?
questions.e: Each fruit is either taken or not: 2⁵ = 32 ways, including taking nothing. Removing the empty choice gives 32 − 1 = 31. The option 32 forgets that at least one fruit must be chosen.

questions.s: A student must answer 4 out of 7 questions, and question 1 is compulsory. In how many ways can the student choose the questions?
questions.e: Question 1 is already chosen, so 3 more are chosen from the other 6: ⁶C₃ = 20. The option 35 = ⁷C₄ ignores the compulsory question, and 15 = ⁶C₄ chooses 4 more instead of 3.

questions.s: A committee of 4 is chosen from 6 boys and 4 girls. In how many ways can this be done if the committee must include at least one girl?
questions.e: All committees: ¹⁰C₄ = 210. Committees with no girl (all boys): ⁶C₄ = 15. So 210 − 15 = 195 contain at least one girl. The option 336 = 4 × ⁹C₃ picks one girl first and then any 3, which counts committees with several girls more than once.

questions.s: In how many ways can 6 different books be shared between Ali and Fatima so that each gets 3 books?
questions.e: Choose Ali's 3 books: ⁶C₃ = 20; Fatima gets the rest automatically. Since the two people are named, no further division is needed. The option 40 doubles the count by also swapping the two people, which is already included.

questions.s: If ⁿC₃ = ⁿC₉, then ⁿC₂ is equal to
questions.e: ⁿC₃ = ⁿC₉ gives n = 3 + 9 = 12, and ¹²C₂ = (12 × 11)/2 = 66. The option 132 = ¹²P₂ forgets to divide by 2, and 78 = ¹³C₂ uses n = 13.

questions.s: In how many ways can Ayesha choose 2 colours from 6 different colours for a poster?
questions.e: Choosing 2 colours ignores order: ⁶C₂ = (6 × 5)/2 = 15. The option 30 = ⁶P₂ treats red-blue and blue-red as different.

questions.s: Which of the following is equal to ¹⁵C₁₁?
questions.e: Choosing 11 objects from 15 is the same as choosing the 4 to leave out: ⁿCᵣ = ⁿCₙ₋ᵣ, so ¹⁵C₁₁ = ¹⁵C₄. The option ¹¹C₄ wrongly changes the total from 15 to 11.

questions.s: The greatest of the numbers ¹⁰C₀, ¹⁰C₁, ¹⁰C₂, …, ¹⁰C₁₀ is
questions.e: For even n the middle coefficient ⁿCₙ/₂ is the largest, so the greatest is ¹⁰C₅ = 252. The option 210 = ¹⁰C₄ is next largest, and 1024 = 2¹⁰ is the sum of all the coefficients, not one of them.

questions.s: A fair die is thrown once. The probability of getting a number greater than 4 is
questions.e: Favourable outcomes are 5 and 6: 2 out of 6, so P = 2/6 = 1/3. The option 1/2 wrongly includes 4, which is not greater than 4.

questions.s: A fair die is thrown once. The probability that the number shown is a factor of 6 is
questions.e: The factors of 6 on a die are 1, 2, 3 and 6: 4 outcomes out of 6, so P = 4/6 = 2/3. The option 1/2 forgets that 1 and 6 are also factors of 6.

questions.s: Two fair coins are tossed together. The probability of getting at least one head is
questions.e: The sample space is HH, HT, TH, TT. Only TT has no head, so P(at least one head) = 1 − 1/4 = 3/4. The option 2/3 wrongly treats the outcomes as 'two heads, one head, no head' with equal chances.

questions.s: Two fair dice are thrown. The probability that the sum of the numbers is 7 is
questions.e: There are 36 equally likely outcomes. A sum of 7 comes from (1,6), (2,5), (3,4), (4,3), (5,2), (6,1): 6 outcomes, so P = 6/36 = 1/6. The option 1/12 counts only the 3 unordered pairs.

questions.s: Two fair dice are thrown. The probability that the sum of the numbers is at least 10 is
questions.e: Sum 10: (4,6), (5,5), (6,4); sum 11: (5,6), (6,5); sum 12: (6,6). That is 6 outcomes out of 36, so P = 1/6. The option 1/12 counts only the sum of exactly 10.

questions.s: Two fair dice are thrown. The probability that both dice show an odd number is
questions.e: Each die is odd with probability 3/6 = 1/2, and the dice are independent, so P = 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4 (9 outcomes out of 36). The option 1/6 counts only the 6 doublets.

questions.s: A card is drawn at random from a well-shuffled pack of 52 playing cards. The probability that it is a king is
questions.e: There are 4 kings among 52 cards: P = 4/52 = 1/13. The option 1/52 is the probability of one particular king, such as the king of hearts.

questions.s: A card is drawn at random from a well-shuffled pack of 52 playing cards. The probability that it is a red face card (jack, queen or king) is
questions.e: Red suits are hearts and diamonds, each with 3 face cards, so there are 6 red face cards: P = 6/52 = 3/26. The option 3/13 = 12/52 counts the face cards of all four suits.

questions.s: A bag contains 5 red and 3 blue balls. Two balls are drawn at random without replacement. The probability that both are red is
questions.e: P = ⁵C₂/⁸C₂ = 10/28 = 5/14 (or 5/8 × 4/7 = 20/56). The option 25/64 = (5/8)² assumes the first ball is replaced.

questions.s: A bag contains 5 red and 3 blue balls. Two balls are drawn at random without replacement. The probability that one is red and the other is blue is
questions.e: Favourable selections: ⁵C₁ × ³C₁ = 15; total selections: ⁸C₂ = 28; so P = 15/28. The option 15/56 = 5/8 × 3/7 covers only the order red-then-blue and forgets blue-then-red.

questions.s: If the probability of an event A is 0.35, then the probability that A does not occur is
questions.e: P(not A) = 1 − P(A) = 1 − 0.35 = 0.65. The option 1.35 adds instead of subtracting and is impossible, since no probability exceeds 1.

questions.s: Three fair coins are tossed. The probability of getting at least one tail is
questions.e: The only outcome with no tail is HHH, with probability (1/2)³ = 1/8. So P(at least one tail) = 1 − 1/8 = 7/8. The option 3/8 is the probability of exactly one tail.

questions.s: A fair die is thrown three times. The probability of getting at least one six is
questions.e: P(no six in three throws) = (5/6)³ = 125/216, so P(at least one six) = 1 − 125/216 = 91/216. The option 125/216 is the probability of no six, and 1/216 is the probability of three sixes.

questions.s: For two events A and B, P(A) = 0.5, P(B) = 0.4 and P(A ∩ B) = 0.2. Then P(A ∪ B) is
questions.e: By the addition law, P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B) = 0.5 + 0.4 − 0.2 = 0.7. The option 0.9 forgets to subtract the overlap, which is then counted twice.

questions.s: A and B are mutually exclusive events with P(A) = 1/3 and P(B) = 1/4. Then P(A ∪ B) is
questions.e: Mutually exclusive events cannot happen together, so P(A ∩ B) = 0 and P(A ∪ B) = 1/3 + 1/4 = 7/12. The option 1/12 multiplies the probabilities, which gives P(A ∩ B) for independent events, not the union.

questions.s: A card is drawn at random from a well-shuffled pack of 52 playing cards. The probability that it is a king or a queen is
questions.e: No card is a king and a queen at the same time, so the events are mutually exclusive: P = 4/52 + 4/52 = 8/52 = 2/13. The option 1/169 = (1/13)² multiplies the probabilities instead of adding them.

questions.s: A card is drawn at random from a well-shuffled pack of 52 playing cards. The probability that it is a heart or a king is
questions.e: P(heart) + P(king) − P(king of hearts) = 13/52 + 4/52 − 1/52 = 16/52 = 4/13. The option 17/52 counts the king of hearts twice.

questions.s: An integer is chosen at random from 1 to 30. The probability that it is divisible by 3 or by 5 is
questions.e: Multiples of 3: 10; multiples of 5: 6; multiples of both (that is, of 15): 2. So 10 + 6 − 2 = 14 numbers and P = 14/30 = 7/15. The option 8/15 = 16/30 forgets to subtract 15 and 30, which were counted twice.

questions.s: For events A and B, P(A) = 0.5, P(B) = 0.6 and P(A ∪ B) = 0.8. Then P(A ∩ B) is
questions.e: From P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B): 0.8 = 1.1 − P(A ∩ B), so P(A ∩ B) = 0.3. The option 1.1 is just P(A) + P(B), which cannot be a probability.

questions.s: Which of the following cannot be the probability of an event?
questions.e: Every probability satisfies 0 ≤ P ≤ 1, so 1.2 is impossible. The value 0 belongs to an impossible event and 1 to a certain event, so both are allowed.

questions.s: A letter is chosen at random from the letters of the word ISLAMABAD. The probability that it is a vowel is
questions.e: ISLAMABAD has 9 letters; the vowels are I, A, A, A, so 4 of the 9 letters are vowels and P = 4/9. The option 2/9 counts the different vowels (I and A) instead of every letter.

questions.s: Five students, including Ali and Bilal, stand in a row in random order. The probability that Ali and Bilal stand next to each other is
questions.e: Total orders: 5! = 120. Orders with the pair together: 4! × 2! = 48. P = 48/120 = 2/5. The option 1/5 forgets that Ali and Bilal can stand in either order within the pair.

questions.s: A committee of 3 is chosen at random from 4 men and 3 women. The probability that it contains at least one woman is
questions.e: Total committees: ⁷C₃ = 35. Committees with no woman: ⁴C₃ = 4. So P(at least one woman) = 1 − 4/35 = 31/35. The option 4/35 is the probability of the complement, an all-male committee.

questions.s: Two fair dice are thrown. The probability that the sum of the numbers is a prime number is
questions.e: Prime sums: 2 (1 way), 3 (2 ways), 5 (4 ways), 7 (6 ways), 11 (2 ways), a total of 15 outcomes out of 36. P = 15/36 = 5/12. Remember that ordered outcomes count: a sum of 7 alone gives 6 of the 15, from (1,6) to (6,1).

questions.s: A bag contains 4 white and 6 black balls. One ball is drawn at random. The probability that it is not white is
questions.e: Not white means black: P = 6/10 = 3/5, which is also 1 − 4/10. The option 2/3 = 4/6 compares white with black instead of with all 10 balls, and 3/2 exceeds 1.

questions.s: A and B are independent events with P(A) = 0.4 and P(B) = 0.5. Then P(A ∩ B) is
questions.e: For independent events the multiplication law gives P(A ∩ B) = P(A) × P(B) = 0.4 × 0.5 = 0.2. The option 0.9 adds the probabilities, which is not even P(A ∪ B) unless the events are mutually exclusive.

questions.s: A fair coin is tossed and a fair die is thrown. The probability of getting a head on the coin and a six on the die is
questions.e: The coin and die are independent: P = 1/2 × 1/6 = 1/12. The option 2/3 = 1/2 + 1/6 adds the probabilities as if only one of the two had to happen.

questions.s: A and B are independent events with P(A) = 1/2 and P(B) = 1/3. Then P(A ∪ B) is
questions.e: P(A ∩ B) = 1/2 × 1/3 = 1/6, so P(A ∪ B) = 1/2 + 1/3 − 1/6 = 4/6 = 2/3. The option 5/6 forgets to subtract the overlap, treating the events as mutually exclusive.

questions.s: Ali hits a target with probability 0.6 and Hamza with probability 0.5, independently. If each fires once, the probability that the target is hit is
questions.e: The target is missed only if both miss: 0.4 × 0.5 = 0.2. So P(hit) = 1 − 0.2 = 0.8. The option 1.1 simply adds the two probabilities and exceeds 1.

questions.s: Ali hits a target with probability 0.6 and Hamza with probability 0.5, independently. If each fires once, the probability that exactly one of them hits the target is
questions.e: Ali hits and Hamza misses: 0.6 × 0.5 = 0.3. Ali misses and Hamza hits: 0.4 × 0.5 = 0.2. These cases are mutually exclusive, so P = 0.3 + 0.2 = 0.5. The option 0.8 is the probability of at least one hit, which includes the case where both hit.

questions.s: Two cards are drawn one after the other from a pack of 52, the first card being replaced before the second is drawn. The probability that both cards are aces is
questions.e: With replacement the draws are independent: P = 4/52 × 4/52 = 1/13 × 1/13 = 1/169. The option 1/221 = 4/52 × 3/51 is the answer without replacement, and 2/13 adds the probabilities.

questions.s: Two cards are drawn at random, without replacement, from a well-shuffled pack of 52. The probability that both are hearts is
questions.e: P = 13/52 × 12/51 = 1/4 × 4/17 = 1/17. The option 1/16 = (1/4)² assumes the first card is put back.

questions.s: For events A and B, P(A ∩ B) = 0.12 and P(B) = 0.4. The conditional probability P(A | B) is
questions.e: P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B)/P(B) = 0.12/0.4 = 0.3. The option 0.52 adds the two numbers, and 0.4 is P(B) itself.

questions.s: A fair die is thrown. Given that the number shown is even, the probability that it is greater than 3 is
questions.e: The condition reduces the sample space to {2, 4, 6}. Of these, 4 and 6 exceed 3, so the probability is 2/3. The option 1/2 = 3/6 ignores the given information and uses the whole die.

questions.s: Two fair coins are tossed. Given that at least one coin shows a head, the probability that both coins show heads is
questions.e: The condition leaves the equally likely outcomes HH, HT, TH. Only HH has two heads, so the probability is 1/3. The option 1/2 wrongly assumes the other coin is a fresh fair toss, and 1/4 ignores the condition.

questions.s: In a class of 40 students in Peshawar, 25 study Physics, 20 study Chemistry and 10 study both subjects. A student chosen at random studies Physics. The probability that this student also studies Chemistry is
questions.e: Given Physics, the sample space is the 25 Physics students, of whom 10 also study Chemistry: P = 10/25 = 2/5. The option 1/4 = 10/40 is the unconditional probability of studying both subjects.

questions.s: In a class of 40 students, 25 study Physics, 20 study Chemistry and 10 study both subjects. A student is chosen at random. The probability that the student studies neither subject is
questions.e: Students taking at least one subject: 25 + 20 − 10 = 35, so 40 − 35 = 5 take neither: P = 5/40 = 1/8. The option 7/8 is the probability of taking at least one subject.

questions.s: A box contains 7 good and 3 defective bulbs. Two bulbs are drawn one after the other without replacement. The probability that the first is good and the second is defective is
questions.e: P = 7/10 × 3/9 = 21/90 = 7/30. The option 21/100 = 7/10 × 3/10 assumes replacement, and 7/15 counts both orders (good then defective, and defective then good).

questions.s: If A and B are mutually exclusive events, then P(A ∩ B) is equal to
questions.e: Mutually exclusive events cannot occur together, so A ∩ B is empty and P(A ∩ B) = 0. The product P(A) × P(B) is the rule for independent events, which is a different idea.

questions.s: A and B are independent events with P(A) = 0.3 and P(B) = 0.6. The probability that neither A nor B occurs is
questions.e: If A and B are independent, so are their complements: P(A′ ∩ B′) = 0.7 × 0.4 = 0.28. The option 0.72 = 1 − 0.28 is the probability that at least one occurs.

questions.s: A and B are independent events with P(A) = 0.2 and P(A ∪ B) = 0.6. Then P(B) is
questions.e: P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A)P(B) gives 0.6 = 0.2 + p − 0.2p, so 0.4 = 0.8p and p = 0.5. The option 0.4 comes from 0.6 − 0.2, which assumes the events are mutually exclusive.

questions.s: An urn contains 2 red and 3 green balls. A ball is drawn, replaced, and a second ball is drawn. The probability that the two balls are of the same colour is
questions.e: P(red, red) = (2/5)² = 4/25 and P(green, green) = (3/5)² = 9/25. These cases are mutually exclusive, so P = 13/25. The option 12/25 is the probability of different colours.

questions.s: A fair die is thrown twice. The probability of getting a six on both throws is
questions.e: The throws are independent: P = 1/6 × 1/6 = 1/36. The option 1/3 = 1/6 + 1/6 adds the probabilities instead of multiplying them.

questions.s: For events A and B, P(A) = 0.6, P(B) = 0.5 and P(A ∩ B) = 0.3. Which statement is correct?
o: A, B are independent, not mutually exclusive
A, B are mutually exclusive, not independent
A, B are independent and mutually exclusive
A, B are neither independent nor exclusive
questions.e: P(A) × P(B) = 0.6 × 0.5 = 0.3 = P(A ∩ B), so A and B are independent. Since P(A ∩ B) = 0.3 ≠ 0, they can happen together and are not mutually exclusive.

questions.s: In a school in Quetta, 60% of the students are girls. 30% of the girls and 20% of the boys wear glasses. The probability that a student chosen at random wears glasses is
questions.e: P(glasses) = P(girl) P(glasses | girl) + P(boy) P(glasses | boy) = 0.6 × 0.3 + 0.4 × 0.2 = 0.18 + 0.08 = 0.26. The option 0.25 simply averages 30% and 20%, ignoring that there are more girls than boys.

questions.s: In a school, 60% of the students are girls. 30% of the girls and 20% of the boys wear glasses. A student chosen at random wears glasses. The probability that this student is a girl is
questions.e: P(girl and glasses) = 0.6 × 0.3 = 0.18 and P(glasses) = 0.18 + 0.4 × 0.2 = 0.26. So P(girl | glasses) = 0.18/0.26 = 9/13. The option 3/10 is P(glasses | girl), the conditional the wrong way round.

questions.s: In how many ways can 7 people sit around a round table if two of them, Bilal and Usman, must not sit next to each other?
questions.e: All circular seatings: (7 − 1)! = 720. With Bilal and Usman as one unit: 6 units give (6 − 1)! = 120, times 2 for their order, so 240. Hence 720 − 240 = 480. The option 240 is the number with the two together.

questions.s: In how many different ways can 4 different keys be put on a key ring?
questions.e: Circular arrangements of 4 objects: (4 − 1)! = 6. A ring can be turned over, so clockwise and anticlockwise orders are the same: 6/2 = 3. The option 6 forgets that the ring can be flipped.

questions.s: The value of ⁵C₂ + ⁵C₃ is
questions.e: ⁵C₂ = 10 and ⁵C₃ = 10, so the sum is 20; by Pascal's rule it equals ⁶C₃ = 20. The option 10 gives only one of the two terms.

questions.s: In how many ways can a president and a secretary be chosen from a society of 8 members, if one person cannot hold both posts?
questions.e: The posts are different, so order matters: 8 choices for president, then 7 for secretary, 8 × 7 = 56. The option 28 = ⁸C₂ treats the two posts as identical, and 64 lets one person hold both.

questions.s: The value of 7!/5! is
questions.e: 7! = 7 × 6 × 5!, so 7!/5! = 7 × 6 = 42. The option 21 also divides by 2!, which would give ⁷C₂, and 210 = 7 × 6 × 5 cancels one factor too few.

questions.s: The value of 4!/(2! × 2!) is
questions.e: 4! = 24 and 2! × 2! = 4, so the value is 24/4 = 6 (it equals ⁴C₂). The option 1 wrongly cancels 4! against 2! + 2!.

questions.s: A 4-letter code is made from the letters A, B, C, D, E, F. Letters may be repeated, but the first letter must be a vowel. How many codes are possible?
questions.e: The first letter is A or E: 2 choices. Each of the other three places has 6 choices: 6³ = 216. Total 2 × 216 = 432. The option 1296 = 6⁴ ignores the vowel condition, and 216 forgets the first letter altogether.

questions.s: Five different books are arranged on a shelf so that a particular dictionary is always in the middle position. The number of arrangements is
questions.e: The dictionary's place is fixed, so the other 4 books fill the remaining 4 places in 4! = 24 ways. The option 120 = 5! ignores the restriction.

questions.s: The number of different arrangements of the letters of the word SANA is
questions.e: SANA has 4 letters with A twice: 4!/2! = 24/2 = 12. The option 6 divides by 2! twice, as if two letters were repeated.

questions.s: In how many ways can 10 students be divided into a group of 6 and a group of 4?
questions.e: Choosing the 4 students for the smaller group fixes the other group: ¹⁰C₄ = (10 × 9 × 8 × 7)/24 = 210. The groups have different sizes, so there is no need to divide by 2; the option 105 does so wrongly. The option 120 = ¹⁰C₃ chooses the wrong number.

questions.s: How many even 5-digit numbers can be formed using all the digits 1, 1, 2, 2, 3 exactly once each?
questions.e: An even number must end in 2. The remaining digits 1, 1, 2, 3 fill the first four places in 4!/2! = 12 ways. The option 30 = 5!/(2! × 2!) counts all arrangements, odd ones included.

questions.s: A convex polygon has 20 diagonals. The number of its sides is
questions.e: A polygon with n sides has ⁿC₂ − n = n(n − 3)/2 diagonals. n(n − 3)/2 = 20 gives n(n − 3) = 40 = 8 × 5, so n = 8. The option 10 uses n(n − 1)/2 = 45, which counts sides as well.

questions.s: Two fair dice are thrown. The probability that the sum of the numbers is 13 is
questions.e: The largest possible sum is 6 + 6 = 12, so a sum of 13 is an impossible event with probability 0. The option 1/36 is the probability of the largest sum, 12.

questions.s: An integer is chosen at random from 1 to 20. The probability that it is a perfect square is
questions.e: The perfect squares from 1 to 20 are 1, 4, 9 and 16: 4 numbers, so P = 4/20 = 1/5. The option 3/20 forgets that 1 = 1² is a perfect square.

questions.s: For each of three people, the day of the week on which they were born is equally likely to be any of the 7 days, independently. The probability that at least two of them were born on the same day of the week is
questions.e: P(all three on different days) = (7 × 6 × 5)/7³ = 210/343 = 30/49. So P(at least two share a day) = 1 − 30/49 = 19/49. The option 30/49 is the complement, and 1/49 is the chance that all three share one day.

questions.s: The sum ¹²C₅ + ¹²C₆ is equal to
questions.e: Pascal's rule ⁿCᵣ + ⁿCᵣ₋₁ = ⁿ⁺¹Cᵣ with n = 12, r = 6 gives ¹³C₆. The option ¹³C₅ uses the smaller lower index, and ²⁴C₁₁ adds the indices, which is not a valid rule.

questions.s: A committee of 5 is chosen from 6 men and 4 women. In how many ways can this be done if the committee includes at most one woman?
questions.e: No woman: ⁶C₅ = 6. Exactly one woman: ⁴C₁ × ⁶C₄ = 4 × 15 = 60. At most one woman means 6 + 60 = 66. The option 60 counts only the exactly-one case.

questions.s: A bag contains 3 red, 5 white and 2 green balls. One ball is drawn at random. The probability that it is green is
questions.e: There are 3 + 5 + 2 = 10 balls, 2 of them green: P = 2/10 = 1/5. The option 1/4 = 2/8 compares green with the other balls instead of with all of them.

questions.s: For events A and B, P(A) = 0.5 and P(B | A) = 0.4. The probability P(A ∩ B) is
questions.e: From the definition of conditional probability, P(A ∩ B) = P(A) × P(B | A) = 0.5 × 0.4 = 0.2. The option 0.8 = 0.4/0.5 divides instead of multiplying.

questions.s: The value of 9!/7! is
questions.e: 9! = 9 × 8 × 7!, so 9!/7! = 9 × 8 = 72. The option 2 comes from wrongly writing 9!/7! as (9 − 7)!, and 36 = ⁹C₂ also divides by 2!.

questions.s: If (n + 2)! = 132 × n!, then n is equal to
questions.e: (n + 2)!/n! = (n + 2)(n + 1) = 132 = 12 × 11, so n + 2 = 12 and n = 10. The options 11 and 12 are the factors themselves, not n.

questions.s: There are 3 roads from town A to town B and 4 roads from town B to town C. In how many ways can Bilal travel from A to C through B?
questions.e: Each of the 3 roads to B can be followed by any of the 4 roads to C: 3 × 4 = 12. The option 7 adds the numbers, which would count choosing a single road.

questions.s: There are 3 roads from A to B and 4 roads from B to C. In how many ways can a person go from A to C through B and return to A through B, if no road is used twice?
questions.e: Going: 3 × 4 = 12 ways. Returning: a different road from C to B (3 left) and a different road from B to A (2 left): 3 × 2 = 6 ways. Total 12 × 6 = 72. The option 144 = 12 × 12 lets the same roads be reused.

questions.s: The value of ⁷P₃ is
questions.e: ⁷P₃ = 7 × 6 × 5 = 210. The option 343 = 7³ allows repetition, and 840 = ⁷P₄ uses one factor too many.

questions.s: The number of different arrangements of all the letters of the word KARACHI is
questions.e: KARACHI has 7 letters with A twice and the rest different: 7!/2! = 5040/2 = 2520. The option 5040 treats the two A's as different.

questions.s: In how many ways can 8 people be seated around a round table?
questions.e: Fix one person to remove equivalent rotations; the remaining 7 can be arranged in 7! = 5040 ways. The option 40320 = 8! counts rotations as different, and 2520 halves the count as for a necklace, which does not apply to people at a table.

questions.s: The value of ¹²C₁₀ is
questions.e: ¹²C₁₀ = ¹²C₂ = (12 × 11)/2 = 66. The option 132 = ¹²P₂ forgets to divide by 2!, and 220 = ¹²C₃.

questions.s: If ⁿC₈ = ⁿC₁₂, then n is equal to
questions.e: ⁿCᵣ = ⁿCₛ with r ≠ s requires r + s = n, so n = 8 + 12 = 20. The option 4 subtracts the indices.

questions.s: In how many ways can a team of 3 boys and 2 girls be chosen from 5 boys and 4 girls?
questions.e: Boys: ⁵C₃ = 10; girls: ⁴C₂ = 6; total 10 × 6 = 60. The option 16 adds the two counts, and 126 = ⁹C₅ ignores the required numbers of boys and girls.

questions.s: A grid is formed by 6 parallel horizontal lines crossed by 5 parallel vertical lines. How many rectangles are formed whose sides lie along these lines?
questions.e: A rectangle is fixed by choosing 2 horizontal lines and 2 vertical lines: ⁶C₂ × ⁵C₂ = 15 × 10 = 150. The option 30 = 6 × 5 counts crossing points, not rectangles.

questions.s: A fair die is thrown once. The probability of getting a number less than 6 is
questions.e: The numbers 1 to 5 are less than 6: 5 outcomes out of 6, so P = 5/6. The option 1/6 is the probability of getting exactly 6, the complement.

questions.s: Two fair dice are thrown. The probability that the sum of the numbers is 8 is
questions.e: A sum of 8 comes from (2,6), (3,5), (4,4), (5,3), (6,2): 5 outcomes out of 36, so P = 5/36. The option 1/12 = 3/36 counts only the unordered pairs.

questions.s: For events A and B, P(A) = 0.7, P(B) = 0.4 and P(A ∪ B) = 0.9. Then P(A ∩ B) is
questions.e: P(A ∩ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∪ B) = 0.7 + 0.4 − 0.9 = 0.2. The option 0.28 = 0.7 × 0.4 assumes independence, which is not given.

questions.s: A card is drawn at random from a well-shuffled pack of 52 playing cards. The probability that it is not a spade is
questions.e: There are 13 spades, so P(spade) = 13/52 = 1/4 and P(not a spade) = 1 − 1/4 = 3/4. The option 12/13 confuses spades with a single rank such as kings.

questions.s: A and B are independent events with P(A) = 0.8 and P(B) = 0.5. The probability that A occurs but B does not is
questions.e: P(A ∩ B′) = P(A) × P(B′) = 0.8 × 0.5 = 0.4. The option 0.3 = 0.8 − 0.5 subtracts the probabilities, and 0.1 = 0.2 × 0.5 is the chance that B occurs but A does not.

questions.s: A bag contains 4 red and 6 blue balls. Three balls are drawn at random without replacement. The probability that all three are blue is
questions.e: P = ⁶C₃/¹⁰C₃ = 20/120 = 1/6 (or 6/10 × 5/9 × 4/8 = 1/6). The option 27/125 = (3/5)³ assumes each ball is replaced.

questions.s: A fair die is thrown. Given that the number shown is prime, the probability that it is odd is
questions.e: The prime outcomes are 2, 3 and 5, which form the reduced sample space. Of these, 3 and 5 are odd, so the probability is 2/3. The option 1/2 is the unconditional probability of an odd number.

questions.s: For events A and B, P(A) = 0.4, P(B) = 0.5 and P(A | B) = 0.6. Then P(B | A) is
questions.e: P(A ∩ B) = P(B) × P(A | B) = 0.5 × 0.6 = 0.3. Then P(B | A) = P(A ∩ B)/P(A) = 0.3/0.4 = 0.75. The option 0.6 assumes P(B | A) equals P(A | B), which is true only when P(A) = P(B).

questions.s: A and B are mutually exclusive events with P(A) = 0.25 and P(B) = 0.45. Then P(A ∪ B) is
questions.e: Mutually exclusive events have no overlap, so P(A ∪ B) = 0.25 + 0.45 = 0.70. The option 0.30 is the probability that neither occurs, and 0.1125 is the product, used for independent events.

questions.s: The first step in proving a statement P(n) for all positive integers n by mathematical induction is to
o: assume that P(k) is true for some k
questions.e: Induction starts with the base case: verify that P(1) is true. Only then is P(k) assumed (the induction hypothesis) and used to prove P(k + 1). Assuming P(k) is the second step, not the first, and proving P(k + 1) ⇒ P(k) runs the chain the wrong way.

questions.s: In the inductive step of a proof by mathematical induction, P(k) is assumed to be true and one must then prove that
questions.e: The inductive step shows P(k) ⇒ P(k + 1); together with the base case this gives P(1), P(2), P(3), … in turn. Proving P(k − 1) moves backwards and proves nothing new, while P(1) belongs to the base step.

questions.s: Which of the following statements is true for every positive integer n?
questions.e: n² + n = n(n + 1) is a product of two consecutive integers, so one factor is even. The others fail: n = 2 gives n² + 1 = 5 (odd), 2² = 4 is not greater than 2² = 4, and 2³ − 2 = 6 is not divisible by 4.

questions.s: Let P(n) be the statement 1 + 3 + 5 + … + (2n − 1) = n². Then P(k + 1) is
questions.e: Replace n by k + 1 everywhere: the last term 2n − 1 becomes 2(k + 1) − 1 = 2k + 1 and the right side becomes (k + 1)². Writing (2k + 3) adds one term too many, and keeping (2k − 1) changes only the right side.

questions.s: The largest integer that divides 4ⁿ − 1 for every positive integer n is
questions.e: For n = 1, 4 − 1 = 3, so no integer larger than 3 can divide every value. By induction, 4ᵏ⁺¹ − 1 = 4(4ᵏ − 1) + 3, so 3 divides every term. 15 divides 4² − 1 but not 4 − 1 = 3.

questions.s: For every positive integer n, the expression n³ + 2n is always divisible by
questions.e: n³ + 2n = n(n² + 2). If n is a multiple of 3 the factor n is; if n leaves remainder 1 or 2, n² + 2 leaves 1 + 2 = 3 or 4 + 2 = 6, both multiples of 3. Values 3, 12, 33 show 2 and 6 fail (n = 1 gives 3, which is odd), and 9 fails too.

questions.s: The inequality 2ⁿ > 2n + 1 holds for all integers n ≥ m. The smallest such m is
questions.e: n = 1: 2 > 3 is false; n = 2: 4 > 5 is false; n = 3: 8 > 7 is true. If 2ᵏ > 2k + 1, then 2ᵏ⁺¹ > 4k + 2 > 2k + 3 for k ≥ 1, so the inequality holds from m = 3 onwards. m = 2 fails because 4 < 5.

questions.s: The statement n! > 2ⁿ is true for all integers n ≥ m, where m is the smallest such starting value. Then m equals
questions.e: 3! = 6 < 8 but 4! = 24 > 16. If k! > 2ᵏ with k ≥ 4, then (k + 1)! = (k + 1)k! > 2·2ᵏ = 2ᵏ⁺¹, so the statement holds from 4 onwards. Choosing 3 is wrong because 6 is not greater than 2³ = 8.

questions.s: The principle of mathematical induction is used to prove statements that depend on
questions.e: Induction works step by step through 1, 2, 3, …, so it proves results indexed by natural numbers n. A real variable or an angle takes values that cannot be listed one after another in this way.

questions.s: It can be proved by induction that 1³ + 2³ + … + n³ = [n(n + 1)/2]². The value of 1³ + 2³ + … + 9³ is
questions.e: With n = 9, n(n + 1)/2 = 9 × 10/2 = 45, and 45² = 2025. 45 forgets to square, 285 is the sum of squares 1² + … + 9², and 1296 = 36² is the sum of cubes only up to 8³.

questions.s: For a statement P(n) it has been proved that P(k) ⇒ P(k + 1) for every positive integer k, but P(1) is false. From these facts alone,
o: P(n) is true for every n ≥ 2
P(n) is false for every positive integer n
induction gives no conclusion about P(n)
P(n) is true for every positive integer n
questions.e: Induction needs both the base case and the inductive step. Without a true starting case the chain never starts, so nothing follows about P(n). For example P(n): n > n + 1 satisfies the step but is never true, while P(n): n ≥ 2 also satisfies the step and is true for n ≥ 2, so neither 'always false' nor 'true from 2' follows.

questions.s: By mathematical induction, 1 + 2 + 2² + … + 2ⁿ⁻¹ equals
questions.e: For n = 1 both sides are 1. If the sum up to 2ᵏ⁻¹ is 2ᵏ − 1, adding 2ᵏ gives 2ᵏ⁺¹ − 1, so the formula is 2ⁿ − 1. 2ⁿ⁺¹ − 1 would be the sum up to 2ⁿ, one term too many.

questions.s: For every positive integer n, 1/(1·2) + 1/(2·3) + … + 1/(n(n + 1)) equals
questions.e: Each term is 1/k − 1/(k + 1), so the sum telescopes to 1 − 1/(n + 1) = n/(n + 1). Check n = 1: 1/2 = 1/2. The option 1/(n + 1) is the part that is subtracted, not the sum.

questions.s: The number of terms in the expansion of (a + b)¹⁵ is
questions.e: (a + b)ⁿ has n + 1 terms, from aⁿ down to bⁿ. For n = 15 that is 16 terms. Answering 15 forgets the term with b⁰ or a⁰.

questions.s: In every term of the expansion of (a + b)ⁿ, the sum of the indices of a and b is
questions.e: The general term is ⁿCᵣ aⁿ⁻ʳ bʳ, and (n − r) + r = n. The number n + 1 is the number of terms, not the sum of the indices in a term.

questions.s: The number of terms in the expansion of (x² + 2x + 1)⁵ is
questions.e: x² + 2x + 1 = (x + 1)², so the expression is (x + 1)¹⁰, which has 10 + 1 = 11 terms. Taking 5 + 1 = 6 ignores that each factor is a square, and 21 counts terms of a general trinomial whose like terms have not been combined.

questions.s: The coefficient of x³ in the expansion of (1 + x)⁸ is
questions.e: The coefficient of xʳ in (1 + x)ⁿ is ⁿCᵣ, so it is ⁸C₃ = (8 × 7 × 6)/(3 × 2 × 1) = 56. 336 = 8 × 7 × 6 forgets to divide by 3!, and 70 = ⁸C₄ is the middle coefficient.

questions.s: The coefficient of x² in the expansion of (1 + 2x)⁶ is
questions.e: The x² term is ⁶C₂(2x)² = 15 × 4x² = 60x². Writing 30 multiplies by 2 instead of 2² = 4, and 15 ignores the 2 completely.

questions.s: The coefficient of x² in the expansion of (x − 2)⁵ is
questions.e: The term containing x² is ⁵C₃ x²(−2)³ = 10 × (−8)x² = −80x². The answer 80 drops the minus sign of (−2)³, an odd power.

questions.s: If ⁿC₇ = ⁿC₅, then n equals
questions.e: ⁿCᵣ = ⁿCₛ with r ≠ s means r + s = n, because ⁿCᵣ = ⁿCₙ₋ᵣ. So n = 7 + 5 = 12. The value 2 comes from subtracting instead of adding.

questions.s: The value of (√2 + 1)⁴ + (√2 − 1)⁴ is
questions.e: In the sum the odd-power terms cancel: 2[(√2)⁴ + ⁴C₂(√2)² + 1] = 2[4 + 12 + 1] = 34. Check: (√2 + 1)² = 3 + 2√2, squared gives 17 + 12√2, and the other bracket gives 17 − 12√2. 17 is only half of the total.

questions.s: The value of (√3 + 1)⁵ − (√3 − 1)⁵ is
questions.e: In the difference only the terms with odd powers of 1 survive, doubled: 2[⁵C₁(√3)⁴ + ⁵C₃(√3)² + ⁵C₅] = 2[5 × 9 + 10 × 3 + 1] = 2 × 76 = 152. 76 forgets the factor 2, and the √3 options keep the wrong set of terms (odd powers of √3).

questions.s: The binomial coefficients in the expansion of (a + b)⁵ are
questions.e: They are ⁵C₀ to ⁵C₅: 1, 5, 10, 10, 5, 1, six numbers, the fifth row of Pascal's triangle after the top 1. 1, 4, 6, 4, 1 belongs to n = 4, and 1, 5, 10, 5, 1 has only five terms.

questions.s: The value of ¹⁰C₈ is
questions.e: ¹⁰C₈ = ¹⁰C₂ = (10 × 9)/2 = 45. 90 = 10 × 9 forgets to divide by 2!, and 720 = 10 × 9 × 8 confuses the calculation with a permutation.

questions.s: For 1 ≤ r ≤ n, ⁿCᵣ + ⁿCᵣ₋₁ equals
questions.e: This is Pascal's rule: two neighbouring entries of row n add up to the entry below them in row n + 1, in position r. For example ⁴C₂ + ⁴C₁ = 6 + 4 = 10 = ⁵C₂. ⁿ⁺¹Cᵣ₋₁ has the wrong position: ⁵C₁ = 5.

questions.s: In the expansion of (a + b)ⁿ in descending powers of a, the (r + 1)th term is
questions.e: The first term is ⁿC₀ aⁿ, the second ⁿC₁ aⁿ⁻¹ b, so the (r + 1)th term is ⁿCᵣ aⁿ⁻ʳ bʳ. The option with ⁿCᵣ₋₁ is the rth term, one place too early, and ⁿCᵣ aʳ bʳ does not have total degree n.

questions.s: The 5th term in the expansion of (2x + 1)⁷ in descending powers of x is
questions.e: T₅ = T₄₊₁ = ⁷C₄(2x)³(1)⁴ = 35 × 8x³ = 280x³. Writing 560x⁴ uses r = 3 for the power of 2x, which gives the 4th term, and 35x³ forgets to cube the 2.

questions.s: The 4th term in the expansion of (x − 1/x)⁸ is
questions.e: T₄ = ⁸C₃ x⁵(−1/x)³ = 56 × (−1)x⁵/x³ = −56x². The sign is negative because (−1)³ = −1; 70 is the middle (5th) term and 28x⁴ is the 3rd term without its correct sign.

questions.s: The 3rd term in the expansion of (3 − x/3)⁶ is
questions.e: T₃ = ⁶C₂ 3⁴(−x/3)² = 15 × 81 × x²/9 = 135x². The sign is positive because the power of −x/3 is even; 1215x² forgets to divide by 3² = 9, and −20x³ is the 4th term.

questions.s: The coefficient of x⁵ in the expansion of (x + 2)⁷ is
questions.e: The x⁵ term is ⁷C₂ x⁵ 2² = 21 × 4x⁵ = 84x⁵. 42 uses 2 instead of 2², and 168 uses 2³, the power that goes with x⁴.

questions.s: The coefficient of x⁷ in the expansion of (x² + 1/x)⁸ is
questions.e: Tᵣ₊₁ = ⁸Cᵣ(x²)⁸⁻ʳ(1/x)ʳ = ⁸Cᵣ x¹⁶⁻³ʳ. Setting 16 − 3r = 7 gives r = 3, so the coefficient is ⁸C₃ = 56. 70 = ⁸C₄ belongs to x⁴.

questions.s: The coefficient of x⁴ in the expansion of (x − 2/x)⁸ is
questions.e: Tᵣ₊₁ = ⁸Cᵣ x⁸⁻ʳ(−2/x)ʳ = ⁸Cᵣ(−2)ʳ x⁸⁻²ʳ. For x⁴, r = 2: 28 × 4 = 112, positive because (−2)² = 4. −112 treats the power of −2 as odd.

questions.s: When n is an even positive integer, the expansion of (a + b)ⁿ has
questions.e: For even n there are n + 1 terms, an odd number, so there is a single middle term, the (n/2 + 1)th. For n = 4 the five terms have the 3rd in the middle. Two middle terms occur only when n is odd.

questions.s: The middle term in the expansion of (x + 1/x)¹⁰ is
questions.e: There are 11 terms, so the middle one is T₆ = ¹⁰C₅ x⁵(1/x)⁵ = 252. 210 = ¹⁰C₄ is the coefficient of the 5th term, and 126 is half of 252.

questions.s: The middle terms in the expansion of (1 + x)⁷ are
questions.e: (1 + x)⁷ has 8 terms, so the 4th and 5th are the middle terms: ⁷C₃x³ = 35x³ and ⁷C₄x⁴ = 35x⁴. A single middle term occurs only for even n; 70 = ⁸C₄ belongs to (1 + x)⁸.

questions.s: The middle term in the expansion of (x/2 − 2/x)⁶ is
questions.e: There are 7 terms, so the middle one is T₄ = ⁶C₃(x/2)³(−2/x)³ = 20 × (x³/8) × (−8/x³) = −20. −160 forgets the 1/8 from (x/2)³, and +20 ignores the odd power of the negative term.

questions.s: The term independent of x in the expansion of (x + 1/x)⁶ is
questions.e: Tᵣ₊₁ = ⁶Cᵣ x⁶⁻²ʳ, which is free of x when r = 3, giving ⁶C₃ = 20. 15 = ⁶C₂ is the coefficient of x², the term next to it.

questions.s: The term independent of x in the expansion of (x² − 1/x)⁶ is
questions.e: Tᵣ₊₁ = ⁶Cᵣ(x²)⁶⁻ʳ(−1/x)ʳ = ⁶Cᵣ(−1)ʳ x¹²⁻³ʳ. 12 − 3r = 0 gives r = 4, so the term is ⁶C₄(−1)⁴ = 15. The minus sign appears only for odd r, and 20 = ⁶C₃ uses the wrong r.

questions.s: The term independent of x in the expansion of (2x² + 1/x)⁹ is
questions.e: Tᵣ₊₁ = ⁹Cᵣ(2x²)⁹⁻ʳ(1/x)ʳ = ⁹Cᵣ 2⁹⁻ʳ x¹⁸⁻³ʳ. 18 − 3r = 0 gives r = 6, so the term is ⁹C₆ × 2³ = 84 × 8 = 672. 84 forgets the factor 2³ from (2x²)³.

questions.s: The term independent of x in the expansion of (√x + 2/x)⁶ is
questions.e: Tᵣ₊₁ = ⁶Cᵣ x^((6 − r)/2) 2ʳ x⁻ʳ, and (6 − r)/2 − r = 0 gives r = 2. The term is ⁶C₂ × 2² = 15 × 4 = 60. 160 = ⁶C₃ × 2³ uses r = 3, as if both parts had the same power of x.

questions.s: In the expansion of (x + 1/x²)⁹, the term independent of x is the
questions.e: Tᵣ₊₁ = ⁹Cᵣ x⁹⁻ʳ x⁻²ʳ = ⁹Cᵣ x⁹⁻³ʳ, free of x when r = 3, which is the (3 + 1)th = 4th term. Choosing the 3rd term confuses r with the position r + 1.

questions.s: If the coefficients of the 2nd and 3rd terms in the expansion of (1 + x)ⁿ are equal, then n equals
questions.e: The coefficients are ⁿC₁ = n and ⁿC₂ = n(n − 1)/2. Setting them equal gives n − 1 = 2, so n = 3; indeed (1 + x)³ = 1 + 3x + 3x² + x³. n = 4 would give 4 and 6.

questions.s: In the expansion of (1 + ax)⁵, the coefficient of x is 15. The coefficient of x² is
questions.e: 5a = 15 gives a = 3. The coefficient of x² is ⁵C₂a² = 10 × 9 = 90. 30 uses a instead of a², and 9 forgets the binomial coefficient ⁵C₂.

questions.s: The first three terms in the expansion of (1 + kx)ⁿ are 1 + 12x + 64x². The value of n is
questions.e: nk = 12 and n(n − 1)k²/2 = 64. Since k = 12/n, this gives (n − 1) × 144/(2n) = 64, so 72(n − 1) = 64n and n = 9 (then k = 4/3). n = 12 assumes k = 1, which would make the x² coefficient 66, not 64.

questions.s: The coefficient of a³b² in the expansion of (a + b)⁵ is
questions.e: The term with b² is ⁵C₂ a³b² = 10a³b². 20 = 5 × 4 forgets to divide by 2!, and 60 = 5 × 4 × 3 is a permutation count.

questions.s: The last term in the expansion of (2 − x)⁵ is
questions.e: The last term is ⁵C₅(−x)⁵ = −x⁵, negative because the power is odd. 32 = 2⁵ is the first term, and −32x⁵ wrongly multiplies the first and last parts together.

questions.s: The coefficient of x⁻² in the expansion of (x − 1/x)⁶ is
questions.e: Tᵣ₊₁ = ⁶Cᵣ(−1)ʳ x⁶⁻²ʳ. 6 − 2r = −2 gives r = 4, so the coefficient is ⁶C₄(−1)⁴ = 15. −15 uses an odd sign, and −20 is the constant term ⁶C₃(−1)³.

questions.s: The expression (1 + x)⁴ − (1 − x)⁴ simplifies to
questions.e: Subtracting cancels the even powers and doubles the odd ones: 2(⁴C₁x + ⁴C₃x³) = 2(4x + 4x³) = 8x + 8x³. 2 + 12x² + 2x⁴ is the sum, not the difference, and 4x + 4x³ forgets to double.

questions.s: The coefficient of x³ in the expansion of (1 − 2x)(1 + x)⁶ is
questions.e: x³ comes from 1 × ⁶C₃x³ and from (−2x) × ⁶C₂x², so the coefficient is 20 − 2 × 15 = −10. 50 adds the two parts instead of subtracting, and 10 drops the sign.

questions.s: The coefficient of x² in (1 + x)⁴ + (1 − x)⁴ is
questions.e: Both expansions have the term ⁴C₂x² = 6x², because (−x)² = x², so the sum has 12x². 6 counts only one bracket; the odd-power terms are the ones that cancel.

questions.s: For a positive integer n, ⁿC₀ + ⁿC₁ + ⁿC₂ + … + ⁿCₙ equals
questions.e: Put x = 1 in (1 + x)ⁿ = ⁿC₀ + ⁿC₁x + … + ⁿCₙxⁿ to get 2ⁿ. 2ⁿ − 1 leaves out ⁿC₀ = 1, which belongs to the sum.

questions.s: The sum of all the coefficients in the expansion of (1 + x)¹⁰ is
questions.e: Setting x = 1 gives the sum of the coefficients: 2¹⁰ = 1024. 512 = 2⁹ is the sum of only the odd-numbered (or only the even-numbered) coefficients.

questions.s: The sum of the coefficients in the expansion of (3x − 2)⁷ is
questions.e: Put x = 1: (3 − 2)⁷ = 1⁷ = 1. Choosing −1 confuses this with (2 − 3)⁷, and 128 = 2⁷ is the sum for (1 + x)⁷.

questions.s: The sum of the coefficients in the expansion of (x + 2y)⁴ is
questions.e: Put x = y = 1: (1 + 2)⁴ = 3⁴ = 81. 16 = 2⁴ treats every coefficient as a plain binomial coefficient and ignores the factor 2 on y.

questions.s: For n ≥ 1, the sum ⁿC₁ + ⁿC₃ + ⁿC₅ + … (all odd-indexed coefficients) equals
questions.e: From x = 1 the full sum is 2ⁿ; from x = −1 the alternating sum is 0, so the odd-indexed and even-indexed sums are equal, each 2ⁿ/2 = 2ⁿ⁻¹. 2ⁿ is the total of all coefficients, not half of them.

questions.s: The value of ¹⁰C₀ + ¹⁰C₂ + ¹⁰C₄ + … + ¹⁰C₁₀ is
questions.e: The even-indexed coefficients make up half of the total 2¹⁰ = 1024, so their sum is 2⁹ = 512. 511 wrongly leaves out ¹⁰C₀ = 1, which is part of the sum.

questions.s: The value of ⁿC₁ + 2·ⁿC₂ + 3·ⁿC₃ + … + n·ⁿCₙ is
questions.e: Since r·ⁿCᵣ = n·ⁿ⁻¹Cᵣ₋₁, the sum is n(ⁿ⁻¹C₀ + … + ⁿ⁻¹Cₙ₋₁) = n·2ⁿ⁻¹. Check n = 2: 2 + 2 × 1 = 4 = 2 × 2. n·2ⁿ gives 8 for n = 2, too large.

questions.s: For n ≥ 1, ⁿC₀ − ⁿC₁ + ⁿC₂ − ⁿC₃ + … + (−1)ⁿ·ⁿCₙ equals
questions.e: Put x = −1 in (1 + x)ⁿ: the result is (1 − 1)ⁿ = 0. 2ⁿ is the sum with all signs positive.

questions.s: The value of ⁷C₀ + 2·⁷C₁ + 2²·⁷C₂ + … + 2⁷·⁷C₇ is
questions.e: The sum is the expansion of (1 + x)⁷ at x = 2, which is 3⁷ = 2187. 2⁷ is the value at x = 1, without the powers of 2.

questions.s: The greatest binomial coefficient in the expansion of (1 + x)⁸ is
questions.e: For even n the greatest coefficient is the middle one, ⁸C₄ = (8 × 7 × 6 × 5)/24 = 70. 56 = ⁸C₃ is the coefficient next to the middle.

questions.s: The sum of the coefficients in the expansion of (1 − 2x + x²)⁵ is
questions.e: Put x = 1: (1 − 2 + 1)⁵ = 0⁵ = 0. In fact the expression is (1 − x)¹⁰, whose coefficients alternate in sign and cancel. 32 = 2⁵ ignores the signs.

questions.s: The remainder when 6⁵¹ is divided by 7 is
questions.e: 6⁵¹ = (7 − 1)⁵¹. Every term of the expansion except the last has a factor 7, and the last is (−1)⁵¹ = −1. A remainder of −1 is the same as 7 − 1 = 6. Answering 1 treats the odd power as even.

questions.s: The remainder when 2⁶² is divided by 7 is
questions.e: 2⁶² = 2² × 2⁶⁰ = 4 × 8²⁰ = 4(7 + 1)²⁰. All terms of (7 + 1)²⁰ except the last 1 are multiples of 7, so 2⁶² leaves the same remainder as 4 × 1 = 4. Answering 1 ignores the extra factor 2².

questions.s: The largest integer that divides 9ⁿ − 8n − 1 for every positive integer n is
questions.e: 9ⁿ = (1 + 8)ⁿ = 1 + 8n + ⁿC₂·8² + ⁿC₃·8³ + …, so 9ⁿ − 8n − 1 is a multiple of 64. For n = 2 it equals 81 − 16 − 1 = 64 exactly, so nothing larger works. 8 and 16 divide it but are not the largest.

questions.s: The last two digits of 11¹⁰ are
questions.e: 11¹⁰ = (1 + 10)¹⁰ = 1 + 10 × 10 + ¹⁰C₂ × 10² + … Every term after the first is a multiple of 100, so the last two digits are 01. 11 assumes the last digits copy the base.

questions.s: Using the first three terms of a binomial expansion, an approximate value of (1.01)⁵ is
questions.e: (1 + 0.01)⁵ ≈ 1 + 5(0.01) + 10(0.01)² = 1 + 0.05 + 0.001 = 1.051. 1.05 keeps only two terms, and 1.105 misplaces the decimal of the third term.

questions.s: Correct to three decimal places, (0.99)⁴ equals
questions.e: (1 − 0.01)⁴ = 1 − 4(0.01) + 6(0.0001) − … = 1 − 0.04 + 0.0006 − 0.000004 ≈ 0.9606, which rounds to 0.961. 0.960 stops after two terms, and 0.959 subtracts the x² term instead of adding it.

questions.s: The expansion of (1 − x)³ is
questions.e: With coefficients 1, 3, 3, 1 and the powers of −x: 1 + 3(−x) + 3(−x)² + (−x)³ = 1 − 3x + 3x² − x³. The signs alternate because even powers of −x are positive; 1 − x³ drops the middle terms.

questions.s: After simplification, the number of terms in (x + y)²⁰ + (x − y)²⁰ is
questions.e: Terms with odd powers of y cancel and those with even powers (y⁰, y², …, y²⁰) double, leaving 11 terms. 21 is the number of terms in one expansion before adding.

questions.s: If ⁿC₂ = 28, then n equals
questions.e: n(n − 1)/2 = 28 gives n(n − 1) = 56 = 8 × 7, so n = 8. 14 comes from dividing 28 by 2 instead of solving n(n − 1) = 56.

questions.s: The coefficient of x¹⁹ in the expansion of (1 + x)²⁰ is
questions.e: The coefficient is ²⁰C₁₉ = ²⁰C₁ = 20. 190 = ²⁰C₂ belongs to x² (or x¹⁸), and 1 is the coefficient of x²⁰.

questions.s: In the expansion of (1 + x)ⁿ, the ratio of the coefficient of xʳ to the coefficient of xʳ⁻¹ is
questions.e: ⁿCᵣ/ⁿCᵣ₋₁ = [n!/(r!(n − r)!)] × [(r − 1)!(n − r + 1)!/n!] = (n − r + 1)/r. Check n = 4, r = 2: 6/4 = 3/2. (n − r)/r gives 1 here, and r/(n − r + 1) is the reciprocal.

questions.s: Three consecutive coefficients in the expansion of (1 + x)ⁿ are 6, 15 and 20. The value of n is
questions.e: (1 + x)⁶ has coefficients 1, 6, 15, 20, 15, 6, 1. Using ratios: 15/6 = (n − r + 1)/r and 20/15 = (n − r)/(r + 1) give 2n + 2 = 7r and 3n − 4 = 7r, so n = 6. For n = 7 the row is 1, 7, 21, 35, …

questions.s: The sum of the coefficients in the expansion of (1 + x)ⁿ is 256. The coefficient of the middle term is
questions.e: 2ⁿ = 256 gives n = 8, so there are 9 terms and the middle one is the 5th, with coefficient ⁸C₄ = 70. 56 = ⁸C₃ belongs to the 4th term, and 35 = ⁷C₃ uses n = 7.

questions.s: The greatest coefficient in the expansion of (1 + 2x)⁵ is
questions.e: The coefficients are ⁵Cᵣ2ʳ: 1, 10, 40, 80, 80, 32. The greatest is 80 (for x³ and x⁴). 32 is the coefficient of x⁵ only, and the greatest binomial coefficient 10 is not the greatest coefficient once the powers of 2 are included.

questions.s: For |x| < 1, the binomial series of (1 + x)⁻¹ is
questions.e: With n = −1 the coefficients are 1, −1, (−1)(−2)/2! = 1, (−1)(−2)(−3)/3! = −1, …, so the signs alternate: 1 − x + x² − x³ + … The series 1 + x + x² + … belongs to (1 − x)⁻¹.

questions.s: When n is a negative integer or a fraction, the binomial series for (1 + x)ⁿ is valid only when
questions.e: For such n the expansion never stops, and the infinite series converges only for |x| < 1. Only for a positive integer n is the expansion finite and true for every x.

questions.s: For |x| < 1, the expansion of (1 − x)⁻² is
questions.e: With n = −2 and −x in place of x: 1 + (−2)(−x) + [(−2)(−3)/2](−x)² + … = 1 + 2x + 3x² + 4x³ + … The alternating series 1 − 2x + 3x² − … is (1 + x)⁻², and 1 + 2x + 4x² + … is (1 − 2x)⁻¹.

questions.s: The binomial expansion of (1 + 2x)^(1/2) in ascending powers of x is valid for
questions.e: The series for (1 + y)^(1/2) needs |y| < 1. Here y = 2x, so |2x| < 1, that is |x| < 1/2. |x| < 1 forgets the factor 2, and |x| < 2 multiplies instead of dividing.

questions.s: The expansion of (2 − 3x)⁻² in ascending powers of x is valid for
questions.e: Write (2 − 3x)⁻² = 2⁻²(1 − 3x/2)⁻². The series needs |3x/2| < 1, so |x| < 2/3. |x| < 3/2 inverts the fraction, and |x| < 1/3 forgets to take out the factor 2.

questions.s: The coefficient of x² in the expansion of (1 + x)^(1/2) is
questions.e: The coefficient is n(n − 1)/2! with n = 1/2: (1/2)(−1/2)/2 = −1/8. The value 1/4 forgets the 2! and the minus sign from n − 1 = −1/2.

questions.s: The coefficient of x³ in the expansion of (1 − x)⁻³ for |x| < 1 is
questions.e: The coefficient is [(−3)(−4)(−5)/3!](−1)³ = (−10)(−1) = 10; in general (1 − x)⁻³ = 1 + 3x + 6x² + 10x³ + … −10 forgets the (−1)³ from (−x)³, and 6 is the coefficient of x².

questions.s: The first three terms in the expansion of (1 − 2x)^(−1/2) are
questions.e: With n = −1/2 and y = −2x: 1 + (−1/2)(−2x) + [(−1/2)(−3/2)/2](−2x)² = 1 + x + (3/8)(4x²) = 1 + x + (3/2)x². The option with (3/8)x² forgets to square the 2 in −2x.

questions.s: Using the binomial series, √1.04 correct to four decimal places is
questions.e: (1 + 0.04)^(1/2) ≈ 1 + (1/2)(0.04) − (1/8)(0.04)² = 1 + 0.02 − 0.0002 = 1.0198. 1.0200 stops after two terms, and 1.0202 adds the x² term although its coefficient −1/8 is negative.

questions.s: Using the binomial series, the cube root of 1001 correct to four decimal places is
questions.e: ∛1001 = 10(1 + 0.001)^(1/3) ≈ 10(1 + 0.001/3) = 10 + 0.00333 = 10.0033; the next term is about −0.000001 and does not affect four places. 10.0010 forgets to divide by 3, and 10.0333 misplaces the decimal.

questions.s: Using the binomial series, √99 correct to three decimal places is
questions.e: √99 = 10(1 − 0.01)^(1/2) ≈ 10[1 − 0.005 − (1/8)(0.0001)] = 10(0.9949875) = 9.949875, which rounds to 9.950. 9.949 cuts off the digits instead of rounding, and 9.900 uses 1 − 0.01 without the square root.

questions.s: If x is so small that x² and higher powers can be neglected, then (1 − 2x)^(1/2)/(1 + x)² is approximately
questions.e: (1 − 2x)^(1/2) ≈ 1 − x and (1 + x)⁻² ≈ 1 − 2x. Their product is 1 − x − 2x + (x² term) ≈ 1 − 3x. 1 + x comes from multiplying by (1 + x)² instead of dividing.

questions.s: The sum of the infinite series 1 + 2(1/3) + 3(1/3)² + 4(1/3)³ + … is
questions.e: 1 + 2x + 3x² + 4x³ + … = (1 − x)⁻² for |x| < 1. With x = 1/3 the sum is (2/3)⁻² = 9/4. 3/2 = (1 − 1/3)⁻¹ is the sum of the geometric series 1 + x + x² + …, not this one.

questions.s: For |x| < 1, the coefficient of xⁿ in the expansion of (1 − x)⁻² is
questions.e: (1 − x)⁻² = 1 + 2x + 3x² + 4x³ + …, so the coefficient of xⁿ is n + 1 (for n = 0 it is 1). The answer n is off by one position.

questions.s: For |x| < 1, the coefficient of x² in the expansion of (1 + x)/(1 − x) is
questions.e: (1 + x)(1 − x)⁻¹ = (1 + x)(1 + x + x² + …). The x² terms are 1 × x² and x × x, so the coefficient is 1 + 1 = 2. Taking only 1 forgets the x × x product.

questions.s: For |x| < 1/2, the coefficient of x³ in the expansion of (1 + 2x)⁻¹ is
questions.e: (1 + 2x)⁻¹ = 1 − 2x + (2x)² − (2x)³ + …, so the x³ coefficient is −2³ = −8. +8 forgets that odd powers have a minus sign, and −6 multiplies 2 by 3 instead of cubing.

questions.s: The coefficient of x² in the expansion of (1 − x)^(−1/2) for |x| < 1 is
questions.e: n(n − 1)/2! with n = −1/2 is (−1/2)(−3/2)/2 = 3/8, and (−x)² = x² keeps it positive. −1/8 is the coefficient for (1 + x)^(1/2), a different index.

questions.s: For |x| < 1, the sum 1 + x + x² + x³ + … equals
questions.e: This is (1 − x)⁻¹ expanded by the binomial series (also a geometric series with ratio x). 1/(1 + x) gives alternating signs, and 1/(1 − x)² gives coefficients 1, 2, 3, …

questions.s: When n is a negative integer, the number of terms in the binomial expansion of (1 + x)ⁿ is
questions.e: For a negative index the factor n − r never becomes zero, so the coefficients never vanish and the series never ends. The count n + 1 applies only to positive integer n.

questions.s: For small x, the first two terms in the expansion of (1 + x)^(1/3) are
questions.e: (1 + x)ⁿ ≈ 1 + nx, and n = 1/3 gives 1 + x/3. 1 + 3x uses the reciprocal of the index, and 1 + x/6 halves it wrongly.

questions.s: For |x| < 1, the coefficient of x² in the expansion of (1 + x)⁻³ is
questions.e: The coefficient is n(n − 1)/2! = (−3)(−4)/2 = 6, positive since two negatives multiply. −6 gets the sign wrong, and −12 also forgets to divide by 2!.

questions.s: If x is small enough for x² and higher powers to be neglected, then (8 + 3x)^(2/3) is approximately
Which of the following gives an infinite series when expanded by the binomial theorem?
questions.e: A fractional index gives coefficients that never become zero, so (1 + x)^(1/2) expands to an infinite series. The other three have positive integer indices and stop after n + 1 terms.

questions.s: For |x| < 1, the coefficient of x² in the expansion of (1 + 2x)/(1 + x) is
questions.e: (1 + 2x)(1 − x + x² − …): the x² terms are 1 × x² and 2x × (−x), so the coefficient is 1 − 2 = −1. +3 adds the two parts with the wrong sign on −x.

questions.s: To prove 2ⁿ ≥ n + 1 for all positive integers n by mathematical induction, the base case to be checked is
questions.e: The base case is P(1): 2¹ ≥ 1 + 1, that is 2 ≥ 2, which is true. 4 ≥ 3 is P(2), and 1 ≥ 1 would be P(0), which is not the first positive integer.

questions.s: For every positive integer n, 1 + 4 + 7 + … + (3n − 2) equals
questions.e: The terms form an arithmetic series with n terms, first term 1 and last term 3n − 2, so the sum is n(1 + 3n − 2)/2 = n(3n − 1)/2. Check n = 2: 1 + 4 = 5 = 2 × 5/2. n(3n + 1)/2 gives 7 for n = 2.

questions.s: The coefficient of x⁴ in the expansion of (1 + x)⁶ is
questions.e: The coefficient is ⁶C₄ = ⁶C₂ = (6 × 5)/2 = 15. 30 = 6 × 5 forgets to divide by 2!, and 20 = ⁶C₃ is the middle coefficient.

questions.s: The 3rd term in the expansion of (2a − b)⁵ in descending powers of a is
questions.e: T₃ = ⁵C₂(2a)³(−b)² = 10 × 8a³ × b² = 80a³b², positive because (−b)² = b². 40a³b² uses 2² instead of 2³, and 80a²b³ has the powers the wrong way round.

questions.s: The middle term in the expansion of (x + 2)⁶ is
questions.e: There are 7 terms, so the middle one is T₄ = ⁶C₃x³2³ = 20 × 8x³ = 160x³. 20x³ forgets the factor 2³, and 240x² = ⁶C₄x²2⁴ is the 5th term.

questions.s: The term independent of x in the expansion of (x − 1/x)⁴ is
questions.e: Tᵣ₊₁ = ⁴Cᵣ(−1)ʳx⁴⁻²ʳ, which is free of x when r = 2: ⁴C₂(−1)² = 6. The sign is positive because the power of −1/x is even.

questions.s: The term independent of x in the expansion of (x³ + 1/x²)⁵ is
questions.e: Tᵣ₊₁ = ⁵Cᵣ(x³)⁵⁻ʳ(x⁻²)ʳ = ⁵Cᵣx¹⁵⁻⁵ʳ, free of x when r = 3, giving ⁵C₃ = 10. 5 = ⁵C₁ uses the wrong r.

questions.s: The value of ⁹C₁ + ⁹C₂ + ⁹C₃ + … + ⁹C₉ is
questions.e: All the coefficients from ⁹C₀ to ⁹C₉ add up to 2⁹ = 512, and this sum leaves out ⁹C₀ = 1, so it equals 511. 512 forgets that ⁹C₀ is missing, and 256 is half of 512.

questions.s: The remainder when 5¹¹ is divided by 24 is
questions.e: 5¹¹ = 5 × 25⁵ = 5(24 + 1)⁵. Every term of (24 + 1)⁵ except the last 1 is a multiple of 24, so 5¹¹ leaves the same remainder as 5 × 1 = 5. Answering 1 ignores the extra factor 5.

questions.s: For small x, the first two terms in the expansion of (1 − x)⁻³ are
