questions.e: f(f(x)) = 3(3x − 4) − 4 = 9x − 12 − 4 = 9x − 16. The option 9x − 12 forgets the final −4, and 9x² − 16 multiplies f by itself instead of composing.

questions.s: If f(x) = 2x + 3 and (f∘g)(x) = 6x − 1, then g(x) is
questions.e: f(g(x)) = 2g(x) + 3 = 6x − 1, so 2g(x) = 6x − 4 and g(x) = 3x − 2. The option 6x − 4 stops before dividing by 2.

questions.s: Which of the following functions from ℝ to ℝ is one-one and so has an inverse?
questions.e: x³ + 1 is strictly increasing, so different inputs always give different outputs. x² and |x| give the same value at x and −x, and cos x repeats every 2π, so they are not one-one on ℝ.

questions.s: The inverse of f(x) = e²ˣ, x ∈ ℝ, is
questions.e: From y = e²ˣ we get 2x = ln y, so x = ½ ln y and f⁻¹(x) = ½ ln x for x > 0. The option 2 ln x multiplies by 2 instead of dividing by it.

questions.s: If f(x) = x/(x − 1), x ≠ 1, then f(f(x)) equals
questions.e: f(f(x)) = [x/(x − 1)] ÷ [x/(x − 1) − 1] = [x/(x − 1)] ÷ [1/(x − 1)] = x. So f is its own inverse; writing x/(x − 1) forgets to apply f a second time.

questions.s: If f(x) = 5x − 7, then f⁻¹(3) is
questions.e: f⁻¹(3) is the x with 5x − 7 = 3, so 5x = 10 and x = 2. The value 8 is f(3), which evaluates f instead of its inverse.

questions.s: The graph of y = f⁻¹(x) is the reflection of the graph of y = f(x) in
questions.e: If (a, b) lies on y = f(x), then (b, a) lies on y = f⁻¹(x); swapping coordinates is reflection in the line y = x. Reflection in the x-axis gives y = −f(x) instead.

questions.s: If f(x) = √x and g(x) = x − 4, then the domain of f∘g is
questions.e: (f∘g)(x) = √(x − 4), which is real when x − 4 ≥ 0, i.e. x ≥ 4. The set [0, ∞) is the domain of f alone, not of the composition.

questions.s: If f(x) = x² − 1 and g(x) = 2x + 1, then (f∘g)(2) − (g∘f)(2) is
questions.e: (f∘g)(2) = f(5) = 24 and (g∘f)(2) = g(3) = 7, so the difference is 24 − 7 = 17. Getting −17 subtracts in the wrong order; 0 assumes composition is commutative, which it is not.

questions.s: If f(x) = (3x + 2)/(5x − 3), x ≠ 3/5, then f⁻¹(x) is
questions.e: From y(5x − 3) = 3x + 2 we get x(5y − 3) = 3y + 2, so x = (3y + 2)/(5y − 3). Thus f⁻¹ = f; this happens for (ax + b)/(cx − a). The reciprocal (5x − 3)/(3x + 2) is not the inverse.

questions.s: The inverse of f(x) = x³ − 2 is
questions.e: y = x³ − 2 gives x³ = y + 2, so x = ∛(y + 2) and f⁻¹(x) = ∛(x + 2). The option ∛x + 2 adds 2 after taking the root, which undoes the steps in the wrong order.

questions.s: If f(x) = 2x and g(x) = x + 3, then (f∘g)(x) − (g∘f)(x) equals
questions.e: (f∘g)(x) = 2(x + 3) = 2x + 6 and (g∘f)(x) = 2x + 3, so the difference is 3. Choosing 0 assumes f∘g = g∘f, which is false in general.

questions.s: If f(x) = 1/(1 − x), x ≠ 0, 1, then f(f(f(x))) equals
questions.e: f(f(x)) = 1/(1 − 1/(1 − x)) = (1 − x)/(−x) = (x − 1)/x. Then f of this is 1/(1 − (x − 1)/x) = 1/(1/x) = x. The option (x − 1)/x is only the second step.
The inverse reverses every ordered pair, so (a, b) becomes (b, a): {(4, 1), (5, 2), (6, 3)}. Taking reciprocals of the images gives 1/f, not f⁻¹.

questions.s: Which of the following is an even function?
questions.e: For x² cos x, replacing x by −x gives (−x)² cos(−x) = x² cos x, so it is even. In x sin x + x the term x sin x is even but the added x is odd, so the sum is neither.

questions.s: Which statement about f(x) = x³ − sin x is correct?
o: It is neither even nor odd
questions.e: f(−x) = −x³ − sin(−x) = −x³ + sin x = −f(x), so f is odd. Each term is odd, and a difference of odd functions is odd; the x³ term stops it from being periodic.

questions.s: Which statement about f(x) = ln((1 + x)/(1 − x)), −1 < x < 1, is correct?
o: It is neither even nor odd
questions.e: f(−x) = ln((1 − x)/(1 + x)) = −ln((1 + x)/(1 − x)) = −f(x), so f is odd. The domain (−1, 1) is symmetric about 0, as the test requires.

questions.s: If f is an odd function and f(3) = −5, then f(−3) is
questions.e: For an odd function f(−x) = −f(x), so f(−3) = −(−5) = 5. The value −5 would be correct for an even function.

questions.s: The graph of an even function is symmetric about
questions.e: f(−x) = f(x) means the points (x, y) and (−x, y) are on the graph together, which is symmetry in the y-axis. Symmetry about the origin belongs to odd functions.

questions.s: Which statement about f(x) = x|x| is correct?
o: It is neither even nor odd
questions.e: f(−x) = (−x)|−x| = −x|x| = −f(x), so f is odd. It looks like it might be even because of |x|, but the factor x changes sign.

questions.s: Every function on ℝ is the sum of an even and an odd function. For f(x) = eˣ, the even part is
questions.e: The even part of f is [f(x) + f(−x)]/2 = (eˣ + e⁻ˣ)/2, which is cosh x. The option (eˣ − e⁻ˣ)/2 is [f(x) − f(−x)]/2, the odd part (sinh x).

questions.s: The graph of y = f(x − 2) is obtained from the graph of y = f(x) by shifting it
questions.e: The value that f had at x = a now occurs where x − 2 = a, i.e. at x = a + 2, so the graph moves 2 units right. Moving left would come from f(x + 2).

questions.s: The graph of y = f(x) + 3 is obtained from the graph of y = f(x) by shifting it
questions.e: Adding 3 to every output raises each point of the graph by 3 units. A horizontal shift would need 3 added or subtracted inside the bracket, as in f(x − 3).

questions.s: The vertex of the parabola y = (x + 1)² − 4 is
questions.e: y = (x + 1)² − 4 is y = x² shifted 1 unit left and 4 units down, so the vertex moves from (0, 0) to (−1, −4). The point (1, −4) misreads x + 1 as a shift to the right.

questions.s: The graph of y = f(−x) is the reflection of the graph of y = f(x) in
questions.e: A point (a, b) on y = f(x) corresponds to (−a, b) on y = f(−x), which is reflection in the y-axis. Reflection in the x-axis gives y = −f(x).

questions.s: The lowest point of the graph of y = |x − 3| is
questions.e: |x − 3| ≥ 0 and equals 0 only at x = 3, so the V-shaped graph touches the x-axis at (3, 0). The point (−3, 0) misreads the shift direction; (0, 3) is the y-intercept.

questions.s: The point (2, 5) lies on the graph of y = f(x). Which point must lie on the graph of y = 2f(x − 1) + 3?
questions.e: We need x − 1 = 2, so x = 3, and then y = 2f(2) + 3 = 2(5) + 3 = 13. The point (3, 16) adds 3 before doubling, and (1, 13) shifts left instead of right.

questions.s: If f(x) = x² + kx + 4 is an even function, then k is
questions.e: f(−x) = x² − kx + 4 must equal x² + kx + 4 for every x, so 2kx = 0 for all x and k = 0. Any other k leaves an odd term kx.

questions.s: The period of f(x) = sin 3x is
questions.e: sin kx has period 2π/k, so sin 3x has period 2π/3. Multiplying by 3 instead (6π or 3π) confuses compressing the graph with stretching it.

questions.s: The period of f(x) = sin 2x + cos 3x is
questions.e: sin 2x has period π and cos 3x has period 2π/3. The smallest number that is a whole multiple of both is 2π (= 2 × π = 3 × 2π/3). π alone fails because cos 3x does not repeat after π.

questions.s: The graph of y = x² is shifted 2 units to the left and then 3 units down. The equation of the new graph is
questions.e: A shift of 2 units left replaces x by x + 2, and a shift of 3 units down subtracts 3: y = (x + 2)² − 3. Using x − 2 would move the graph to the right.

questions.s: Which of the following functions is neither even nor odd?
questions.e: For x² + x, f(−x) = x² − x, which is neither f(x) nor −f(x). The other functions contain only even powers (or cos) or only odd powers, so they are even or odd.

questions.s: If f is an even function and g is an odd function on ℝ, then the composite f∘g is
o: neither even nor odd in general
questions.e: (f∘g)(−x) = f(g(−x)) = f(−g(x)) = f(g(x)), using g odd and then f even. So f∘g is even. The product f·g would be odd, which is a different combination.

questions.s: The graph of the constant function f(x) = 7 is
o: a line parallel to the y-axis
a line parallel to the x-axis
questions.e: y = 7 for every x, so the graph is the horizontal line 7 units above the x-axis, with slope 0. A line parallel to the y-axis, x = 7, is not even a function.

questions.s: The value of lim (x → 2) (x² − 4)/(x − 2) is
questions.e: Factorise: (x² − 4)/(x − 2) = x + 2 for x ≠ 2, so the limit is 2 + 2 = 4. Direct substitution gives 0/0, which is indeterminate, not a reason to say the limit does not exist.

questions.s: The value of lim (x → 3) (2x² − 5x + 1) is
questions.e: A polynomial is continuous, so substitute: 2(9) − 5(3) + 1 = 18 − 15 + 1 = 4. The value 34 comes from adding 15 instead of subtracting it.

questions.s: The value of lim (x → 1) (x³ − 1)/(x − 1) is
questions.e: x³ − 1 = (x − 1)(x² + x + 1), so the expression equals x² + x + 1 for x ≠ 1, and the limit is 1 + 1 + 1 = 3. This matches the rule lim (xⁿ − aⁿ)/(x − a) = naⁿ⁻¹ with n = 3, a = 1.

questions.s: The value of lim (x → ∞) (3x² + 2x)/(5x² − 1) is
questions.e: Divide top and bottom by x²: (3 + 2/x)/(5 − 1/x²) → 3/5 as x → ∞. When the degrees are equal, the limit is the ratio of the leading coefficients, not 0 or ∞.

questions.s: The value of lim (x → 0) (√(x + 4) − 2)/x is
questions.e: Multiply by the conjugate: (x + 4 − 4)/[x(√(x + 4) + 2)] = 1/(√(x + 4) + 2) → 1/(2 + 2) = 1/4. Getting 1/2 forgets to add the two square roots in the conjugate.

questions.s: The value of lim (x → 2) (x⁵ − 32)/(x − 2) is
questions.e: Use lim (xⁿ − aⁿ)/(x − a) = naⁿ⁻¹ with n = 5 and a = 2: 5 × 2⁴ = 5 × 16 = 80. The value 16 is only a⁴, forgetting the factor n.

questions.s: The value of lim (x → ∞) [√(x² + 3x) − x] is
questions.e: Multiply by the conjugate: 3x/(√(x² + 3x) + x) = 3/(√(1 + 3/x) + 1) → 3/2. It is tempting to say ∞ − ∞ = 0, but the form is indeterminate and must be simplified first.

questions.s: The value of lim (x → −1) (x² + 3x + 2)/(x² − 1) is
questions.e: Factorise: (x + 1)(x + 2)/[(x + 1)(x − 1)] = (x + 2)/(x − 1) for x ≠ −1. At x = −1 this is 1/(−2) = −1/2. A sign slip in x − 1 gives 1/2.

questions.s: The value of lim (x → ∞) (2x + 7)/(x − 3) is
questions.e: Divide by x: (2 + 7/x)/(1 − 3/x) → 2/1 = 2. The value −7/3 is what you get by putting x = 0, not by letting x grow without bound.

questions.s: The value of lim (x → 4) (x − 4)/(√x − 2) is
questions.e: Write x − 4 = (√x − 2)(√x + 2), so the expression equals √x + 2 for x ≠ 4, and the limit is 2 + 2 = 4. The value 1/4 is the limit of the reciprocal expression.

questions.s: The value of lim (x → ∞) (x² + 1)/(2x³ − x) is
questions.e: Divide by x³: (1/x + 1/x³)/(2 − 1/x²) → 0/2 = 0. The denominator has the higher degree, so the fraction shrinks to 0; 1/2 would need equal degrees.

questions.s: The value of lim (x → 0) [(1 + x)³ − 1]/x is
questions.e: (1 + x)³ − 1 = 3x + 3x² + x³, so dividing by x gives 3 + 3x + x² → 3. Substituting directly gives 0/0, which does not mean the limit is 0.

questions.s: If lim (x → 2) f(x) = 5 and lim (x → 2) g(x) = −3, then lim (x → 2) [2f(x) − g(x)] is
questions.e: By the limit laws, the limit is 2(5) − (−3) = 10 + 3 = 13. The value 7 treats −g(x) as −3 instead of +3.

questions.s: The value of lim (x → 1) (x⁴ − 1)/(x³ − 1) is
questions.e: Divide numerator and denominator by x − 1: the limits of (x⁴ − 1)/(x − 1) and (x³ − 1)/(x − 1) are 4 and 3, so the answer is 4/3. Writing 3/4 inverts the ratio.

questions.s: The value of lim (x → 3) (x² − 9)/(x² − 2x − 3) is
questions.e: Factorise: (x − 3)(x + 3)/[(x − 3)(x + 1)] = (x + 3)/(x + 1), which at x = 3 is 6/4 = 3/2. Writing 2/3 turns the fraction upside down.

questions.s: The value of lim (x → 0) [√(1 + x) − √(1 − x)]/x is
questions.e: Multiply by the conjugate: [(1 + x) − (1 − x)]/[x(√(1 + x) + √(1 − x))] = 2/(√(1 + x) + √(1 − x)) → 2/2 = 1. Forgetting the 2 in the numerator gives 1/2.

questions.s: The value of lim (x → ∞) (5 − 3x)/(2x + 1) is
questions.e: Divide by x: (5/x − 3)/(2 + 1/x) → −3/2. The leading coefficients are −3 and 2; dropping the minus sign gives 3/2.

questions.s: The value of lim (x → 2) [1/(x − 2) − 4/(x² − 4)] is
questions.e: Combine: [(x + 2) − 4]/(x² − 4) = (x − 2)/[(x − 2)(x + 2)] = 1/(x + 2) → 1/4. Each term alone is unbounded, but their difference has a finite limit.

questions.s: The value of lim (n → ∞) (1 + 2 + 3 + … + n)/n² is
questions.e: 1 + 2 + … + n = n(n + 1)/2, so the expression is (n² + n)/(2n²) = (1 + 1/n)/2 → 1/2. Saying 0 treats each term k/n² as vanishing without counting how many terms there are.

questions.s: The value of lim (x → 0) (x² + 3x)/(2x) is
questions.e: For x ≠ 0, (x² + 3x)/(2x) = (x + 3)/2, which tends to 3/2. Cancelling x but forgetting the 2 in the denominator gives 3.

questions.s: The value of lim (x → 0) (sin 5x)/x is
questions.e: Write (sin 5x)/x = 5 × (sin 5x)/(5x), and (sin 5x)/(5x) → 1, so the limit is 5. The value 1 forgets the factor needed to match the angle 5x.

questions.s: The value of lim (x → 0) (tan x)/x is
questions.e: (tan x)/x = (sin x/x) × (1/cos x) → 1 × 1 = 1. The form 0/0 at x = 0 is indeterminate; it does not give 0.

questions.s: The value of lim (x → 0) (sin 4x)/(sin 7x) is
questions.e: Write it as [(sin 4x)/(4x)] × [(7x)/(sin 7x)] × (4/7); the first two factors tend to 1, so the limit is 4/7. The value 7/4 inverts the ratio.

questions.s: The value of lim (x → 0) (1 − cos x)/x² is
questions.e: 1 − cos x = 2 sin²(x/2), so the expression is 2 sin²(x/2)/x² = ½ [sin(x/2)/(x/2)]² → ½. Getting 1 forgets that the angle is x/2.

questions.s: The value of lim (x → 0) (1 − cos 4x)/x² is
questions.e: 1 − cos 4x = 2 sin² 2x, so the expression is 2 (sin 2x/x)² → 2 × 2² = 8. The value 16 forgets the factor ½ hidden in 1 − cos θ = 2 sin²(θ/2).

questions.s: The value of lim (x → 0) (tan x − sin x)/x³ is
questions.e: tan x − sin x = tan x (1 − cos x), so the expression is (tan x/x) × (1 − cos x)/x² → 1 × ½ = ½. Cancelling tan x with sin x and writing 0 ignores the x³ in the denominator.

questions.s: If θ is measured in degrees, then lim (θ → 0) (sin θ)/θ equals
questions.e: θ degrees is πθ/180 radians, so (sin θ°)/θ = (π/180) × sin(πθ/180)/(πθ/180) → π/180. The standard result 1 holds only when the angle is in radians.

questions.s: The value of lim (x → 0) (sin 2x + sin 3x)/x is
questions.e: Split the fraction: (sin 2x)/x → 2 and (sin 3x)/x → 3, so the limit is 2 + 3 = 5. Multiplying the two values instead of adding them gives 6.

questions.s: The value of lim (x → π) (sin x)/(π − x) is
questions.e: Put t = π − x, so t → 0 and sin x = sin(π − t) = sin t. The limit becomes (sin t)/t → 1. A sign slip with sin(π − t) leads to −1.

questions.s: The value of lim (x → 0) x cot x is
questions.e: x cot x = (x/sin x) × cos x → 1 × 1 = 1. The form 0 × ∞ is indeterminate, so it cannot simply be taken as 0.

questions.s: The result lim (x → 0) (sin x)/x = 1 is true when x is measured in
questions.e: The result comes from comparing arc length rθ with sin θ, which needs θ in radians. In degrees the limit is π/180, so the unit does matter.

questions.s: The value of lim (x → 0) (sin² 3x)/x² is
questions.e: (sin² 3x)/x² = [(sin 3x)/x]² and (sin 3x)/x → 3, so the limit is 3² = 9. Writing 3 forgets to square.

questions.s: The value of lim (x → 0) (1 − cos x)/(x sin x) is
questions.e: Write it as [(1 − cos x)/x²] × [x/sin x] → ½ × 1 = ½. Treating 1 − cos x like sin x and cancelling gives 1, which is wrong.

questions.s: The value of lim (x → 0) (tan 3x)/(2x) is
questions.e: (tan 3x)/(2x) = (3/2) × (tan 3x)/(3x) → 3/2 × 1 = 3/2. The value 2/3 inverts the coefficients.

questions.s: The value of lim (x → π/2) (cos x)/(x − π/2) is
questions.e: Put t = x − π/2, so cos x = cos(π/2 + t) = −sin t. The limit is (−sin t)/t → −1. Forgetting that cos(π/2 + t) is negative gives 1.

questions.s: The value of lim (x → 0) (cos x − cos 3x)/x² is
questions.e: Write cos x − cos 3x = (1 − cos 3x) − (1 − cos x). Using (1 − cos kx)/x² → k²/2, the limit is 9/2 − 1/2 = 4. Using k instead of k² gives 3/2 − 1/2 = 1, and adding instead of subtracting gives 5.

questions.s: The value of lim (x → 0) (sin x)/(2x) is
questions.e: (sin x)/(2x) = ½ × (sin x)/x → ½. The constant 2 in the denominator stays; the value 2 puts it in the numerator.

questions.s: The value of lim (x → 0) (x + sin x)/x is
questions.e: (x + sin x)/x = 1 + (sin x)/x → 1 + 1 = 2. Stopping at the first term gives 1.

questions.s: The value of lim (x → 0) (1 − cos 2x)/(x tan x) is
questions.e: 1 − cos 2x = 2 sin² x, so the expression is 2 × (sin x/x) × (sin x/tan x) = 2 × (sin x/x) × cos x → 2. Using 1 − cos 2x = sin² x without the 2 gives 1.

questions.s: The value of lim (x → 0) sin(x²)/(1 − cos x) is
questions.e: sin(x²)/x² → 1 and (1 − cos x)/x² → ½, so the limit is 1 ÷ ½ = 2. Multiplying by ½ instead of dividing gives ½.

questions.s: The value of lim (n → ∞) (1 + 1/n)ⁿ is
questions.e: This limit defines the number e ≈ 2.718. It is the form 1^∞, which is indeterminate: the base tends to 1 but the power grows, so the answer is not 1.

questions.s: The value of lim (x → ∞) (1 + 3/x)ˣ is
questions.e: Put x = 3t: (1 + 1/t)^(3t) = [(1 + 1/t)ᵗ]³ → e³. In general (1 + k/x)ˣ → eᵏ; 3e multiplies instead of raising to the power.

questions.s: The value of lim (x → 0) (1 + 2x)^(1/x) is
questions.e: Write (1 + 2x)^(1/x) = [(1 + 2x)^(1/(2x))]² and (1 + h)^(1/h) → e as h → 0, so the limit is e². The value e^(1/2) divides by 2 instead of multiplying.

questions.s: The value of lim (x → 0) (eˣ − 1)/x is
questions.e: This is the standard result (aˣ − 1)/x → ln a with a = e, and ln e = 1. Substituting x = 0 gives 0/0, which is indeterminate, not 0.

questions.s: The value of lim (x → 0) (2ˣ − 1)/x is
questions.e: Using lim (aˣ − 1)/x = ln a with a = 2 gives ln 2. The value 1 holds only for base e.

questions.s: The value of lim (x → 0) (3ˣ − 2ˣ)/x is
questions.e: Split: (3ˣ − 1)/x − (2ˣ − 1)/x → ln 3 − ln 2 = ln(3/2). Adding the logarithms gives ln 6, and subtracting in the wrong order gives ln(2/3).

questions.s: The value of lim (x → ∞) (1 − 2/x)^(3x) is
questions.e: (1 + k/x)ˣ → eᵏ with k = −2, so (1 − 2/x)^(3x) = [(1 − 2/x)ˣ]³ → (e⁻²)³ = e⁻⁶. Losing the minus sign gives e⁶.

questions.s: The value of lim (x → 0) (e⁴ˣ − 1)/x is
questions.e: (e⁴ˣ − 1)/x = 4 × (e⁴ˣ − 1)/(4x) → 4 × 1 = 4. The answer e⁴ comes from substituting x = 1 instead of taking the limit at 0.

questions.s: The value of lim (x → ∞) ((x + 2)/(x − 1))ˣ is
questions.e: Write the base as (1 + 2/x)/(1 − 1/x). Then (1 + 2/x)ˣ → e² and (1 − 1/x)ˣ → e⁻¹, so the limit is e² ÷ e⁻¹ = e³. Treating the base as 1 + 2/x only gives e².

questions.s: The value of lim (x → 0) ln(1 + x)/x is
questions.e: ln(1 + x)/x = ln[(1 + x)^(1/x)] and (1 + x)^(1/x) → e, so the limit is ln e = 1. Writing e confuses the inner limit with the final answer.

questions.s: The value of lim (x → 0) (eˣ − e⁻ˣ)/x is
questions.e: Split: (eˣ − 1)/x + (1 − e⁻ˣ)/x. The first tends to 1, and (1 − e⁻ˣ)/x = (e⁻ˣ − 1)/(−x) → 1, so the total is 2. Writing 0 treats the two terms as cancelling.

questions.s: The value of lim (x → 0) (5ˣ − 1)/(3ˣ − 1) is
questions.e: Divide top and bottom by x: (5ˣ − 1)/x → ln 5 and (3ˣ − 1)/x → ln 3, so the limit is ln 5/ln 3. The option ln(5/3) is ln 5 − ln 3, a difference rather than a quotient.

questions.s: Correct to three decimal places, the number e = lim (n → ∞) (1 + 1/n)ⁿ is
The value of lim (n → ∞) (1 + 1/(2n))ⁿ is
questions.e: Put m = 2n: (1 + 1/m)^(m/2) = [(1 + 1/m)ᵐ]^(1/2) → e^(1/2) = √e. The value e² multiplies the exponent by 2 instead of halving it.

questions.s: The value of lim (x → 0) (1 + 3x)^(2/x) is
questions.e: (1 + 3x)^(2/x) = [(1 + 3x)^(1/(3x))]⁶, and the bracket tends to e, so the limit is e⁶. Adding the numbers 2 and 3 gives e⁵, which has no basis.

questions.s: The value of lim (x → 0) (10ˣ − 1)/x is
questions.e: By lim (aˣ − 1)/x = ln a with a = 10, the limit is ln 10 ≈ 2.303. The value 1 would need log to base 10, but the result uses the natural logarithm.

questions.s: The value of lim (x → ∞) (1 + 1/x)^(x + 2) is
questions.e: (1 + 1/x)^(x + 2) = (1 + 1/x)ˣ × (1 + 1/x)² → e × 1 = e. The extra power 2 acts on a base tending to 1, so it does not change the limit to e².

questions.s: The value of lim (x → 1) (x − 1)/ln x is
questions.e: Put x = 1 + h with h → 0: the expression is h/ln(1 + h), the reciprocal of ln(1 + h)/h → 1, so the limit is 1. The 0/0 form at x = 1 does not mean the limit is 0.

questions.s: The value of lim (x → 0) ln(1 + 4x)/x is
questions.e: ln(1 + 4x)/x = 4 × ln(1 + 4x)/(4x) → 4 × 1 = 4. The option ln 4 confuses this with (4ˣ − 1)/x.

questions.s: The value of lim (x → 0) x/(e²ˣ − 1) is
questions.e: (e²ˣ − 1)/x → 2, so its reciprocal x/(e²ˣ − 1) → 1/2. The value 2 forgets that the fraction is upside down.

questions.s: The function f(x) = 3x − 1 for x < 2 and f(x) = x + k for x ≥ 2 is continuous at x = 2. The value of k is
questions.e: The left-hand limit is 3(2) − 1 = 5 and f(2) = 2 + k. Continuity needs 2 + k = 5, so k = 3. The option 5 sets k equal to the limit itself and forgets the 2.

questions.s: The value of lim (x → 0⁻) |x|/x is
questions.e: For x < 0, |x| = −x, so |x|/x = −1 and the left-hand limit is −1. The value 1 is the right-hand limit, from x > 0.

questions.s: The value of lim (x → 0) |x|/x is
questions.e: |x|/x = 1 for x > 0 and −1 for x < 0, so the right-hand limit is 1 and the left-hand limit is −1. As they differ, the two-sided limit does not exist; 0 is not their average in any valid sense.

questions.s: Let f(x) = (x² − 9)/(x − 3) for x ≠ 3 and f(3) = k. If f is continuous at x = 3, then k is
questions.e: For x ≠ 3, f(x) = x + 3, so lim (x → 3) f(x) = 6, and continuity needs k = 6. The value 0 comes from substituting into the numerator only.

questions.s: Let f(x) = (sin 3x)/x for x ≠ 0 and f(0) = k. If f is continuous at x = 0, then k is
questions.e: lim (x → 0) (sin 3x)/x = 3 × (sin 3x)/(3x) → 3, so k must be 3. The value 1 forgets the factor 3 from the angle.

questions.s: The function f(x) = 1/(x − 5) is discontinuous at
questions.e: f is not defined where the denominator is zero, x − 5 = 0, i.e. x = 5, so it cannot be continuous there. At every other real x it is a quotient of continuous functions with non-zero denominator.

questions.s: The function f(x) = x + 2 for x ≤ 1 and f(x) = ax² for x > 1 is continuous at x = 1. The value of a is
questions.e: f(1) = 1 + 2 = 3 and the right-hand limit is a(1)² = a, so continuity requires a = 3. Using x + 2 = 2 at x = 1 (dropping the x) gives 2.

questions.s: Let f(x) = ax + b for x < 2, f(2) = 10 and f(x) = bx − a for x > 2. If f is continuous at x = 2, then (a, b) is
questions.e: Continuity needs 2a + b = 10 and 2b − a = 10. From the first, b = 10 − 2a; then 20 − 4a − a = 10 gives a = 2 and b = 6. The pairs (3, 4) and (4, 2) satisfy only the left-hand condition.

questions.s: Let f(x) = x² for x < 0 and f(x) = x + 1 for x ≥ 0. Which statement is correct?
questions.e: From the right, f(x) = x + 1 → 1, and from the left, f(x) = x² → 0. Since the one-sided limits differ, f is not continuous at 0, and f(0) = 0 + 1 = 1, not 0.

questions.s: Which of the following functions is continuous for every real x?
questions.e: x² and sin x are continuous everywhere, so their sum is too. 1/x fails at 0, tan x at odd multiples of π/2, and ln x is not defined for x ≤ 0.

questions.s: f(x) = (x² − 4x + 3)/(x² − 1) is not defined at x = 1. To make f continuous at x = 1, f(1) must be defined as
questions.e: Factorise: (x − 1)(x − 3)/[(x − 1)(x + 1)] = (x − 3)/(x + 1) for x ≠ ±1, which tends to −2/2 = −1 as x → 1. Taking f(1) = 0 from the numerator alone is wrong because the denominator is also 0.

questions.s: Let f(x) = (1 − cos 2x)/x² for x ≠ 0 and f(0) = k. If f is continuous at x = 0, then k is
questions.e: 1 − cos 2x = 2 sin² x, so f(x) = 2 (sin x/x)² → 2, and k = 2. Using (1 − cos kx)/x² → k² without the factor ½ gives 4.

questions.s: Let f(x) = 2x + 1 for x < 3 and f(x) = 10 − x for x ≥ 3. The value of lim (x → 3) f(x) is
questions.e: Left-hand limit: 2(3) + 1 = 7. Right-hand limit: 10 − 3 = 7. They agree, so the limit is 7 (and f is continuous at 3, since f(3) = 7).

questions.s: Let f(x) = (1 + x)^(1/x) for x ≠ 0. For f to be continuous at x = 0, f(0) must be
questions.e: lim (x → 0) (1 + x)^(1/x) = e, so f(0) must equal e. Saying 1 treats 1^∞ as 1, but this form is indeterminate.

questions.s: A function f is continuous at x = a if
questions.e: Continuity needs f(a) defined, the limit at a to exist, and the two to be equal; the condition lim f(x) = f(a) contains all three. A limit can exist while f(a) is undefined or different, so the second option alone is not enough.

questions.s: The number of points at which f(x) = (x + 1)/(x² − 5x + 6) is discontinuous is
questions.e: x² − 5x + 6 = (x − 2)(x − 3) = 0 at x = 2 and x = 3, where f is undefined; it is continuous elsewhere. So there are 2 points. The zero of the numerator, x = −1, causes no discontinuity.

questions.s: f(x) = (x³ + 8)/(x + 2) is not defined at x = −2. The value of f(−2) that makes f continuous there is
questions.e: x³ + 8 = (x + 2)(x² − 2x + 4), so f(x) = x² − 2x + 4 for x ≠ −2, which tends to 4 + 4 + 4 = 12. A sign slip in the middle term gives 4 − 4 + 4 = 4.

questions.s: The function f(x) = kx² for x ≤ 2 and f(x) = 3 for x > 2 is continuous at x = 2. The value of k is
questions.e: f(2) = 4k and the right-hand limit is 3, so 4k = 3 and k = 3/4. The value 3/2 uses 2k instead of k(2)².

questions.s: The value of lim (x → 3⁻) (x − 3)/|x − 3| is
questions.e: For x < 3, x − 3 < 0 so |x − 3| = −(x − 3), and the fraction equals −1. The value 1 is the right-hand limit.

questions.s: Let f(x) = (sin x)/x for x ≠ 0 and f(0) = 0. Which statement is correct?
o: f is continuous at x = 0 as defined
f has a removable discontinuity at 0
f is discontinuous for every real x
questions.e: lim (x → 0) (sin x)/x = 1 exists but differs from f(0) = 0, so f is discontinuous at 0; redefining f(0) = 1 removes the break. Away from 0, f is a quotient of continuous functions, so it is continuous there.

questions.s: If f(x) = 4x − 3, then [f(x + h) − f(x)]/h, h ≠ 0, equals
questions.e: f(x + h) − f(x) = 4x + 4h − 3 − (4x − 3) = 4h, and dividing by h gives 4, the slope of the line. Forgetting to divide by h leaves 4h.

questions.s: If f(x) = x², then [f(x + h) − f(x)]/h, h ≠ 0, equals
questions.e: (x + h)² − x² = 2xh + h², and dividing by h gives 2x + h. The option 2x is the limit as h → 0, not the quotient itself; 2xh + h² forgets to divide.

questions.s: A taxi in Lahore charges C(d) = 150 + 40d rupees for a ride of d km. The fare for a 5 km ride is
questions.e: C(5) = 150 + 40 × 5 = 150 + 200 = Rs 350. Rs 200 leaves out the fixed charge of Rs 150, and Rs 190 uses d = 1.

questions.s: If f(x) = ax + b, f(1) = 5 and f(3) = 11, then f(5) is
questions.e: Subtracting a + b = 5 from 3a + b = 11 gives 2a = 6, so a = 3 and b = 2. Then f(5) = 15 + 2 = 17. The value 15 forgets b.

questions.s: If f(x + 1) = x² + 3x for every real x, then f(x) is
questions.e: Put t = x + 1, so x = t − 1 and f(t) = (t − 1)² + 3(t − 1) = t² + t − 2. Hence f(x) = x² + x − 2; check f(2) = 4 = 1 + 3. The option x² + 5x + 4 is f(x + 2), found by replacing x with x + 1 instead of x − 1.

questions.s: If f(x) = x² − 1 and g(x) = x + 1, then (f/g)(x) for x ≠ −1 is
questions.e: (f/g)(x) = (x² − 1)/(x + 1) = (x − 1)(x + 1)/(x + 1) = x − 1. The option 1/(x − 1) is g/f, the quotient the wrong way up.

questions.s: The function f(x) = 2x + 3 is defined on the set {−1, 0, 1, 2}. Its range is
questions.e: f(−1) = 1, f(0) = 3, f(1) = 5 and f(2) = 7, so the range is {1, 3, 5, 7}. The set {−1, 0, 1, 2} is the domain, not the range.

questions.s: For which domain is f(x) = x² a one-one function?
questions.e: On [0, ∞) the function x² is strictly increasing, so no two inputs share an output. Any domain containing a pair a and −a with a ≠ 0, such as [−2, 2] or [−1, ∞), gives f(a) = f(−a).

questions.s: If f(x) = ax + b with a > 0 and f(f(x)) = 4x + 9 for all x, then f(x) is
questions.e: f(f(x)) = a(ax + b) + b = a²x + ab + b. So a² = 4, giving a = 2 (as a > 0), and 3b = 9, giving b = 3. The function −2x − 9 also satisfies the equation but has a < 0; 2x + 9/2 forgets the ab term.

questions.s: The value of lim (x → −∞) (2x + 1)/√(x² + 1) is
questions.e: For x < 0, √(x² + 1) = |x|√(1 + 1/x²) = −x√(1 + 1/x²). So the expression is (2 + 1/x)/(−√(1 + 1/x²)) → −2. Taking √(x²) = x gives 2, which is the limit as x → +∞.

questions.s: The value of lim (x → 1) (x² + x − 2)/(x − 1) is
questions.e: x² + x − 2 = (x − 1)(x + 2), so the expression equals x + 2 for x ≠ 1 and the limit is 3. The 0/0 form at x = 1 is not the value of the limit.

questions.s: Compared with the graph of y = f(x), the graph of y = 2f(x) is
o: stretched horizontally by a factor of 2
stretched vertically by a factor of 2
questions.e: Every output is doubled while the inputs stay the same, so each point (a, b) moves to (a, 2b): a vertical stretch by factor 2. A shift up by 2 would be f(x) + 2.

questions.s: Compared with the graph of y = f(x), the graph of y = f(2x) is
o: shrunk horizontally by a factor of 2
stretched horizontally by a factor of 2
stretched vertically by a factor of 2
questions.e: The value f had at x = a now occurs at x = a/2, so each point (a, b) moves to (a/2, b): the graph is compressed towards the y-axis by factor 2. A horizontal stretch by 2 would be f(x/2).

questions.s: The range of f(x) = 4 − |x| is
questions.e: |x| ≥ 0, so 4 − |x| ≤ 4, with 4 reached at x = 0, and it takes every smaller value. The range is (−∞, 4]; [4, ∞) reverses the inequality caused by the minus sign.

questions.s: If f(x) = (x + |x|)/2, then f(−3) + f(3) is
questions.e: f(−3) = (−3 + 3)/2 = 0 and f(3) = (3 + 3)/2 = 3, so the sum is 3. Taking |−3| as −3 gives f(−3) = −3 and a total of 0.

questions.s: The value of lim (x → 0) (3x² − 2x)/x is
questions.e: For x ≠ 0, (3x² − 2x)/x = 3x − 2, which tends to −2. Dropping the sign of the −2x term gives 2.

questions.s: Let f(x) = x² + 1 for x ≠ 2 and f(2) = 3. The value of lim (x → 2) f(x) is
questions.e: The limit depends only on values near 2, not at 2, so lim (x → 2) (x² + 1) = 5. The value 3 is f(2); since 5 ≠ 3, f is discontinuous at 2, but the limit still exists.

questions.s: The inverse of f(x) = log₂ x, x > 0, is
questions.e: y = log₂ x means x = 2ʸ, so f⁻¹(x) = 2ˣ. The option log x / log 2 is just log₂ x again (change of base), and 1/log₂ x is the reciprocal.

questions.s: The value of lim (x → 0) (sin x)/(x + tan x) is
questions.e: Divide top and bottom by x: (sin x/x)/(1 + tan x/x) → 1/(1 + 1) = 1/2. Treating the denominator like x alone gives 1.

questions.s: If f(x) = 2x − 5 and g(x) = (x + 5)/2, then (g∘f)(7) is
questions.e: f(7) = 9 and g(9) = 14/2 = 7. In fact g is the inverse of f, so (g∘f)(x) = x for every x. The value 9 is f(7) alone.

questions.s: The domain of f(x) = (x + 2)/(x − 7) is
questions.e: Only the denominator can make f undefined: x − 7 = 0 at x = 7. The numerator may be zero, which just gives f(−2) = 0, so −2 stays in the domain.

questions.s: If f(x) = x² − 5x, then f(−1) is
The range of f(x) = 2 + √(x − 1) is
questions.e: √(x − 1) takes every value in [0, ∞), so 2 + √(x − 1) takes every value in [2, ∞), with 2 reached at x = 1. The set [1, ∞) is the domain.

questions.s: If f(x) = x + 4 and g(x) = 3x, then (g∘f)(1) is
questions.e: (g∘f)(1) = g(f(1)) = g(5) = 15. The value 7 is (f∘g)(1) = f(3), which applies the functions in the wrong order.

questions.s: The inverse of f(x) = 4 − 3x is
questions.e: y = 4 − 3x gives 3x = 4 − y, so x = (4 − y)/3 and f⁻¹(x) = (4 − x)/3. Check: f((4 − x)/3) = 4 − (4 − x) = x. The option (x − 4)/3 has the sign reversed.

questions.s: Which statement about f(x) = x⁴ + 3x² is correct?
o: It is neither even nor odd
questions.e: Only even powers of x appear, so f(−x) = x⁴ + 3x² = f(x) and f is even. Its graph is symmetric about the y-axis.

questions.s: Which statement about f(x) = sin x + cos x is correct?
o: It is neither even nor odd
questions.e: f(−x) = −sin x + cos x, which equals neither f(x) nor −f(x) (e.g. f(π/2) = 1 but f(−π/2) = −1 and f(0) = 1 ≠ 0). sin x is odd and cos x is even, and their sum is neither.

questions.s: The value of lim (x → −2) (x² + 1)/(x − 1) is
questions.e: The denominator is not zero at x = −2, so substitute: (4 + 1)/(−2 − 1) = 5/(−3) = −5/3. Dropping the sign of the denominator gives 5/3.

questions.s: The value of lim (x → 5) (x² − 25)/(x − 5) is
questions.e: (x² − 25)/(x − 5) = x + 5 for x ≠ 5, so the limit is 10. The value 0 comes from substituting into the numerator alone.

questions.s: The value of lim (x → ∞) (4x³ − 2)/(2x³ + x) is
questions.e: Divide by x³: (4 − 2/x³)/(2 + 1/x²) → 4/2 = 2. With equal degrees the limit is the ratio of leading coefficients, not 4 or ∞.

questions.s: The value of lim (x → 0) 3x/(sin x) is
questions.e: 3x/(sin x) = 3 × x/(sin x) and x/(sin x) → 1, so the limit is 3. The value 1/3 inverts the constant.

questions.s: The value of lim (x → 0) (sin 5x)/(tan 2x) is
questions.e: Write [(sin 5x)/(5x)] × [(2x)/(tan 2x)] × (5/2); the first two factors tend to 1, so the limit is 5/2. Multiplying 5 and 2 gives 10, which is wrong.

questions.s: The value of lim (x → ∞) (1 + 1/x)^(4x) is
questions.e: (1 + 1/x)^(4x) = [(1 + 1/x)ˣ]⁴ → e⁴. The power 4 acts on e, so 4e is wrong.

questions.s: The value of lim (x → 0) (eˣ − 1)/(3x) is
questions.e: (eˣ − 1)/x → 1, so (eˣ − 1)/(3x) → 1/3. The value 3 puts the constant in the numerator.

questions.s: The value of lim (x → 0) (4ˣ − 1)/x is
questions.e: Using lim (aˣ − 1)/x = ln a with a = 4 gives ln 4 (= 2 ln 2). The value 1 is correct only when the base is e.

questions.s: The function f(x) = 2x + 5 for x < 1 and f(x) = 3x + k for x ≥ 1 is continuous at x = 1. The value of k is
questions.e: The left-hand limit is 2 + 5 = 7 and f(1) = 3 + k, so 3 + k = 7 gives k = 4. The value 7 forgets to subtract the 3.

questions.s: Which of the following functions is discontinuous at x = 0?
questions.e: 1/x is not defined at x = 0, so it cannot be continuous there. x², sin x and eˣ are continuous for every real x.

questions.s: Let f(x) = (√(x + 9) − 3)/x for x ≠ 0 and f(0) = k. If f is continuous at x = 0, then k is
questions.e: Multiply by the conjugate: (x + 9 − 9)/[x(√(x + 9) + 3)] = 1/(√(x + 9) + 3) → 1/6, so k = 1/6. Taking only one root, 1/3, forgets to add the 3 in the conjugate.

questions.s: The graph of y = f(x + 3) − 1 is obtained from the graph of y = f(x) by shifting it
questions.e: Replacing x by x + 3 moves the graph 3 units left, and subtracting 1 moves it 1 unit down. Reading x + 3 as a shift to the right is the common mistake.

questions.s: If f(x) = 3x + 2 and g(x) = x² − 1, then the solutions of (f∘g)(x) = 11 are
questions.e: (f∘g)(x) = 3(x² − 1) + 2 = 3x² − 1 = 11, so x² = 4 and x = ±2. Using (g∘f)(x) = (3x + 2)² − 1 instead leads to different values.

questions.s: The value of lim (x → ∞) x[√(x² + 1) − x] is
questions.e: Multiply by the conjugate: x/(√(x² + 1) + x) = 1/(√(1 + 1/x²) + 1) → 1/2. Saying 0 assumes the bracket vanishes, but it is multiplied by x, which grows.

questions.s: The range of f(x) = (x² − 1)/(x² + 1), x ∈ ℝ, is
questions.e: f(x) = 1 − 2/(x² + 1). As x² + 1 runs over [1, ∞), 2/(x² + 1) runs over (0, 2], so f runs over [−1, 1). The value −1 occurs at x = 0, but 1 is never reached, so [−1, 1] is wrong.

questions.s: The domain of f(x) = 1/ln x is
questions.e: ln x needs x > 0, and the denominator must be non-zero, so ln x ≠ 0, i.e. x ≠ 1. Hence the domain is (0, 1) ∪ (1, ∞). The set (0, ∞) forgets that ln 1 = 0.

questions.s: The value of lim (x → 0) (8ˣ − 2ˣ)/x is
questions.e: Split: (8ˣ − 1)/x − (2ˣ − 1)/x → ln 8 − ln 2 = 3 ln 2 − ln 2 = 2 ln 2. Subtracting the bases first gives ln 6, which is wrong; 3 ln 2 is only the first part.

questions.s: Which statement about f(x) = |x| at x = 0 is correct?
o: the left- and right-hand limits at 0 differ
questions.e: From the left |x| = −x → 0 and from the right |x| = x → 0, so the limit is 0 = f(0) and f is continuous. The graph has a sharp corner at 0, but a corner is not a break.

questions.s: The slope of the tangent to the curve y = x³ − 2x at x = 2 is
questions.e: dy/dx = 3x² − 2, so at x = 2 the slope is 12 − 2 = 10. The value 12 forgets the −2 from differentiating −2x, and 4 is y(2), the height of the point rather than the slope.

questions.s: The equation of the tangent to y = x² at the point (3, 9) is
questions.e: dy/dx = 2x = 6 at x = 3, so y − 9 = 6(x − 3), giving y = 6x − 9. y = 6x + 9 has the right slope but does not pass through (3, 9); y = 3x uses x instead of 2x for the slope.

questions.s: The slope of the normal to the curve y = x² + 1 at x = 2 is
questions.e: The tangent slope is dy/dx = 2x = 4, and the normal slope is the negative reciprocal, −1/4. The value 4 is the tangent slope, and 1/4 takes the reciprocal but forgets the minus sign.

questions.s: The equation of the normal to the curve y = 1/x at the point (1, 1) is
questions.e: dy/dx = −1/x² = −1 at x = 1, so the normal has slope 1 and passes through (1, 1): y − 1 = x − 1, i.e. y = x. The line x + y = 2 has slope −1, so it is the tangent, not the normal.

questions.s: The point on the curve y = x² − 4x + 5 at which the tangent is parallel to the x-axis is
questions.e: A tangent parallel to the x-axis has slope 0: dy/dx = 2x − 4 = 0 gives x = 2, and y = 4 − 8 + 5 = 1. The point (−2, 17) comes from solving 2x + 4 = 0, a sign error.

questions.s: The point on the curve y = x² at which the tangent is parallel to the line y = 4x − 1 is
questions.e: Parallel lines have equal slopes, so 2x = 4 and x = 2, giving the point (2, 4). (4, 16) sets x equal to the slope instead of 2x, and at (−2, 4) the slope is −4.

questions.s: The equation of the tangent to the curve y = eˣ at the point where it crosses the y-axis is
questions.e: The curve crosses the y-axis at (0, 1), where dy/dx = e⁰ = 1, so the tangent is y − 1 = x, i.e. y = x + 1. y = ex is the tangent at x = 1 (the one through the origin), and y = 1 has slope 0.

questions.s: The equation of the tangent to the curve y = ln x at x = 1 is
questions.e: At x = 1, y = ln 1 = 0 and dy/dx = 1/x = 1, so the tangent is y − 0 = 1(x − 1), i.e. y = x − 1. y = x has the right slope but passes through the origin, not through (1, 0).

questions.s: The slope of the tangent to the circle x² + y² = 25 at the point (3, 4) is
questions.e: Differentiating implicitly, 2x + 2y(dy/dx) = 0, so dy/dx = −x/y = −3/4 at (3, 4). The value 4/3 is the slope of the radius to (3, 4), which is the normal direction; −4/3 inverts the fraction.

questions.s: Tangents are drawn to the curve y = x² from the point (0, −4). The slopes of these tangents are
questions.e: The tangent at (a, a²) is y = 2ax − a². It passes through (0, −4) when −a² = −4, so a = ±2 and the slopes 2a are ±4. The answer ±2 gives the x-coordinates of the points of contact, not the slopes.

questions.s: The angle that the tangent to y = x² − x at x = 0 makes with the positive direction of the x-axis is
questions.e: dy/dx = 2x − 1 = −1 at x = 0, so tan θ = −1 and θ = 3π/4 (measured in [0, π)). The answer π/4 drops the minus sign, which would give a rising tangent instead of a falling one.

questions.s: If the tangent to a curve at a point has slope m (m ≠ 0), then the normal at that point has slope
questions.e: The normal is perpendicular to the tangent, so the product of their slopes is −1, giving −1/m. The value 1/m forgets the sign and −m forgets the reciprocal; neither line would be perpendicular.

questions.s: The equation of the tangent to y = sin x at x = π is
questions.e: At x = π, y = 0 and dy/dx = cos π = −1, so y − 0 = −(x − π), i.e. y = π − x. y = x − π uses slope +1, forgetting that cos π is −1; y = −x has the right slope but misses the point (π, 0).

questions.s: The tangent to the curve y = 1/x at the point (2, 1/2) meets the coordinate axes at A and B. The area of triangle OAB, where O is the origin, is
questions.e: dy/dx = −1/x² = −1/4, so the tangent is y − 1/2 = −(x − 2)/4. Its x-intercept is 4 and its y-intercept is 1, so the area is ½ × 4 × 1 = 2. The answer 4 is the product of the intercepts without the factor ½.

questions.s: For the curve x = t², y = 2t, the slope of the tangent at the point where t = 1/2 is
questions.e: dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt) = 2/(2t) = 1/t, which is 2 at t = 1/2. The value 1/2 is (dx/dt)/(dy/dt), the reciprocal of the slope.

questions.s: The tangent to the curve y = x³ at the point (1, 1) meets the curve again at
questions.e: The tangent is y = 3x − 2. Solving x³ = 3x − 2 gives x³ − 3x + 2 = (x − 1)²(x + 2) = 0, and the double root x = 1 is the point of contact, so the other point is x = −2, y = −8. The point (−1, −1) lies on the curve but not on the tangent.

questions.s: The equation of the normal to the curve y = x² at the point (1, 1) is
questions.e: The tangent slope is 2, so the normal slope is −1/2: y − 1 = −(x − 1)/2, which gives x + 2y = 3. The line 2x − y = 1 has slope 2, so it is the tangent; x − 2y + 1 = 0 has slope +1/2, a sign error.

questions.s: At a point where the tangent to a curve is parallel to the y-axis, the value of dy/dx is
questions.e: A vertical tangent makes an angle of 90° with the x-axis and tan 90° is undefined, so dy/dx is not defined there (dx/dy = 0 instead). dy/dx = 0 is the condition for a tangent parallel to the x-axis.

questions.s: The point on the curve y = √x at which the tangent has slope 1/4 is
questions.e: dy/dx = 1/(2√x) = 1/4 gives √x = 2, so x = 4 and y = 2. The point (16, 4) comes from 1/√x = 1/4, forgetting the factor 2 in the derivative.

questions.s: The equation of the normal to the curve y = 2x² − 3x + 1 at the point where x = 1 is
questions.e: At x = 1, y = 0 and dy/dx = 4x − 3 = 1, so the normal has slope −1 through (1, 0): y = −(x − 1), i.e. x + y = 1. The line x − y = 1 has slope 1, so it is the tangent.

questions.s: If the line y = 4x + k is a tangent to the curve y = x², then k equals
questions.e: The slope 2x must equal 4, so the point of contact is (2, 4). Substituting in the line, 4 = 8 + k, so k = −4. The value 4 comes from writing k = 8 − 4 with the subtraction reversed.

questions.s: Tangents are drawn to the curve y = x² − 5x + 6 at the points where it cuts the x-axis. The angle between these two tangents is
questions.e: The curve cuts the x-axis at x = 2 and x = 3, where dy/dx = 2x − 5 is −1 and 1. Since the product of the slopes is −1, the tangents are perpendicular. Each tangent makes 45° with the x-axis, which tempts the answer 45°, but the angle between them is 90°.

questions.s: The function f(x) = x² − 6x is increasing for
questions.e: f′(x) = 2x − 6 > 0 when x > 3, so f increases for x > 3 and decreases for x < 3. The answer x > 6 uses the root of x² − 6x = 0 instead of the root of f′(x) = 0.

questions.s: The function f(x) = 5 − 2x is
questions.e: f′(x) = −2 < 0 for every x, so f is decreasing everywhere. The constant term 5 does not make it constant; only its derivative, −2, decides the behaviour.

questions.s: The function f(x) = x³ − 3x is decreasing on the interval
questions.e: f′(x) = 3x² − 3 = 3(x − 1)(x + 1), which is negative between the roots, so f decreases for −1 < x < 1. Outside this interval f′(x) > 0, so 'x < −1 or x > 1' is where f increases.

questions.s: Which of the following is correct for the function f(x) = x³ + 3x?
o: It is increasing for all real x
It is decreasing for all real x
It is increasing only for x > 0
questions.e: f′(x) = 3x² + 3 is at least 3 for every x, so f is increasing on the whole real line and has no stationary point. The option −1 < x < 1 is the decreasing interval of x³ − 3x, where the sign of the 3x term is reversed.

questions.s: The function f(x) = eˣ − x is increasing for
questions.e: f′(x) = eˣ − 1 > 0 exactly when eˣ > 1, i.e. x > 0. For x < 0 we have eˣ < 1, so f decreases there; 'all real x' ignores this, and x > 1 confuses eˣ > 1 with x > 1.

questions.s: The function f(x) = x ln x (x > 0) is increasing for
questions.e: By the product rule f′(x) = ln x + 1, which is positive when ln x > −1, i.e. x > 1/e. The answer x > 1 comes from requiring ln x > 0 and forgetting the +1 term.

questions.s: The function f(x) = 2x³ − 9x² + 12x is decreasing on the interval
questions.e: f′(x) = 6x² − 18x + 12 = 6(x − 1)(x − 2), which is negative between the roots, so f decreases on (1, 2). On (−∞, 1) and (2, ∞) the derivative is positive and f increases.

questions.s: The function f(x) = x³ + kx is increasing for all real x if and only if
questions.e: f′(x) = 3x² + k must be non-negative for every x; its least value is k (at x = 0), so k ≥ 0 is needed. If k < 0, then f′ is negative near x = 0 and f decreases there, so 'k ≤ 0' is wrong.

questions.s: In the interval 0 ≤ x ≤ 2π, the function f(x) = sin x is decreasing on
questions.e: f′(x) = cos x is negative for π/2 < x < 3π/2, so sin x decreases there. On (π, 2π) sin x is negative, but being negative is not the same as decreasing: it rises again after 3π/2.

questions.s: If f′(x) < 0 for every x in an interval (a, b), then on (a, b) the function f is
questions.e: A negative derivative means the tangent slopes downward everywhere in the interval, so f is strictly decreasing there. Concavity depends on the sign of f″(x), not of f′(x).

questions.s: For x > 0, the function f(x) = x + 1/x is decreasing on
questions.e: f′(x) = 1 − 1/x² < 0 when x² < 1, i.e. 0 < x < 1 for positive x. For x > 1 the derivative is positive, so f increases there.

questions.s: The stationary (critical) points of f(x) = x⁴ − 2x² occur at
questions.e: f′(x) = 4x³ − 4x = 4x(x − 1)(x + 1) = 0 gives x = 0, 1 and −1. Cancelling the factor x by mistake loses x = 0 and leaves only ±1.

questions.s: The function f(x) = x² is decreasing on
questions.e: f′(x) = 2x is negative for x < 0, so x² decreases for x < 0 and increases for x > 0. The function is not monotonic on all of ℝ, so neither 'all real x' nor 'no interval' is right.

questions.s: The point of inflection of the curve y = x³ − 6x² + 5 is
questions.e: y″ = 6x − 12 = 0 at x = 2, and y″ changes sign there; y(2) = 8 − 24 + 5 = −11. The points (0, 5) and (4, −27) are where y′ = 3x² − 12x = 0, i.e. the stationary points.

questions.s: The curve y = x³ − 3x² is concave downward for
questions.e: y″ = 6x − 6 < 0 when x < 1, so the curve is concave downward there and concave upward for x > 1. The interval x > 2 comes from y′ = 3x² − 6x, which is about increasing, not concavity.

questions.s: The function f(x) = x e⁻ˣ is increasing for
questions.e: f′(x) = e⁻ˣ − x e⁻ˣ = e⁻ˣ(1 − x). Since e⁻ˣ > 0 always, f′(x) > 0 exactly when x < 1. Forgetting the minus sign from differentiating e⁻ˣ gives e⁻ˣ(1 + x) and a wrong interval.

questions.s: The function f(x) = x² e⁻ˣ is increasing on the interval
questions.e: f′(x) = 2x e⁻ˣ − x² e⁻ˣ = x e⁻ˣ(2 − x), which is positive when 0 < x < 2. Outside [0, 2] the factors x and (2 − x) have opposite signs, so f decreases on (−∞, 0) and on (2, ∞).

questions.s: On the interval (0, π), the function f(x) = cos x is
questions.e: f′(x) = −sin x, and sin x > 0 on (0, π), so f′(x) < 0 and cos x decreases from 1 to −1. 'Increasing then decreasing' describes sin x on this interval, not cos x.

questions.s: The function f(x) = 2x³ − 3x² − 12x + 7 is increasing for
questions.e: f′(x) = 6x² − 6x − 12 = 6(x − 2)(x + 1), which is positive outside the roots, so x < −1 or x > 2. The interval −1 < x < 2 is where f decreases; 'x < −2 or x > 1' swaps the signs of the roots.

questions.s: The least value of f(x) = x² − 4x + 7 is
questions.e: f′(x) = 2x − 4 = 0 at x = 2, and f″(x) = 2 > 0, so the minimum is f(2) = 4 − 8 + 7 = 3. The value 2 is the x-coordinate of the minimum point, not the minimum value.

questions.s: If f′(c) = 0 and f″(c) > 0, then at x = c the function f has
questions.e: f′(c) = 0 makes c a stationary point, and f″(c) > 0 means the curve is concave upward there, so it is a local minimum. A negative second derivative would indicate a maximum.

questions.s: The local maximum value of f(x) = x³ − 3x + 2 is
questions.e: f′(x) = 3x² − 3 = 0 at x = ±1, and f″(x) = 6x is negative at x = −1, so the maximum is f(−1) = −1 + 3 + 2 = 4. The value 0 is the local minimum f(1).

questions.s: The minimum value of f(x) = x + 4/x for x > 0 is
questions.e: f′(x) = 1 − 4/x² = 0 gives x = 2 (x > 0), and f″(x) = 8/x³ > 0 there, so the minimum is 2 + 4/2 = 4. The value 2 is where the minimum occurs; 5 is f(1) or f(4), which are larger.

questions.s: The function f(x) = 2x³ − 15x² + 36x + 1 has a local maximum at
questions.e: f′(x) = 6x² − 30x + 36 = 6(x − 2)(x − 3), so the stationary points are x = 2 and x = 3. f″(x) = 12x − 30 is −6 at x = 2 (maximum) and +6 at x = 3 (minimum).

questions.s: The maximum value of f(x) = sin x + cos x is
questions.e: f′(x) = cos x − sin x = 0 gives tan x = 1, x = π/4, where f = 1/√2 + 1/√2 = √2, and f″(π/4) = −√2 < 0. The value 2 assumes both sin x and cos x can equal 1 at the same x, which never happens.

questions.s: The greatest value of f(x) = x(6 − x) is
questions.e: f(x) = 6x − x², so f′(x) = 6 − 2x = 0 at x = 3 and f″ = −2 < 0. The maximum is f(3) = 3 × 3 = 9. The value 3 is the point where the maximum occurs.

questions.s: The minimum value of f(x) = x eˣ is
questions.e: f′(x) = eˣ(1 + x) = 0 at x = −1, and f′ changes from negative to positive there, so the minimum is f(−1) = −e⁻¹ = −1/e. The value −e comes from writing e⁻¹ as e.

questions.s: The maximum value of f(x) = (ln x)/x for x > 0 is
questions.e: f′(x) = (1 − ln x)/x² = 0 at x = e; f′ is positive before e and negative after, so the maximum is f(e) = 1/e. The value e is the point where the maximum occurs, not the maximum value.

questions.s: The greatest value of f(x) = x³ − 12x on the interval −3 ≤ x ≤ 3 is
questions.e: f′(x) = 3x² − 12 = 0 at x = ±2. Comparing f(−3) = 9, f(−2) = 16, f(2) = −16 and f(3) = −9, the greatest is 16. The value 9 is the endpoint value f(−3), which is smaller than the interior maximum.

questions.s: The least value of f(x) = x³ − 3x² + 1 on the interval −1 ≤ x ≤ 3 is
questions.e: f′(x) = 3x² − 6x = 0 at x = 0 and x = 2. The values are f(−1) = −3, f(0) = 1, f(2) = −3 and f(3) = 1, so the least value is −3, reached at x = −1 and x = 2. The value 1 is the local maximum f(0).

questions.s: For f(x) = x⁴, f′(0) = 0 and f″(0) = 0. At x = 0 the function has
o: neither a maximum nor a minimum
questions.e: The second-derivative test fails, so check the sign of f′(x) = 4x³: it is negative for x < 0 and positive for x > 0, so x = 0 is a local minimum (indeed x⁴ ≥ 0). f″(0) = 0 does not make it an inflection point, because f″(x) = 12x² does not change sign.

questions.s: At x = 0, the curve y = x³ has
questions.e: y′ = 3x² is zero at x = 0 but positive on both sides, so there is no maximum or minimum. y″ = 6x changes sign at x = 0, so the origin is a (stationary) point of inflection.

questions.s: The number of stationary points of the curve y = x³ + x is
questions.e: y′ = 3x² + 1 is never zero, since 3x² + 1 ≥ 1 for every x, so the curve has no stationary points. Solving 3x² − 1 = 0 by a sign slip would wrongly give two points.

questions.s: The local minimum value of f(x) = x⁴ − 8x² is
questions.e: f′(x) = 4x³ − 16x = 4x(x² − 4) = 0 at x = 0, ±2. f″(x) = 12x² − 16 is positive at x = ±2, giving minima f(±2) = 16 − 32 = −16. The value 0 is the local maximum at x = 0.

questions.s: On the interval (0, π), the function f(x) = sin 2x attains its maximum at
questions.e: f′(x) = 2 cos 2x = 0 gives 2x = π/2 or 3π/2, i.e. x = π/4 or 3π/4. f″(x) = −4 sin 2x is negative at π/4, so the maximum is at π/4; x = 3π/4 is the minimum. π/2 is where sin x, not sin 2x, peaks.

questions.s: The maximum value of f(x) = 1/(x² + 2x + 5) is
questions.e: f is largest when the denominator g(x) = x² + 2x + 5 is smallest: g′(x) = 2x + 2 = 0 at x = −1, where g = 4. So the maximum of f is 1/4. The value 1/5 is f(0), which is not the maximum.

questions.s: The local maximum value of f(x) = x³ − 6x² + 9x + 2 is
questions.e: f′(x) = 3x² − 12x + 9 = 3(x − 1)(x − 3). f″(x) = 6x − 12 is negative at x = 1, so the maximum is f(1) = 1 − 6 + 9 + 2 = 6. The value 2 is the local minimum f(3).

questions.s: If f(x) = ax² + bx has a local minimum value −2 at x = 1, then (a, b) is
questions.e: f′(1) = 2a + b = 0 and f(1) = a + b = −2. Subtracting gives a = 2, so b = −4; a > 0 confirms a minimum. (4, −8) also makes f′(1) = 0 but gives f(1) = −4, and (−2, 4) gives a maximum.

questions.s: If f(x) = x³ + ax² + bx has stationary points at x = 1 and x = 3, then
questions.e: f′(x) = 3x² + 2ax + b must equal 3(x − 1)(x − 3) = 3x² − 12x + 9, so 2a = −12 and b = 9, giving a = −6. The pair a = −4, b = 3 comes from matching (x − 1)(x − 3) without the leading factor 3.

questions.s: The minimum value of f(x) = eˣ + e⁻ˣ is
questions.e: f′(x) = eˣ − e⁻ˣ = 0 gives eˣ = e⁻ˣ, so x = 0, and f″(0) = 2 > 0. The minimum is f(0) = 1 + 1 = 2. The value 1 counts only one of the two terms.

questions.s: The local maximum value of f(x) = x(1 − x)² is
questions.e: f′(x) = (1 − x)² − 2x(1 − x) = (1 − x)(1 − 3x), so the stationary points are x = 1 and x = 1/3. f′ changes from positive to negative at 1/3, giving f(1/3) = (1/3)(2/3)² = 4/27. The value 1/3 is where the maximum occurs, not its value.

questions.s: The curve y = x² − 6x + 10 has a stationary point at
questions.e: y′ = 2x − 6 = 0 gives x = 3, where y = 9 − 18 + 10 = 1. The value 1 is the y-coordinate (the minimum value), and x = −3 comes from a sign error in solving 2x − 6 = 0.

questions.s: Two positive numbers have sum 20. The greatest possible value of their product is
questions.e: With numbers x and 20 − x, P = 20x − x² and P′ = 20 − 2x = 0 at x = 10, so the numbers are 10 and 10 and P = 100. Pairs such as 8 and 12 give 96, which is less.

questions.s: A rectangle has area 64 m². Its least possible perimeter is
questions.e: With sides x and 64/x, P = 2x + 128/x and P′ = 2 − 128/x² = 0 at x = 8, so the rectangle is an 8 m square with perimeter 32 m. A 4 m by 16 m rectangle gives 40 m; 16 m is just the sum of two sides.

questions.s: Ali has 200 m of fencing to enclose a rectangular field beside a straight river. No fence is needed along the river. The greatest area he can enclose is
questions.e: Let each side perpendicular to the river be x, so the side parallel to it is 200 − 2x and A = x(200 − 2x). A′ = 200 − 4x = 0 at x = 50, giving A = 50 × 100 = 5000 m². The value 2500 m² is the best square when all four sides are fenced.

questions.s: An open box is made from a square sheet of side 12 cm by cutting equal squares of side x cm from each corner and folding up the sides. The volume is greatest when x equals
questions.e: V = x(12 − 2x)², so V′ = (12 − 2x)² − 4x(12 − 2x) = (12 − 2x)(12 − 6x). V′ = 0 at x = 6 or x = 2; x = 6 gives zero volume, so the maximum is at x = 2 (V = 128 cm³). x = 3 gives only 108 cm³.

questions.s: The product of two positive numbers is 16. The least possible value of their sum is
questions.e: With numbers x and 16/x, S = x + 16/x and S′ = 1 − 16/x² = 0 at x = 4, with S″ > 0, so S = 4 + 4 = 8. Pairs such as 2 and 8 give 10, and 1 and 16 give 17, both larger.

questions.s: The point on the curve y = x² nearest to the point (0, 3) has y-coordinate
questions.e: For a point (x, x²), the squared distance is D = x² + (x² − 3)². Writing u = x², D = u + (u − 3)² and dD/du = 1 + 2(u − 3) = 0 gives u = 5/2. So y = 5/2; the answer 3 assumes the nearest point is level with (0, 3).

questions.s: A closed cylindrical can of fixed volume has the least total surface area when its height h and radius r satisfy
questions.e: With V = πr²h fixed, S = 2πr² + 2V/r and S′ = 4πr − 2V/r² = 0 gives V = 2πr³, so πr²h = 2πr³ and h = 2r: the height equals the diameter. h = r would make the height equal to the radius.

questions.s: A ball is thrown upward so that its height after t seconds is h = 40t − 5t² metres. Its greatest height is
questions.e: dh/dt = 40 − 10t = 0 at t = 4 s, so the greatest height is 40(4) − 5(16) = 160 − 80 = 80 m. The value 160 m forgets to subtract the 5t² term.

questions.s: A shop's daily revenue from selling x items is R(x) = 60x − x² rupees. The maximum daily revenue is
questions.e: R′(x) = 60 − 2x = 0 at x = 30, and R″ = −2 < 0, so the maximum is R(30) = 1800 − 900 = Rs 900. Rs 1800 is only the 60x term at x = 30, without subtracting x².

questions.s: A rectangle is inscribed in a semicircle of radius 5 cm with one side on the diameter. The greatest possible area of the rectangle is
questions.e: Let the base be 2x and height √(25 − x²), so A² = 4x²(25 − x²). Maximising, d(A²)/dx = 200x − 16x³ = 0 gives x² = 25/2, so A = 2x·x = 2 × 25/2 = 25 cm². The value 50 cm² is for a rectangle in the full circle (a square of side 5√2).

questions.s: Positive numbers x and y satisfy x + y = 12. The product x²y is greatest when x equals
questions.e: P = x²(12 − x) = 12x² − x³, so P′ = 24x − 3x² = 3x(8 − x) = 0 gives x = 8 (x = 0 gives P = 0). Then y = 4 and P = 256. The value 6 maximises xy, not x²y.

questions.s: Hamza finds that the cost of running his van is f(v) = v/8 + 200/v rupees per kilometre at a steady speed of v km/h. The speed that makes the cost per kilometre least is
questions.e: f′(v) = 1/8 − 200/v² = 0 gives v² = 1600, so v = 40 km/h, and f″(v) = 400/v³ > 0 confirms a minimum (cost Rs 10 per km). At 50 km/h the cost is 6.25 + 4 = Rs 10.25 per km, which is higher.

questions.s: Two numbers differ by 10. The least possible value of their product is
questions.e: With numbers x and x + 10, P = x² + 10x and P′ = 2x + 10 = 0 at x = −5, so the numbers are −5 and 5 and P = −25. The value 0 (from 0 and 10) is not the least, because a negative product is possible.

questions.s: A rectangle has one vertex at the origin, two sides along the positive axes, and the opposite vertex on the line x + 2y = 8. The greatest possible area of the rectangle is
questions.e: If the far vertex is (x, y) with y = (8 − x)/2, then A = x(8 − x)/2. A′ = (8 − 2x)/2 = 0 at x = 4, so y = 2 and A = 8. The value 16 is the area of the triangle cut off by the line, ½ × 8 × 4.

questions.s: A particle moves along a line so that s = t³ − 3t metres after t seconds. Its acceleration at t = 2 s is
questions.e: v = ds/dt = 3t² − 3 and a = dv/dt = 6t, so at t = 2 the acceleration is 12 m/s². The value 9 is the velocity at t = 2, and 2 is the displacement s(2).

questions.s: A body moves so that s = t³ − 6t² + 4t metres after t seconds. Its acceleration is zero when t equals
questions.e: v = 3t² − 12t + 4 and a = 6t − 12, which is zero at t = 2 s. The value 4 s comes from setting 3t² − 12t = 0, which belongs to the velocity, not the acceleration.

questions.s: The radius of a circular ink spot increases at 2 cm/s. The rate at which its area increases when the radius is 5 cm is
questions.e: A = πr², so dA/dt = 2πr(dr/dt) = 2π × 5 × 2 = 20π cm²/s. The value 10π omits the rate dr/dt = 2, and 25π is just the area at r = 5.

questions.s: Each edge of a cube increases at 3 cm/s. The rate of increase of its volume when the edge is 10 cm is
questions.e: V = x³, so dV/dt = 3x²(dx/dt) = 3 × 100 × 3 = 900 cm³/s. The value 300 cm³/s is dV/dx = 3x² without multiplying by the rate of 3 cm/s.

questions.s: Air is pumped into a spherical balloon so that its volume increases at 400π cm³/s. The rate at which the radius increases when the radius is 5 cm is
questions.e: V = (4/3)πr³ gives dV/dt = 4πr²(dr/dt). With r = 5, 400π = 100π(dr/dt), so dr/dt = 4 cm/s. The value 1/4 cm/s comes from dividing the wrong way round.

questions.s: A 5 m ladder leans against a vertical wall. Its foot slides away from the wall at 1 m/s. When the foot is 3 m from the wall, the top slides down the wall at
questions.e: With x² + y² = 25, differentiating gives x(dx/dt) + y(dy/dt) = 0. At x = 3, y = 4, so 3(1) + 4(dy/dt) = 0 and dy/dt = −3/4: the top slides down at 3/4 m/s. The value 4/3 m/s swaps x and y.

questions.s: The cost of producing x units is C(x) = 500 + 20x + 0.5x² rupees. The marginal cost C′(x) when x = 30 is
questions.e: C′(x) = 20 + 2(0.5)x = 20 + x, so C′(30) = Rs 50. The value Rs 35 comes from differentiating 0.5x² as 0.5x, forgetting the factor 2 from the power.

questions.s: The rate of change of the area of a square with respect to its side, when the side is 4 cm, is
questions.e: A = x², so dA/dx = 2x = 8 cm² per cm at x = 4. The value 16 is the area itself, not its rate of change.

questions.s: Water flows into a vertical cylindrical tank of radius 4 m at 8π m³/min. The water level rises at
questions.e: V = πr²h = 16πh, so dV/dt = 16π(dh/dt). Then 8π = 16π(dh/dt) gives dh/dt = 1/2 m/min. The value 2 m/min divides 8π by 4π, using r instead of r².

questions.s: A point moves along the curve y = x² with x increasing. At which point are x and y changing at the same rate?
questions.e: dy/dt = 2x(dx/dt), so dy/dt = dx/dt when 2x = 1, i.e. x = 1/2 and y = 1/4. At (1, 1), y changes twice as fast as x.

questions.s: Using differentials with y = √x at x = 25, the approximate value of √26 is
questions.e: dy = (1/(2√x))dx = (1/10)(1) = 0.1, so √26 ≈ 5 + 0.1 = 5.1. The value 5.2 forgets the factor ½ in the derivative of √x.

questions.s: Using differentials with y = x^(1/3) at x = 8, the approximate value of (8.12)^(1/3) is
A particle moves so that s = 2t³ − 9t² + 12t metres after t seconds. It is momentarily at rest when
questions.e: At rest means v = ds/dt = 6t² − 18t + 12 = 6(t − 1)(t − 2) = 0, so t = 1 s and t = 2 s. Setting s = 0 instead of v = 0 leads to wrong times such as t = 0.

questions.s: The radius of a circle increases at 0.5 cm/s. When the radius is 10 cm, its circumference increases at
questions.e: C = 2πr, so dC/dt = 2π(dr/dt) = 2π × 0.5 = π cm/s, whatever the radius. Using the area formula instead would bring in r and give a wrong, larger rate.

questions.s: The population of a town t years from now is modelled by P = 1000e^(0.02t). The rate of growth of the population at t = 0 is
questions.e: dP/dt = 1000 × 0.02 × e^(0.02t), which is 20 per year at t = 0. The value 1000 is the population at t = 0, not its rate of change.

questions.s: Zainab, 1.5 m tall, walks away from a 6 m high lamp post at 1.2 m/s. The rate at which the length of her shadow increases is
questions.e: If x is her distance from the post and s her shadow length, similar triangles give s/1.5 = (x + s)/6, so 4.5s = 1.5x and s = x/3. Hence ds/dt = 1.2/3 = 0.4 m/s. The value 1.6 m/s is the speed of the tip of the shadow, x + s.

questions.s: In the Maclaurin series of eˣ, the coefficient of x³ is
questions.e: eˣ = 1 + x + x²/2! + x³/3! + …, so the coefficient of x³ is 1/3! = 1/6. The value 1/3 divides by 3 instead of 3!, and 1/24 is the coefficient of x⁴.

questions.s: The first two non-zero terms of the Maclaurin series of sin x are
questions.e: sin x = x − x³/3! + x⁵/5! − …, so the first two terms are x − x³/6. 1 − x²/2 starts the series for cos x, and x + x³/6 has the wrong sign.

questions.s: In the Maclaurin series of cos x, the coefficient of x⁴ is
questions.e: cos x = 1 − x²/2! + x⁴/4! − …, and the x⁴ term has a plus sign, so the coefficient is 1/4! = 1/24. The value −1/24 gets the alternating sign wrong; −1/2 is the coefficient of x².

questions.s: In the Maclaurin series of ln(1 + x), the coefficient of x³ is
questions.e: ln(1 + x) = x − x²/2 + x³/3 − …, so the coefficient of x³ is +1/3. Note that the denominators are n, not n!, so 1/6 is wrong, and the x³ term is positive.

questions.s: In the Maclaurin series of e^(2x), the coefficient of x³ is
questions.e: Replacing x by 2x in eˣ gives the term (2x)³/3! = 8x³/6, so the coefficient is 4/3. The value 1/6 forgets to cube the 2, and 8/3 divides by 3 instead of 3!.

questions.s: In the Maclaurin series of a function f(x), the coefficient of xⁿ is
questions.e: The Maclaurin series is f(0) + f′(0)x + f″(0)x²/2! + …, so the xⁿ term is f⁽ⁿ⁾(0)xⁿ/n!. The derivatives are evaluated at 0, not at 1, and divided by n!, not by n.

questions.s: The first three terms of the Maclaurin series of e⁻ˣ are
questions.e: Replace x by −x in eˣ = 1 + x + x²/2! + …: the terms are 1 − x + (−x)²/2 = 1 − x + x²/2. The x² term stays positive because (−x)² = x², so 1 − x − x²/2 is wrong.

questions.s: The first three terms of the Maclaurin series of √(1 + x) are
questions.e: For f(x) = (1 + x)^(1/2), f(0) = 1, f′(0) = 1/2 and f″(0) = −1/4, so the x² coefficient is (−1/4)/2! = −1/8, giving 1 + x/2 − x²/8. The option with −x²/4 forgets to divide f″(0) by 2!.

questions.s: Up to the term in x³, the Maclaurin series of tan x is
questions.e: tan x = sin x/cos x ≈ (x − x³/6)(1 + x²/2 + …) = x + x³/2 − x³/6 = x + x³/3. Equivalently f′(0) = 1 and f‴(0) = 2, giving 2/3! = 1/3. The option x + x³/6 is sin x with the sign changed, not tan x.

questions.s: Using the Maclaurin series of sin x, the value of lim(x→0) (sin x − x)/x³ is
questions.e: sin x − x = −x³/6 + x⁵/120 − …, so (sin x − x)/x³ = −1/6 + x²/120 − … → −1/6. The value 1/6 loses the minus sign of the x³ term, and 0 wrongly assumes sin x − x vanishes faster than x³.

questions.s: The Maclaurin series of ln(1 − x) begins
questions.e: Replace x by −x in ln(1 + x) = x − x²/2 + x³/3 − …: every term becomes negative, giving −x − x²/2 − x³/3 − …. The series has no constant term because ln 1 = 0, and x − x²/2 + … is the series for ln(1 + x).

questions.s: In the Maclaurin series of cos 3x, the coefficient of x² is
questions.e: cos 3x = 1 − (3x)²/2! + … = 1 − 9x²/2 + …, so the coefficient is −9/2. The value −3/2 forgets to square the 3, and −9 forgets to divide by 2!.

questions.s: Up to the term in x³, the Maclaurin series of eˣ sin x is
questions.e: Multiply (1 + x + x²/2 + x³/6)(x − x³/6) and keep terms up to x³: x + x² + x³/2 − x³/6 = x + x² + x³/3. The option with x³/2 forgets the −x³/6 from sin x.

questions.s: The Maclaurin series of a function f begins 3 − 2x + 5x² + … . The value of f″(0) is
questions.e: The coefficient of x² is f″(0)/2!, so f″(0)/2 = 5 and f″(0) = 10. The value 5 reads the coefficient as f″(0) itself, forgetting the 2!.

questions.s: Which of the following functions has a Maclaurin series containing only even powers of x?
questions.e: cos x = 1 − x²/2! + x⁴/4! − …, which has only even powers because cos x is an even function. sin x has only odd powers, and eˣ and ln(1 + x) contain both.

questions.s: Using the first three terms of the Maclaurin series of eˣ, the approximate value of e^0.1 is
questions.e: e^0.1 ≈ 1 + 0.1 + (0.1)²/2 = 1 + 0.1 + 0.005 = 1.105. The value 1.110 forgets to divide (0.1)² by 2!, and 1.100 uses only two terms.

questions.s: By definition (first principles), the derivative of f(x) is
questions.e: The derivative is the limit of the difference quotient, the average rate of change [f(x + h) − f(x)]/h, as h → 0. Without dividing by h the limit is simply 0 for a continuous function, so the first option is not the derivative.

questions.s: The value of lim h→0 [(x + h)² − x²]/h is
questions.e: Expanding, (x + h)² − x² = 2xh + h², so the quotient is 2x + h. Letting h → 0 gives 2x. The expression 2x + h is only the quotient before the limit is taken.

questions.s: Using first principles, lim h→0 [√(x + h) − √x]/h for x > 0 equals
questions.e: Multiply top and bottom by √(x + h) + √x: the numerator becomes h, so the quotient is 1/[√(x + h) + √x]. As h → 0 this tends to 1/(2√x). Forgetting that the denominator has two equal terms gives 1/√x.

questions.s: The value of lim h→0 [1/(x + h) − 1/x]/h, x ≠ 0, is
questions.e: Combine the fractions: 1/(x + h) − 1/x = −h/[x(x + h)]. Dividing by h and letting h → 0 gives −1/x². The sign is negative because 1/x decreases as x increases, so 1/x² is wrong.

questions.s: If f(x) = x³, then lim h→0 [f(2 + h) − f(2)]/h equals
questions.e: The limit is f′(2) by definition. Since f′(x) = 3x², f′(2) = 3 × 4 = 12. The value 8 is f(2) itself, not its derivative.

questions.s: The value of lim h→0 [cos(x + h) − cos x]/h is
questions.e: This is the derivative of cos x from first principles. Using cos(x + h) − cos x = −2 sin(x + h/2) sin(h/2) and lim (sin(h/2))/(h/2) = 1, the limit is −sin x. Dropping the minus sign, a common slip, gives sin x.

questions.s: If f′(a) = 4, then lim h→0 [f(a + 3h) − f(a)]/h equals
questions.e: Write the quotient as 3 × [f(a + 3h) − f(a)]/(3h). As h → 0, 3h → 0 as well, so the bracket tends to f′(a) = 4 and the limit is 3 × 4 = 12. Answering 4 ignores that the step is 3h while the division is only by h.

questions.s: For f(x) = x², the value of lim h→0 [f(3 + h) − f(3 − h)]/(2h) is
questions.e: f(3 + h) − f(3 − h) = (9 + 6h + h²) − (9 − 6h + h²) = 12h, so the quotient is 12h/(2h) = 6. This equals f′(3) = 2 × 3 = 6. Answering 12 forgets the factor 2 in the denominator.

questions.s: d/dx (5x⁴ − 3x² + 7) equals
questions.e: Differentiate term by term with d/dx(xⁿ) = nxⁿ⁻¹: 5x⁴ → 20x³, −3x² → −6x and the constant 7 → 0. Keeping the 7 is wrong because the derivative of a constant is zero.

questions.s: The derivative of 1/x³ with respect to x is
questions.e: Write 1/x³ = x⁻³; then d/dx(x⁻³) = −3x⁻⁴ = −3/x⁴. Reducing the power to −2 instead of −4 gives −3/x², a common error with negative indices.

questions.s: If y = x√x, then dy/dx equals
questions.e: x√x = x^(3/2), so dy/dx = (3/2)x^(1/2) = (3/2)√x. The option (2/3)x^(3/2) is a mix-up with integration, where the power rises.

questions.s: d/dx (π² + e³) equals
questions.e: π² + e³ is a constant number (it contains no x), and the derivative of any constant is 0. Treating π or e as the variable gives 2π + 3e², which is wrong here.

questions.s: If y = (x² + 1)/x, then dy/dx at x = 2 is
questions.e: Split first: y = x + 1/x, so dy/dx = 1 − 1/x². At x = 2 this is 1 − 1/4 = 3/4. The value 5/2 is y(2), and 5/4 comes from adding instead of subtracting 1/x².

questions.s: If f(x) = x⁻² + 2√x, then f′(1) equals
questions.e: f′(x) = −2x⁻³ + 2 × 1/(2√x) = −2/x³ + 1/√x. At x = 1, f′(1) = −2 + 1 = −1. Taking the derivative of x⁻² as +2x⁻³ gives 3.

questions.s: For x ≠ 0, d/dx [(x³ − 4x)/x²] equals
questions.e: Simplify first: (x³ − 4x)/x² = x − 4/x = x − 4x⁻¹. Its derivative is 1 + 4x⁻² = 1 + 4/x². The option 1 − 4/x² forgets that d/dx(−4x⁻¹) = +4x⁻².

questions.s: If f(x) = x^(2/3), then f′(8) equals
d/dx (x² sin x) equals
questions.e: By the product rule, (uv)′ = u′v + uv′ with u = x² and v = sin x: 2x sin x + x² cos x. Multiplying the two derivatives gives 2x cos x, which is not the product rule.

questions.s: The derivative of x eˣ is
questions.e: Product rule: d/dx(x eˣ) = 1·eˣ + x·eˣ = eˣ(x + 1). Differentiating only eˣ and keeping x gives x eˣ, which misses the first term.

questions.s: If y = (x² + 1)(x³ − 2), then dy/dx at x = 1 is
questions.e: dy/dx = 2x(x³ − 2) + (x² + 1)(3x²). At x = 1: 2(−1) + 2(3) = −2 + 6 = 4. The value 6 is just the product of the two derivatives 2x × 3x² at x = 1.

questions.s: d/dx (x ln x), x > 0, equals
questions.e: Product rule: 1·ln x + x·(1/x) = ln x + 1. Writing only ln x forgets the second term, x × 1/x = 1.

questions.s: If u(2) = 3, u′(2) = −1, v(2) = 4 and v′(2) = 5, then the derivative of u(x)v(x) at x = 2 is
questions.e: (uv)′ = u′v + uv′ = (−1)(4) + (3)(5) = −4 + 15 = 11. The value −5 is u′v′, which is not the product rule, and 19 ignores the negative sign of u′(2).

questions.s: d/dx (eˣ sin x) equals
questions.e: Product rule: eˣ sin x + eˣ cos x = eˣ(sin x + cos x). Differentiating only the sine factor gives eˣ cos x and misses the eˣ sin x term.

questions.s: If y = x(x − 1)(x − 2), then dy/dx at x = 0 is
questions.e: Expanding, y = x³ − 3x² + 2x, so dy/dx = 3x² − 6x + 2, which is 2 at x = 0. Answering 0 confuses y(0) = 0 with the slope; only the term (x − 1)(x − 2) = 2 survives at x = 0.

questions.s: If y = x² eˣ ln x, then dy/dx equals
o: x eˣ(2 ln x + x ln x)
eˣ(2x ln x + x² ln x + x²)
x eˣ(2 ln x + x ln x + 1)
questions.e: For three factors, (uvw)′ = u′vw + uv′w + uvw′: 2x eˣ ln x + x² eˣ ln x + x² eˣ(1/x). The last term is x eˣ, so dy/dx = x eˣ(2 ln x + x ln x + 1). Writing x² for the last term forgets that d/dx(ln x) = 1/x cancels one x.

questions.s: d/dx [x/(x + 1)] equals
questions.e: Quotient rule: [(x + 1)(1) − x(1)]/(x + 1)² = 1/(x + 1)². Reversing the order in the numerator, x − (x + 1), gives the wrong sign −1/(x + 1)².

questions.s: d/dx [(2x + 3)/(x − 1)] equals
questions.e: Quotient rule: [2(x − 1) − (2x + 3)(1)]/(x − 1)² = (2x − 2 − 2x − 3)/(x − 1)² = −5/(x − 1)². Taking the numerator in the wrong order, u v′ − v u′, flips the sign to +5/(x − 1)².

questions.s: For x ≠ 0, d/dx (sin x / x) equals
questions.e: Quotient rule with u = sin x, v = x: (v u′ − u v′)/v² = (x cos x − sin x)/x². Dividing the derivatives, cos x/1, is not the quotient rule, and (sin x − x cos x)/x² has the numerator in the wrong order.

questions.s: If y = x²/(x² + 1), then dy/dx at x = 1 is
questions.e: dy/dx = [2x(x² + 1) − x²(2x)]/(x² + 1)² = 2x/(x² + 1)². At x = 1 this is 2/4 = 1/2. Forgetting to square the denominator gives 2/2 = 1.

questions.s: If f(1) = 2, f′(1) = 3, g(1) = 1 and g′(1) = −2, then the derivative of f(x)/g(x) at x = 1 is
questions.e: (f/g)′ = (f′g − fg′)/g² = [3(1) − 2(−2)]/1² = 3 + 4 = 7. Ignoring the sign of g′(1) gives 3 − 4 = −1, and f′/g′ = −3/2 is not the quotient rule.

questions.s: d/dx (eˣ/x), x ≠ 0, equals
questions.e: Quotient rule: (x eˣ − eˣ·1)/x² = eˣ(x − 1)/x². The form eˣ(1 − x)/x² comes from writing u v′ − v u′ in the numerator, which reverses the sign.

questions.s: The derivative of 3/(2x − 1) is
questions.e: Write it as 3(2x − 1)⁻¹; then the derivative is −3(2x − 1)⁻² × 2 = −6/(2x − 1)². The option −3/(2x − 1)² forgets the factor 2 from the inner function 2x − 1.

questions.s: If y = (1 − tan x)/(1 + tan x), then dy/dx at x = 0 is
questions.e: Quotient rule: dy/dx = [−sec²x(1 + tan x) − (1 − tan x)sec²x]/(1 + tan x)² = −2sec²x/(1 + tan x)². At x = 0, sec 0 = 1 and tan 0 = 0, so dy/dx = −2. Equivalently y = tan(π/4 − x), whose derivative −sec²(π/4 − x) = −2 at x = 0; −1 forgets that sec²(π/4) = 2.

questions.s: d/dx (3x + 2)⁵ equals
questions.e: Chain rule: 5(3x + 2)⁴ × d/dx(3x + 2) = 5(3x + 2)⁴ × 3 = 15(3x + 2)⁴. The answer 5(3x + 2)⁴ forgets to multiply by the derivative of the inner function.

questions.s: The derivative of √(x² + 9) is
questions.e: Chain rule: (1/2)(x² + 9)^(−1/2) × 2x = x/√(x² + 9). The option 2x/√(x² + 9) forgets the factor 1/2 from the power rule, and 1/(2√(x² + 9)) forgets the inner derivative 2x.

questions.s: If y = (x² − 3)⁴, then dy/dx at x = 2 is
questions.e: dy/dx = 4(x² − 3)³ × 2x. At x = 2, x² − 3 = 1, so dy/dx = 4 × 1 × 4 = 16. The value 4 forgets the inner derivative 2x = 4.

questions.s: d/dx sin(x²) equals
questions.e: Chain rule: cos(x²) × d/dx(x²) = 2x cos(x²). Writing cos(x²) alone misses the inner derivative, and 2x cos x wrongly changes the angle from x² to x.

questions.s: The derivative of sin²x is
questions.e: sin²x = (sin x)², so the derivative is 2 sin x × cos x = sin 2x. The option 2 sin x applies the power rule but forgets to multiply by the derivative of sin x.

questions.s: d/dx [1/(x² + 1)²] equals
questions.e: Write it as (x² + 1)⁻²: the derivative is −2(x² + 1)⁻³ × 2x = −4x/(x² + 1)³. The option −2/(x² + 1)³ forgets the inner derivative 2x, and +4x loses the minus sign of the power rule.

questions.s: If g(x) = f(3x) and f′(6) = 2, then g′(2) equals
questions.e: By the chain rule g′(x) = 3f′(3x), so g′(2) = 3f′(6) = 3 × 2 = 6. Answering 2 forgets the factor 3 from the inner function 3x.

questions.s: For x > 0, d/dx √(1 + √x) equals
questions.e: Apply the chain rule twice: [1/(2√(1 + √x))] × d/dx(√x) = [1/(2√(1 + √x))] × [1/(2√x)] = 1/(4√x √(1 + √x)). The first option stops after the outer square root and misses the factor 1/(2√x).

questions.s: If y = f(x²) and f′(4) = 3, then dy/dx at x = −2 is
questions.e: dy/dx = f′(x²) × 2x. At x = −2, x² = 4, so dy/dx = 3 × (−4) = −12. Using 2x = 4 instead of −4 gives 12, and forgetting the factor 2 gives −6.

questions.s: If y = u³ and u = 2x² + 1, then dy/dx at x = 1 is
questions.e: dy/dx = (dy/du)(du/dx) = 3u² × 4x. At x = 1, u = 3, so dy/dx = 3 × 9 × 4 = 108. The value 27 is dy/du alone, without du/dx = 4.

questions.s: If x² + y² = 25, then dy/dx equals
questions.e: Differentiate both sides with respect to x: 2x + 2y(dy/dx) = 0, so dy/dx = −x/y. The option −y/x inverts the ratio by solving for dx/dy instead.

questions.s: If xy = 6, then dy/dx at the point (2, 3) is
questions.e: Product rule on xy: y + x(dy/dx) = 0, so dy/dx = −y/x = −3/2 at (2, 3). The value −2/3 swaps x and y in the ratio.

questions.s: If x² + xy + y² = 7, then dy/dx equals
questions.e: Differentiating: 2x + (y + x y′) + 2y y′ = 0, so y′(x + 2y) = −(2x + y) and y′ = −(2x + y)/(x + 2y). Missing the y from the product rule on xy gives −2x/(x + 2y).

questions.s: For the parabola y² = 4ax (a constant), dy/dx equals
questions.e: Differentiate: 2y(dy/dx) = 4a, so dy/dx = 4a/(2y) = 2a/y. The option 4a/y forgets that d/dx(y²) = 2y·y′, not y′ alone.

questions.s: If x³ + y³ = 3xy, then dy/dx equals
questions.e: Differentiating: 3x² + 3y² y′ = 3y + 3x y′, so y′(y² − x) = y − x² and y′ = (y − x²)/(y² − x). The option −x²/y² ignores the right side 3xy, whose derivative needs the product rule.

questions.s: If sin y = x, then dy/dx equals
questions.e: Differentiate with respect to x: cos y × (dy/dx) = 1, so dy/dx = 1/cos y = sec y. The option sec x writes the wrong variable; cos y alone is dx/dy, not dy/dx.

questions.s: If x²y + y³ = 10, then dy/dx at the point (3, 1) is
questions.e: Differentiating: 2xy + x² y′ + 3y² y′ = 0, so y′ = −2xy/(x² + 3y²). At (3, 1): −6/(9 + 3) = −1/2. Forgetting the 3y² term gives −6/9 = −2/3.

questions.s: If √x + √y = 3, then dy/dx equals
questions.e: Differentiating: 1/(2√x) + [1/(2√y)] y′ = 0, so y′ = −√y/√x = −√(y/x). The option −√(x/y) inverts the ratio, which happens when solving for dx/dy by mistake.

questions.s: If y² = x, then dy/dx equals
questions.e: Differentiate both sides with respect to x: 2y(dy/dx) = 1, so dy/dx = 1/(2y). The option 2y is dx/dy, the reciprocal of what is asked.

questions.s: If x + y = sin y, then dy/dx equals
questions.e: Differentiating: 1 + y′ = cos y · y′, so y′(cos y − 1) = 1 and y′ = 1/(cos y − 1). Moving the terms carelessly gives 1/(1 − cos y), which has the wrong sign.

questions.s: If x = t² and y = 2t, then dy/dx equals
questions.e: dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt) = 2/(2t) = 1/t. Dividing the other way, (dx/dt)/(dy/dt) = t, gives dx/dy instead.

questions.s: If x = a cos θ and y = a sin θ, then dy/dx equals
questions.e: dx/dθ = −a sin θ and dy/dθ = a cos θ, so dy/dx = a cos θ/(−a sin θ) = −cot θ. Losing the minus sign from the derivative of cos θ gives cot θ.

questions.s: If x = 3t + 1 and y = t³ − 2, then dy/dx at t = 2 is
questions.e: dy/dt = 3t² and dx/dt = 3, so dy/dx = t², which is 4 at t = 2. The value 12 is dy/dt alone, without dividing by dx/dt = 3.

questions.s: If x = eᵗ and y = e⁻ᵗ, then dy/dx equals
questions.e: dy/dt = −e⁻ᵗ and dx/dt = eᵗ, so dy/dx = −e⁻ᵗ/eᵗ = −e^(−2t). The option −1 wrongly cancels e⁻ᵗ against eᵗ as if they were equal.

questions.s: If x = t + 1/t and y = t − 1/t, then dy/dx equals
questions.e: dx/dt = 1 − 1/t² and dy/dt = 1 + 1/t². Multiplying both by t², dy/dx = (t² + 1)/(t² − 1). The first option is dx/dy, the ratio taken upside down.

questions.s: If x = sec θ and y = tan θ, then dy/dx equals
questions.e: dy/dθ = sec²θ and dx/dθ = sec θ tan θ, so dy/dx = sec θ/tan θ = (1/cos θ)(cos θ/sin θ) = cosec θ. Its reciprocal, sin θ, is dx/dy.

questions.s: For the cycloid x = a(θ − sin θ), y = a(1 − cos θ), dy/dx equals
questions.e: dy/dx = a sin θ/[a(1 − cos θ)]. Using sin θ = 2 sin(θ/2)cos(θ/2) and 1 − cos θ = 2 sin²(θ/2), this is cos(θ/2)/sin(θ/2) = cot(θ/2). The option tan(θ/2) is the reciprocal, which comes from dividing dx/dθ by dy/dθ.

questions.s: If x = t² and y = t³, then d²y/dx² equals
questions.e: dy/dx = 3t²/(2t) = 3t/2. Then d²y/dx² = d/dt(3t/2) ÷ dx/dt = (3/2)/(2t) = 3/(4t). Stopping at d/dt(3t/2) = 3/2 forgets to divide by dx/dt.

questions.s: If x = 2 cos t and y = 3 sin t, then dy/dx at t = π/4 is
questions.e: dy/dx = 3 cos t/(−2 sin t) = −(3/2)cot t. At t = π/4, cot t = 1, so dy/dx = −3/2. The value −2/3 inverts the ratio of the coefficients.

questions.s: d/dx (tan x) equals
