questions.e: tan x = sin x/cos x, and the quotient rule gives (cos²x + sin²x)/cos²x = 1/cos²x = sec²x. The option sec x tan x is the derivative of sec x, and −cosec²x is that of cot x.

questions.s: The derivative of cosec x is
questions.e: cosec x = (sin x)⁻¹, so its derivative is −(sin x)⁻² cos x = −(1/sin x)(cos x/sin x) = −cosec x cot x. Dropping the minus sign gives cosec x cot x; derivatives of the co-functions carry a minus sign.

questions.s: d/dx (cos 3x) equals
questions.e: By the chain rule, d/dx cos(3x) = −sin(3x) × 3 = −3 sin 3x. The option −sin 3x forgets the factor 3 from the inner function 3x.

questions.s: d/dx (sec x + tan x) equals
questions.e: d/dx sec x = sec x tan x and d/dx tan x = sec²x, so the sum is sec x tan x + sec²x = sec x(tan x + sec x). The option sec x tan x + 1 wrongly takes the derivative of tan x as 1.

questions.s: If y = cot 2x, then dy/dx at x = π/8 is
questions.e: dy/dx = −2 cosec²(2x). At x = π/8, 2x = π/4 and cosec²(π/4) = 2, so dy/dx = −2 × 2 = −4. Forgetting the factor 2 from the chain rule gives −2.

questions.s: d/dx (sin x cos x) equals
questions.e: Product rule: cos x · cos x + sin x(−sin x) = cos²x − sin²x = cos 2x. Writing sin x cos x = (1/2)sin 2x gives the same result; 2 cos 2x forgets the factor 1/2, and cos²x + sin²x has the wrong sign in the second term.

questions.s: The derivative of cos³x is
questions.e: Chain rule: 3cos²x × d/dx(cos x) = 3cos²x(−sin x) = −3 cos²x sin x. The option 3 cos²x forgets to multiply by the derivative of cos x.

questions.s: If y = sin x°, where x is measured in degrees, then dy/dx equals
questions.e: x° = πx/180 radians, so y = sin(πx/180) and dy/dx = (π/180)cos(πx/180) = (π/180) cos x°. The rule d/dx sin x = cos x holds only in radians, so cos x° alone is wrong; 180/π uses the conversion upside down.

questions.s: For 0 < x < π/4, if y = √(1 + sin 2x), then dy/dx equals
questions.e: 1 + sin 2x = sin²x + cos²x + 2 sin x cos x = (sin x + cos x)², and sin x + cos x > 0 here, so y = sin x + cos x. Then dy/dx = cos x − sin x. The option cos x + sin x is y itself, not its derivative.

questions.s: d/dx [sin x/(1 + cos x)] equals
questions.e: sin x/(1 + cos x) = 2 sin(x/2)cos(x/2)/[2cos²(x/2)] = tan(x/2). Its derivative is (1/2)sec²(x/2). The option sec²(x/2) forgets the factor 1/2 from the inner function x/2.

questions.s: If y = tan²x, then dy/dx at x = π/4 is
questions.e: dy/dx = 2 tan x sec²x. At x = π/4, tan x = 1 and sec²x = 2, so dy/dx = 2 × 1 × 2 = 4. The value 2 uses sec²(π/4) = 1, which is wrong because sec(π/4) = √2.

questions.s: d/dx (2 sin x − 3 cos x) equals
questions.e: d/dx(2 sin x) = 2 cos x and d/dx(−3 cos x) = −3(−sin x) = 3 sin x, so the sum is 2 cos x + 3 sin x. Forgetting that d/dx cos x = −sin x gives 2 cos x − 3 sin x.

questions.s: For −1 < x < 1, d/dx (sin⁻¹x) equals
questions.e: If y = sin⁻¹x then sin y = x, so cos y · y′ = 1 and y′ = 1/cos y = 1/√(1 − x²), taking cos y > 0 for −π/2 < y < π/2. The negative version, −1/√(1 − x²), is the derivative of cos⁻¹x.

questions.s: d/dx [tan⁻¹(2x)] equals
questions.e: d/dx tan⁻¹u = u′/(1 + u²) with u = 2x: 2/(1 + 4x²). The option 1/(1 + 4x²) forgets the chain rule factor 2, and 2/(1 + 2x²) forgets to square the 2.

questions.s: For −1 < x < 1, d/dx [cos⁻¹(x²)] equals
questions.e: d/dx cos⁻¹u = −u′/√(1 − u²) with u = x², so the derivative is −2x/√(1 − x⁴). The option −2x/√(1 − x²) forgets that u² = x⁴, and −1/√(1 − x⁴) leaves out u′ = 2x.

questions.s: For x > 1, d/dx (sec⁻¹x) equals
questions.e: If y = sec⁻¹x, then sec y = x, so sec y tan y · y′ = 1 and y′ = 1/(sec y tan y) = 1/(x√(x² − 1)), since tan y = √(x² − 1) > 0 here. The negative form belongs to cosec⁻¹x.

questions.s: d/dx (cot⁻¹x) equals
questions.e: Since cot⁻¹x = π/2 − tan⁻¹x, its derivative is −1/(1 + x²). The option −cosec²x is the derivative of cot x, not of its inverse.

questions.s: For x < 1, d/dx tan⁻¹[(1 + x)/(1 − x)] equals
questions.e: (1 + x)/(1 − x) = (tan π/4 + tan θ)/(1 − tan π/4 tan θ) with x = tan θ, so the function equals π/4 + tan⁻¹x for x < 1. Its derivative is 1/(1 + x²). The option 1/(1 − x)² is only part of the chain rule: the full working also divides by 1 + [(1 + x)/(1 − x)]².

questions.s: For −1 < x < 1, d/dx sin⁻¹[2x/(1 + x²)] equals
questions.e: Put x = tan θ: 2x/(1 + x²) = sin 2θ, so for |x| < 1 the function is 2θ = 2 tan⁻¹x. Its derivative is 2/(1 + x²). Answering 1/(1 + x²) forgets the factor 2 from 2θ.

questions.s: For −1 < x < 1, d/dx (x sin⁻¹x) equals
questions.e: Product rule: 1·sin⁻¹x + x · 1/√(1 − x²) = sin⁻¹x + x/√(1 − x²). The option x/√(1 − x²) differentiates only the second factor and loses the sin⁻¹x term.

questions.s: If y = tan⁻¹(√x), then dy/dx at x = 1 is
questions.e: dy/dx = [1/(1 + x)] × [1/(2√x)]. At x = 1 this is (1/2)(1/2) = 1/4. Answering 1/2 forgets the chain-rule factor 1/(2√x).

questions.s: For −1 < x < 1, d/dx (sin⁻¹x + cos⁻¹x) equals
questions.e: The derivatives are 1/√(1 − x²) and −1/√(1 − x²), which cancel to 0. This matches the identity sin⁻¹x + cos⁻¹x = π/2, a constant; π/2 is the value of the sum, not its derivative.

questions.s: d/dx (e^(3x)) equals
questions.e: Chain rule: e^(3x) × d/dx(3x) = 3e^(3x). The option 3x e^(3x − 1) wrongly applies the power rule, which is only for xⁿ with a constant power.

questions.s: The derivative of 2ˣ is
questions.e: 2ˣ = e^(x ln 2), so its derivative is ln 2 × e^(x ln 2) = 2ˣ ln 2. The option x 2ˣ⁻¹ treats the variable power as if it were a constant power.

questions.s: d/dx [e^(x²)] equals
questions.e: Chain rule: e^(x²) × d/dx(x²) = 2x e^(x²). Writing e^(x²) alone forgets the inner derivative 2x.

questions.s: If y = e^(sin x), then dy/dx at x = 0 is
questions.e: dy/dx = cos x · e^(sin x). At x = 0, cos 0 = 1 and e^(sin 0) = e⁰ = 1, so dy/dx = 1. Answering 0 confuses sin 0 = 0 with the value of the derivative.

questions.s: d/dx [(eˣ + e⁻ˣ)/2] equals
questions.e: d/dx eˣ = eˣ and d/dx e⁻ˣ = −e⁻ˣ, so the derivative is (eˣ − e⁻ˣ)/2. Keeping the plus sign forgets the chain-rule factor −1 from the power −x.

questions.s: d/dx (e^(2x) cos x) equals
questions.e: Product rule: 2e^(2x) cos x + e^(2x)(−sin x) = e^(2x)(2 cos x − sin x). The option e^(2x)(cos x − sin x) forgets the factor 2 in the derivative of e^(2x).

questions.s: If a > 0 is a constant, d/dx [a^(x²)] equals
questions.e: a^(x²) = e^(x² ln a), so its derivative is e^(x² ln a) × 2x ln a = 2x a^(x²) ln a. The option 2x a^(x²) treats a as if it were e, forgetting the factor ln a.

questions.s: If y = eˣ/(1 + eˣ), then dy/dx at x = 0 is
questions.e: Quotient rule: dy/dx = [eˣ(1 + eˣ) − eˣ·eˣ]/(1 + eˣ)² = eˣ/(1 + eˣ)². At x = 0 this is 1/2² = 1/4. The value 1/2 is y(0), not the derivative.

questions.s: d/dx [e^(5 − 2x)] equals
questions.e: Chain rule: e^(5 − 2x) × d/dx(5 − 2x) = −2e^(5 − 2x). Losing the minus sign of the inner derivative gives 2e^(5 − 2x).

questions.s: For x > 0, d/dx [ln(3x)] equals
questions.e: ln(3x) = ln 3 + ln x, and ln 3 is a constant, so the derivative is 1/x. By the chain rule as well, 3/(3x) = 1/x; the option 3/x forgets to divide by 3x.

questions.s: d/dx [ln(x² + 1)] equals
questions.e: d/dx ln u = u′/u with u = x² + 1, giving 2x/(x² + 1). The option 1/(x² + 1) forgets to multiply by u′ = 2x.

questions.s: For x > 0, d/dx (log₁₀x) equals
questions.e: Change of base: log₁₀x = ln x/ln 10, so the derivative is 1/(x ln 10). The option 1/x holds only for the natural logarithm, base e.

questions.s: For 0 < x < π, d/dx [ln(sin x)] equals
questions.e: d/dx ln u = u′/u: cos x/sin x = cot x. The option 1/sin x forgets to multiply by the derivative of sin x, which is cos x.

questions.s: For 0 < x < π/2, d/dx [ln(sec x + tan x)] equals
questions.e: The derivative is (sec x tan x + sec²x)/(sec x + tan x) = sec x(tan x + sec x)/(sec x + tan x) = sec x. The option 1/(sec x + tan x) forgets to multiply by the derivative of the inside.

questions.s: For x > 0, if y = xˣ, then dy/dx equals
questions.e: Take logs: ln y = x ln x, so (1/y)y′ = ln x + 1 and y′ = xˣ(1 + ln x). The option x·xˣ⁻¹ uses the power rule, and xˣ ln x uses the exponential rule; neither works when both base and power vary.

questions.s: For −1 < x < 1, d/dx ln√[(1 + x)/(1 − x)] equals
questions.e: Use log laws first: y = (1/2)[ln(1 + x) − ln(1 − x)], so y′ = (1/2)[1/(1 + x) + 1/(1 − x)] = (1/2) × 2/(1 − x²) = 1/(1 − x²). The option 2/(1 − x²) forgets the factor 1/2 from the square root.

questions.s: For x > 1, d/dx [ln(ln x)] equals
questions.e: Chain rule: [1/ln x] × d/dx(ln x) = (1/ln x)(1/x) = 1/(x ln x). The option 1/ln x stops after the outer logarithm and forgets the inner derivative 1/x.

questions.s: If y = x⁴, then d²y/dx² equals
questions.e: dy/dx = 4x³ and d²y/dx² = 12x². The option 24x is the third derivative, one step too far, and 4x³ is only the first derivative.

questions.s: If y = sin x, then d²y/dx² equals
questions.e: dy/dx = cos x and d²y/dx² = −sin x, so y″ = −y. The option −cos x comes from applying the minus sign at the first step, which belongs to the derivative of cos x.

questions.s: If y = e^(2x), then d²y/dx² equals
questions.e: Each differentiation brings down a factor 2: y′ = 2e^(2x) and y″ = 4e^(2x). The option 2e^(2x) is only the first derivative.

questions.s: If y = ln x (x > 0), then d³y/dx³ equals
questions.e: y′ = x⁻¹, y″ = −x⁻², y‴ = 2x⁻³ = 2/x³. The option −1/x² is the second derivative, and −2/x³ misses that two minus signs multiply to plus.

questions.s: If y = x⁵, then d⁵y/dx⁵ equals
questions.e: Differentiating x⁵ five times gives 5 × 4 × 3 × 2 × 1 = 5! = 120, a constant. The value 0 is the sixth derivative, since the derivative of the constant 120 is zero.

questions.s: If y = A cos 3x + B sin 3x, where A and B are constants, then d²y/dx² + ky = 0 when k equals
questions.e: y′ = −3A sin 3x + 3B cos 3x and y″ = −9A cos 3x − 9B sin 3x = −9y. So y″ + 9y = 0 and k = 9. Choosing 3 forgets that the factor 3 appears twice, once for each differentiation.

questions.s: If y = x eˣ, then d²y/dx² equals
questions.e: y′ = eˣ + x eˣ = eˣ(x + 1). Differentiating again: y″ = eˣ(x + 1) + eˣ = eˣ(x + 2). The option eˣ(x + 1) is only the first derivative.

questions.s: If y = cos 2x, then d⁴y/dx⁴ equals
questions.e: y′ = −2 sin 2x, y″ = −4 cos 2x, y‴ = 8 sin 2x and y⁽⁴⁾ = 16 cos 2x. After four steps the sign returns to positive; −16 cos 2x loses track of the signs, and 8 cos 2x uses 2 × 4 instead of 2⁴.

questions.s: If f(x) = x³ − 6x² + 4x, then f″(1) equals
questions.e: f′(x) = 3x² − 12x + 4 and f″(x) = 6x − 12, so f″(1) = 6 − 12 = −6. The value −5 is f′(1), the first derivative, not the second.

questions.s: If y = tan⁻¹x, which of the following is correct?
questions.e: y′ = 1/(1 + x²), so (1 + x²)y′ = 1. Differentiating both sides: 2xy′ + (1 + x²)y″ = 0. The relation (1 − x²)y″ − xy′ = 0 is the one satisfied by y = sin⁻¹x, not tan⁻¹x.

questions.s: If y = x⁵, then dy/dx equals
questions.e: By the power rule d/dx(xⁿ) = nxⁿ⁻¹, so d/dx(x⁵) = 5x⁴. The option x⁶/6 is the antiderivative (integration), not the derivative.

questions.s: The derivative of sin 3x with respect to x is
questions.e: By the chain rule, d/dx sin(3x) = cos(3x) × 3 = 3 cos 3x. Writing cos 3x forgets the derivative of the inner function 3x, and the minus sign belongs to the derivative of cos, not sin.

questions.s: The derivative of x²eˣ is
questions.e: By the product rule, d/dx(x²eˣ) = 2x·eˣ + x²·eˣ = eˣ(x² + 2x). The option 2x eˣ differentiates each factor and multiplies the results, which is not the product rule.

questions.s: If y = x/(x + 1), then dy/dx equals
questions.e: By the quotient rule, dy/dx = [(x + 1)(1) − x(1)]/(x + 1)² = 1/(x + 1)². The option −1/(x + 1)² comes from subtracting the terms of the numerator in the wrong order.

questions.s: The derivative of (2x + 1)⁵ is
questions.e: By the chain rule, d/dx(2x + 1)⁵ = 5(2x + 1)⁴ × 2 = 10(2x + 1)⁴. The option 5(2x + 1)⁴ forgets to multiply by 2, the derivative of the inside.

questions.s: The derivative of ln(x² + 1) is
questions.e: d/dx ln u = u′/u, so with u = x² + 1 the derivative is 2x/(x² + 1). The option 1/(x² + 1) forgets the chain-rule factor 2x.

questions.s: The derivative of tan⁻¹x is
questions.e: If y = tan⁻¹x then tan y = x, so sec²y (dy/dx) = 1 and dy/dx = 1/(1 + tan²y) = 1/(1 + x²). 1/√(1 − x²) is the derivative of sin⁻¹x, and sec² x is the derivative of tan x.

questions.s: The derivative of sin⁻¹(2x) is
questions.e: d/dx sin⁻¹u = u′/√(1 − u²); with u = 2x this is 2/√(1 − 4x²). The option 1/√(1 − 4x²) forgets the factor u′ = 2, and 2/√(1 − 2x²) forgets to square the 2.

questions.s: The value of lim(h→0) [(x + h)² − x²]/h is
questions.e: (x + h)² − x² = 2xh + h², so the quotient is 2x + h, which tends to 2x as h → 0. This is d/dx(x²) from first principles; 2x + h is the quotient before taking the limit.

questions.s: If x² + xy + y² = 7, then dy/dx equals
questions.e: Differentiating implicitly, 2x + (y + x dy/dx) + 2y dy/dx = 0, so (x + 2y) dy/dx = −(2x + y) and dy/dx = −(2x + y)/(x + 2y). The option −x/y ignores the xy term, which needs the product rule.

questions.s: If x = a cos t and y = a sin t, then dy/dx equals
questions.e: dy/dt = a cos t and dx/dt = −a sin t, so dy/dx = (a cos t)/(−a sin t) = −cot t. The option −tan t divides dx/dt by dy/dt, the wrong way round.

questions.s: If y = sin 2x, then d²y/dx² equals
questions.e: dy/dx = 2 cos 2x and d²y/dx² = −4 sin 2x, each step bringing a factor 2 from the chain rule. The option −2 sin 2x includes the factor 2 only once.

questions.s: The derivative of eˣ ln x (x > 0) is
questions.e: By the product rule, d/dx(eˣ ln x) = eˣ ln x + eˣ(1/x) = eˣ(ln x + 1/x). The option eˣ/x multiplies the two separate derivatives, which is not the product rule.

questions.s: If y = xˣ (x > 0), then dy/dx equals
questions.e: Take logs: ln y = x ln x, so (1/y) dy/dx = ln x + 1 and dy/dx = xˣ(1 + ln x). The option x·xˣ⁻¹ treats the exponent as a constant (power rule), and xˣ ln x treats the base as a constant.

questions.s: For a constant a > 0, a ≠ 1, the derivative of aˣ is
questions.e: Writing aˣ = e^(x ln a) gives d/dx aˣ = ln a · e^(x ln a) = aˣ ln a. The option x aˣ⁻¹ wrongly applies the power rule, which is for a variable base and constant exponent.

questions.s: If y = e^(ax), where a is a constant, then the nth derivative of y is
questions.e: Each differentiation of e^(ax) multiplies it by a, so y′ = a e^(ax), y″ = a² e^(ax) and in general yₙ = aⁿ e^(ax). The option n a e^(ax) adds the factors a instead of multiplying them, and the exponent ax never changes.

questions.s: If y = sin⁻¹x, then (1 − x²)y″ − xy′ equals
questions.e: y′ = (1 − x²)^(−1/2), so y″ = x(1 − x²)^(−3/2). Then (1 − x²)y″ = x(1 − x²)^(−1/2) = xy′, and the expression is 0. Answering 1 comes from multiplying y′ by √(1 − x²) instead of differentiating it.

questions.s: The derivative of sec x is
questions.e: sec x = (cos x)⁻¹, so its derivative is −(cos x)⁻²(−sin x) = sin x/cos²x = sec x tan x. sec² x is the derivative of tan x, and the minus sign belongs to the derivative of cosec x.

questions.s: The derivative of cos²x is
questions.e: By the chain rule, d/dx (cos x)² = 2 cos x × (−sin x) = −2 sin x cos x = −sin 2x. The option sin 2x forgets that the derivative of cos x is −sin x.

questions.s: The slope of the tangent to the curve y = 3x² − x at x = 1 is
questions.e: dy/dx = 6x − 1, which is 5 at x = 1. The value 6 forgets the −1 from differentiating −x, and 2 is the height y(1) = 3 − 1.

questions.s: The equation of the normal to the curve y = x³ at the point (1, 1) is
questions.e: The tangent slope is 3x² = 3, so the normal slope is −1/3: y − 1 = −(x − 1)/3, i.e. x + 3y = 4. The line 3x − y = 2 is the tangent, and x − 3y + 2 = 0 has slope +1/3, a sign error.

questions.s: The function f(x) = x³ − 12x is increasing for
questions.e: f′(x) = 3x² − 12 = 3(x − 2)(x + 2) is positive outside the roots, so f increases for x < −2 and for x > 2. The interval −2 < x < 2 is where f decreases, and 'x > 2 only' misses the left-hand interval.

questions.s: The minimum value of f(x) = x² − 8x + 20 is
questions.e: f′(x) = 2x − 8 = 0 at x = 4 and f″ = 2 > 0, so the minimum is f(4) = 16 − 32 + 20 = 4. The value 20 is f(0), the y-intercept, which is not the least value.

questions.s: The greatest value of f(x) = x³ − 3x on the interval 0 ≤ x ≤ 2 is
questions.e: f′(x) = 3x² − 3 = 0 at x = 1 in the interval, where f(1) = −2 is a minimum. Comparing with the endpoints f(0) = 0 and f(2) = 8 − 6 = 2, the greatest value is 2. Checking only the stationary point would wrongly give −2.

questions.s: Bilal has 60 m of fencing to enclose a rectangular garden on all four sides. The greatest area he can enclose is
questions.e: With sides x and 30 − x, A = 30x − x² and A′ = 30 − 2x = 0 at x = 15, so the garden is a 15 m square of area 225 m². A 10 m by 20 m rectangle gives only 200 m².

questions.s: A car moves so that its distance is s = 4t² + 2t metres after t seconds. Its velocity at t = 3 s is
questions.e: v = ds/dt = 8t + 2, so at t = 3 the velocity is 24 + 2 = 26 m/s. The value 42 is the distance s(3) = 36 + 6, not the velocity, and 8 m/s is the acceleration.

questions.s: In the Maclaurin series of ln(1 + x), the coefficient of x² is
questions.e: For f(x) = ln(1 + x), f′(x) = 1/(1 + x) and f″(x) = −1/(1 + x)², so f″(0)/2! = −1/2. The value 1/2 misses the alternating sign of the series x − x²/2 + x³/3 − ….

questions.s: Up to the term in x³, the Maclaurin series of sin 2x is
questions.e: Replace x by 2x in sin x = x − x³/6 + …: 2x − (2x)³/6 = 2x − 8x³/6 = 2x − 4x³/3. The option 2x − x³/3 forgets to cube the 2, and 2x − 8x³/3 divides by 3 instead of 3!.

questions.s: The derivative of tan⁻¹[(1 + x)/(1 − x)], x ≠ 1, is
questions.e: With u = (1 + x)/(1 − x), u′ = 2/(1 − x)² and 1 + u² = 2(1 + x²)/(1 − x)², so u′/(1 + u²) = 1/(1 + x²). This matches tan⁻¹u = π/4 + tan⁻¹x. The value 2/(1 + x²) forgets the factor 2 in 1 + u².

questions.s: If y = eˣ sin x, then y″ − 2y′ + 2y equals
questions.e: y′ = eˣ(sin x + cos x) and y″ = eˣ(sin x + cos x + cos x − sin x) = 2eˣ cos x. Then y″ − 2y′ + 2y = 2eˣ cos x − 2eˣ sin x − 2eˣ cos x + 2eˣ sin x = 0. The option 2eˣ cos x is y″ alone.

questions.s: The value of ∫₀² (3x² + 1) dx is
questions.e: An antiderivative is x³ + x, so the value is (8 + 2) − 0 = 10. The answer 8 integrates only the 3x² term and forgets that ∫₀² 1 dx = 2.

questions.s: The value of ∫₁⁴ (1/√x) dx is
questions.e: ∫x^(−1/2) dx = 2√x, so the value is 2√4 − 2√1 = 4 − 2 = 2. The value 1 comes from forgetting the factor 2 and computing √4 − √1.

questions.s: The value of ∫₀^π sin x dx is
questions.e: [−cos x]₀^π = −cos π + cos 0 = 1 + 1 = 2. Getting −2 comes from writing the antiderivative of sin x as +cos x; 0 would be the value over a full period from 0 to 2π.

questions.s: The value of ∫₀¹ eˣ dx is
questions.e: [eˣ]₀¹ = e¹ − e⁰ = e − 1. Writing e forgets that the lower limit gives e⁰ = 1, not 0.

questions.s: The value of ∫₁^e (1/x) dx is
questions.e: [ln x]₁^e = ln e − ln 1 = 1 − 0 = 1. The value e − 1 treats 1/x as if its antiderivative were x.

questions.s: The value of ∫₀^(π/3) sec²x dx is
questions.e: Since d/dx(tan x) = sec²x, the value is tan(π/3) − tan 0 = √3. The option 1/√3 is tan(π/6), obtained by mixing up the angles; 2 is sec(π/3).

questions.s: The value of ∫₋₂¹ |x| dx is
questions.e: Split at 0: ∫₋₂⁰ (−x) dx = 2 and ∫₀¹ x dx = 1/2, giving 5/2. Ignoring the modulus gives [x²/2]₋₂¹ = 1/2 − 2 = −3/2, which cannot be right because |x| ≥ 0.

questions.s: If ∫₀³ f(x) dx = 7 and ∫₀⁵ f(x) dx = 12, then ∫₃⁵ f(x) dx equals
questions.e: ∫₀⁵ f = ∫₀³ f + ∫₃⁵ f, so ∫₃⁵ f = 12 − 7 = 5. Adding the two given values (19) uses the additivity property the wrong way round.

questions.s: The value of ∫₂² (x⁵ − 3x) dx is
questions.e: When the upper and lower limits are equal the definite integral is 0, whatever the integrand. The value 26 is just f(2) = 32 − 6, which is not an integral.

questions.s: If ∫₁⁴ g(x) dx = 6, then ∫₄¹ 2g(x) dx equals
questions.e: Reversing the limits changes the sign and the constant 2 comes outside: ∫₄¹ 2g dx = −2 × 6 = −12. The answer 12 forgets the sign change; −6 forgets the factor 2.

questions.s: The value of ∫₋₂² (x³ − 5x) dx is
questions.e: x³ − 5x is an odd function, and the integral of an odd function over [−a, a] is 0. Directly: [x⁴/4 − 5x²/2] gives (4 − 10) − (4 − 10) = 0.

questions.s: The value of ∫₋₁¹ (x³ + 3x² + x) dx is
questions.e: x³ and x are odd, so their integrals over [−1, 1] vanish; 3x² is even, so its integral is 2∫₀¹ 3x² dx = 2. Choosing 0 wrongly treats the whole integrand as odd.

questions.s: The value of ∫ from −π/2 to π/2 of (sin x + cos x) dx is
questions.e: sin x is odd, so it contributes 0; cos x is even, so it contributes 2∫₀^(π/2) cos x dx = 2[sin x]₀^(π/2) = 2. The value 0 assumes both terms are odd.

questions.s: The value of ∫₀² (2x + 1)³ dx is
questions.e: An antiderivative is (2x + 1)⁴/8 (divide by 4 for the power and by 2 for the inner derivative), giving (625 − 1)/8 = 78. The value 156 divides by 4 only and forgets the factor 2 from the inner function.

questions.s: The value of ∫₀^(π/2) cos²x dx is
questions.e: cos²x = (1 + cos 2x)/2, so the integral is [x/2 + sin 2x/4]₀^(π/2) = π/4. The value π/2 forgets to halve, integrating 1 + cos 2x instead of its half.

questions.s: The value of ∫₀^(π/2) sin³x cos x dx is
questions.e: Put u = sin x, du = cos x dx, limits 0 to 1: ∫₀¹ u³ du = 1/4. The value 1/3 uses the power 3 as the divisor instead of 4.

questions.s: The value of ∫₀¹ x/(x² + 1) dx is
questions.e: The numerator is half the derivative of x² + 1, so the integral is ½[ln(x² + 1)]₀¹ = ½ ln 2. The value π/4 is ∫₀¹ 1/(x² + 1) dx, a different integrand.

questions.s: The value of ∫₀^√3 1/(1 + x²) dx is
questions.e: [tan⁻¹x]₀^√3 = tan⁻¹√3 − 0 = π/3. The value π/6 is tan⁻¹(1/√3), a common mix-up of the special angles.

questions.s: The value of ∫₀^(1/2) 1/√(1 − x²) dx is
questions.e: [sin⁻¹x]₀^(1/2) = sin⁻¹(1/2) = π/6. The value π/3 is cos⁻¹(1/2), which comes from using the wrong inverse function.

questions.s: The value of ∫₀^(ln 2) e^(2x) dx is
questions.e: [e^(2x)/2]₀^(ln 2) = (e^(2 ln 2) − 1)/2 = (4 − 1)/2 = 3/2. The value 3 forgets to divide by 2, the derivative of the exponent.

questions.s: The value of ∫₀¹ x eˣ dx is
questions.e: By parts, ∫x eˣ dx = x eˣ − ∫eˣ dx = (x − 1)eˣ, so the value is 0·e − (−1)e⁰ = 1. The value e keeps only [x eˣ]₀¹ and forgets to subtract ∫₀¹ eˣ dx = e − 1.

questions.s: The value of ∫₀^π x sin x dx is
questions.e: By parts, ∫x sin x dx = −x cos x + sin x. At π this is −π(−1) + 0 = π, and at 0 it is 0, so the value is π. The value 2 comes from dropping the x and integrating sin x alone.

questions.s: The value of ∫₁^e ln x dx is
questions.e: By parts, ∫ln x dx = x ln x − x, so the value is (e − e) − (0 − 1) = 1. The value e keeps only [x ln x]₁^e and forgets to subtract ∫₁^e 1 dx = e − 1.

questions.s: The value of ∫₀^(π/2) sin x/(sin x + cos x) dx is
questions.e: Call it I. Using ∫₀^a f(x) dx = ∫₀^a f(a − x) dx with a = π/2 turns sin x into cos x, so I also equals ∫ cos x/(sin x + cos x) dx. Adding, 2I = ∫₀^(π/2) 1 dx = π/2, so I = π/4. The value π/2 is 2I, forgetting to halve.

questions.s: The value of ∫₀^(π/2) ln(tan x) dx is
questions.e: Replacing x by π/2 − x turns ln(tan x) into ln(cot x) = −ln(tan x), so I = −I and I = 0. The integrand is negative on (0, π/4) and positive on (π/4, π/2), and the two parts cancel exactly.

questions.s: The value of ∫₀³ 5 dx is
questions.e: The integral of a constant c over [a, b] is c(b − a), so the value is 5 × 3 = 15. The value 8 adds 5 and 3 instead of multiplying.

questions.s: Let f(x) = x² for 0 ≤ x ≤ 1 and f(x) = 3 for 1 < x ≤ 3. Then ∫₀³ f(x) dx equals
questions.e: Split at x = 1: ∫₀¹ x² dx = 1/3 and ∫₁³ 3 dx = 6, so the total is 19/3. The value 7 replaces the first piece by f(1) = 1 instead of integrating x².

questions.s: The value of ∫₀⁴ |x − 2| dx is
questions.e: On [0, 2] the integrand is 2 − x and on [2, 4] it is x − 2; each piece is a triangle of area 2, so the total is 4. Ignoring the modulus gives [x²/2 − 2x]₀⁴ = 0.

questions.s: If ∫₀^k 2x dx = 9 and k > 0, then k equals
questions.e: ∫₀^k 2x dx = [x²]₀^k = k², so k² = 9 and k = 3. The value 9 sets k itself equal to the integral, and 81 squares 9.

questions.s: If ∫₁^a (2x − 1) dx = 6 and a > 1, then a equals
questions.e: [x² − x]₁^a = (a² − a) − 0 = 6, so a² − a − 6 = 0, (a − 3)(a + 2) = 0 and a = 3 since a > 1. The root −2 is rejected by the condition a > 1.

questions.s: The value of ∫₀^(π/6) cos x dx is
questions.e: [sin x]₀^(π/6) = sin(π/6) − 0 = 1/2. The value √3/2 is cos(π/6), obtained by evaluating the integrand instead of its antiderivative.

questions.s: The value of ∫₀^π cos x dx is
questions.e: [sin x]₀^π = sin π − sin 0 = 0; the positive area on (0, π/2) cancels the negative area on (π/2, π). The value 2 is ∫₀^π sin x dx, or the total area, not the integral.

questions.s: The value of ∫₀^(π/4) tan²x dx is
questions.e: tan²x = sec²x − 1, so the integral is [tan x − x]₀^(π/4) = 1 − π/4. The value π/4 − 1 reverses the sign; it is negative, but tan²x ≥ 0 gives a positive integral.

questions.s: The value of ∫₀^(π/6) cos 3x dx is
questions.e: [sin 3x/3]₀^(π/6) = sin(π/2)/3 = 1/3. The value 1 forgets to divide by 3, and 3 multiplies instead of dividing.

questions.s: The value of ∫₀^(π/2) sin 2x dx is
questions.e: [−cos 2x/2]₀^(π/2) = (−cos π + cos 0)/2 = (1 + 1)/2 = 1. The value 2 forgets the factor 1/2 from the inner derivative.

questions.s: If F(x) = ∫₁^x (t³ + 1) dt, then F′(x) equals
questions.e: By the fundamental theorem of calculus, the derivative of ∫ₐ^x f(t) dt with respect to x is f(x), so F′(x) = x³ + 1. The option x⁴/4 + x is the antiderivative, not its derivative, and 3x² differentiates the integrand.

questions.s: The value of ∫₁² 1/(2x + 1) dx is
questions.e: ∫1/(2x + 1) dx = ½ ln(2x + 1), so the value is ½(ln 5 − ln 3) = ½ ln(5/3). The value ln(5/3) forgets the ½ that comes from the coefficient of x.

questions.s: The value of ∫₀³ 1/(x + 1) dx is
questions.e: [ln(x + 1)]₀³ = ln 4 − ln 1 = ln 4 = 2 ln 2. The value ln 3 substitutes the limits into ln x instead of ln(x + 1).

questions.s: The value of ∫₀¹ x²/(x³ + 1) dx is
questions.e: With u = x³ + 1, du = 3x² dx, the integral becomes (1/3)∫₁² du/u = (1/3) ln 2. The value 3 ln 2 multiplies by 3 instead of dividing.

questions.s: The value of ∫₁² (x² − 1)/x² dx is
questions.e: (x² − 1)/x² = 1 − x⁻², whose antiderivative is x + 1/x; the value is (2 + 1/2) − (1 + 1) = 1/2. Writing the antiderivative as x − 1/x is a sign slip that gives 3/2.

questions.s: The value of ∫₀^(π/2) √(1 − cos 2x) dx is
questions.e: 1 − cos 2x = 2 sin²x, and sin x ≥ 0 on [0, π/2], so the integrand is √2 sin x. Then √2[−cos x]₀^(π/2) = √2. The value 2 forgets the square root and integrates 2 sin x.

questions.s: The value of ∫₀^(π/4) sec x tan x dx is
questions.e: d/dx(sec x) = sec x tan x, so the value is sec(π/4) − sec 0 = √2 − 1. The value √2 forgets that sec 0 = 1, and 1 − √2 reverses the order of the limits.

questions.s: For every function f continuous on [0, a], which of the following is correct?
questions.e: The substitution u = a − x maps [0, a] onto itself and reverses the direction; the reversal cancels the minus sign from du = −dx, so ∫₀^a f(x) dx = ∫₀^a f(a − x) dx. Keeping the minus sign gives the wrong version with −∫; the doubling rule needs the extra condition f(a − x) = f(x).

questions.s: The value of ∫₀¹ x(1 − x)⁵ dx is
questions.e: Using ∫₀¹ f(x) dx = ∫₀¹ f(1 − x) dx, the integral equals ∫₀¹ (1 − x)x⁵ dx = 1/6 − 1/7 = 1/42. The value 1/30 = 1/5 − 1/6 comes from using powers 4 and 5 instead of 5 and 6.

questions.s: The value of ∫₀^(π/2) sin x cos x dx is
questions.e: With u = sin x the integral is ∫₀¹ u du = 1/2. Alternatively ½∫ sin 2x dx = ½ × 1. The value 1/4 halves twice.

questions.s: If f is an even function and ∫₀³ f(x) dx = 4, then ∫₋₃³ f(x) dx equals
questions.e: For an even function the areas on [−3, 0] and [0, 3] are equal, so ∫₋₃³ f = 2 × 4 = 8. The value 0 is the rule for odd functions.

questions.s: If f is an odd function and ∫₀² f(x) dx = 5, then ∫₋₂⁰ f(x) dx equals
questions.e: For odd f, f(−x) = −f(x), so the integral over [−2, 0] is the negative of the integral over [0, 2], giving −5. The value 0 is ∫₋₂² f, the whole symmetric interval, not the left half.

questions.s: The value of ∫₀^π |cos x| dx is
questions.e: |cos x| is cos x on [0, π/2] and −cos x on [π/2, π]; each piece gives 1, so the total is 2. Dropping the modulus gives ∫₀^π cos x dx = 0.

questions.s: The value of ∫₋₁¹ x² dx is
questions.e: [x³/3]₋₁¹ = 1/3 − (−1/3) = 2/3. The value 0 wrongly treats x² as odd; 1/3 uses only the upper limit.

questions.s: The value of ∫₀⁴ √x dx is
questions.e: ∫x^(1/2) dx = (2/3)x^(3/2), and 4^(3/2) = 8, so the value is 16/3. The value 8 forgets the factor 2/3, and 12 multiplies by 3/2 instead.

questions.s: The area of the region bounded by y = x², the x-axis and the lines x = 0 and x = 3 is
questions.e: Area = ∫₀³ x² dx = [x³/3]₀³ = 27/3 = 9 square units. The value 27 forgets to divide by 3 when integrating x².

questions.s: The area of the region bounded by y = 2x + 1, the x-axis and the lines x = 0 and x = 2 is
questions.e: Area = ∫₀² (2x + 1) dx = [x² + x]₀² = 4 + 2 = 6 square units. The value 5 is just the height y(2), and 4 forgets the constant term.

questions.s: The total area enclosed between the curve y = sin x and the x-axis from x = 0 to x = 2π is
questions.e: The arch on [0, π] has area ∫₀^π sin x dx = 2, and the arch on [π, 2π] lies below the axis with the same area 2, so the total is 4. The value 0 is the signed integral, in which the two arches cancel.

questions.s: The area of the region enclosed by the parabola y = 4 − x² and the x-axis is
questions.e: The curve meets the x-axis at x = ±2, so the area is ∫₋₂² (4 − x²) dx = 2[4x − x³/3]₀² = 2(8 − 8/3) = 32/3. The value 16/3 covers only the half from 0 to 2.

questions.s: The area of the region enclosed between the line y = x and the parabola y = x² is
questions.e: They meet at x = 0 and x = 1, and x ≥ x² there, so the area is ∫₀¹ (x − x²) dx = 1/2 − 1/3 = 1/6. Adding the two integrals instead of subtracting gives 5/6.

questions.s: The area of the region enclosed between the parabola y = x² and the line y = 1 is
questions.e: They meet at x = ±1, and 1 ≥ x² between them, so the area is ∫₋₁¹ (1 − x²) dx = 2(1 − 1/3) = 4/3. The value 2/3 takes only one side of the y-axis, and 2 is the area of the whole 2 × 1 rectangle.

questions.s: The area under the curve y = 1/x between x = 1 and x = e², above the x-axis, is
questions.e: Area = [ln x]₁^(e²) = ln e² − ln 1 = 2. The value e² − 1 treats the antiderivative of 1/x as x.

questions.s: The area of the region bounded by y = eˣ, the x-axis and the lines x = 0 and x = ln 3 is
questions.e: Area = [eˣ]₀^(ln 3) = 3 − e⁰ = 3 − 1 = 2. The value 3 forgets that the lower limit contributes e⁰ = 1.

questions.s: The total area enclosed between the curve y = x³, the x-axis and the lines x = −1 and x = 1 is
questions.e: The curve is below the axis on [−1, 0] and above it on [0, 1]; each part has area ∫₀¹ x³ dx = 1/4, so the total is 1/2. The value 0 is the signed integral ∫₋₁¹ x³ dx, in which the two parts cancel.

questions.s: The area of the region enclosed between the parabola y = x² and the line y = 3x is
questions.e: x² = 3x gives x = 0 and x = 3, and 3x ≥ x² between them, so the area is ∫₀³ (3x − x²) dx = 27/2 − 9 = 9/2. The value 27/2 is the area under the line alone, without subtracting the parabola.

questions.s: The area of the region enclosed by the parabola y² = 4x and the line x = 1 is
questions.e: The region is symmetric about the x-axis, with upper boundary y = 2√x, so the area is 2∫₀¹ 2√x dx = 4 × (2/3) = 8/3. The value 4/3 finds only the half above the x-axis.

questions.s: The area of the region bounded by y = √x, the x-axis and the line x = 9 is
questions.e: Area = ∫₀⁹ x^(1/2) dx = (2/3)·9^(3/2) = (2/3)·27 = 18. The value 27 forgets the factor 2/3.

questions.s: Using integration, the area of the region bounded by the line y = 4 − x and the two coordinate axes is
questions.e: The line meets the x-axis at x = 4, so the area is ∫₀⁴ (4 − x) dx = 16 − 8 = 8, matching the triangle ½ × 4 × 4. The value 16 is the square 4 × 4, forgetting the ½.

questions.s: The area under the curve y = cos x from x = 0 to x = π/2 is
questions.e: Area = [sin x]₀^(π/2) = 1 − 0 = 1. The value 2 is the area of a full arch of sine from 0 to π, a different region.

questions.s: The area of the region between the curves y = cos x and y = sin x from x = 0 to x = π/4 is
questions.e: On [0, π/4], cos x ≥ sin x, so the area is ∫ (cos x − sin x) dx = [sin x + cos x]₀^(π/4) = √2 − 1. The value √2 forgets to subtract the value 1 at the lower limit.

questions.s: The area of the region bounded by y = x² + 1, the x-axis and the lines x = −1 and x = 2 is
questions.e: Area = [x³/3 + x]₋₁² = (8/3 + 2) − (−1/3 − 1) = 14/3 + 4/3 = 6. Taking the lower-limit value as +4/3 instead of −4/3 gives 14/3 − 4/3 = 10/3.

questions.s: The area of the region enclosed by the parabola y = 9 − x² and the x-axis is
questions.e: The curve cuts the axis at x = ±3, so the area is 2∫₀³ (9 − x²) dx = 2(27 − 9) = 36. The value 18 covers only one half, and 54 is the bounding 6 × 9 rectangle.

questions.s: The area of the region enclosed between the curves y = x² and y = √x is
questions.e: They meet at x = 0 and x = 1, and √x ≥ x² there, so the area is ∫₀¹ (√x − x²) dx = 2/3 − 1/3 = 1/3. The value 2/3 is the area under y = √x alone.

questions.s: The area of the region enclosed between the graph of y = |x| and the line y = 2 is
questions.e: They meet at x = ±2, so the area is ∫₋₂² (2 − |x|) dx = 2∫₀² (2 − x) dx = 2 × 2 = 4. The value 8 is the whole 4 × 2 rectangle, forgetting to subtract the area under y = |x|.

questions.s: The total area of the regions enclosed between the curves y = x³ and y = x is
questions.e: x³ = x at x = −1, 0, 1. On [0, 1] the area is ∫(x − x³) dx = 1/2 − 1/4 = 1/4, and by symmetry the loop on [−1, 0] also has area 1/4, giving 1/2. The value 0 adds signed integrals that cancel.

questions.s: The area under the curve y = sec²x from x = 0 to x = π/4 is
questions.e: Area = [tan x]₀^(π/4) = 1 − 0 = 1. The value √2 is sec(π/4), which comes from using sec x as the antiderivative.

questions.s: The area of the region bounded by y = 1/(1 + x²), the x-axis and the lines x = −1 and x = 1 is
questions.e: Area = [tan⁻¹x]₋₁¹ = π/4 − (−π/4) = π/2. The value π/4 uses only the part from 0 to 1.

questions.s: If f(x) ≥ g(x) for a ≤ x ≤ b, the area of the region between y = f(x) and y = g(x) from x = a to x = b is
questions.e: The area between two curves is the integral of (upper curve − lower curve); since f is above g, it is ∫ₐᵇ [f(x) − g(x)] dx. Taking g − f gives the negative of the area.

questions.s: The area of the region bounded by y = 2ˣ, the x-axis and the lines x = 0 and x = 2 is
questions.e: ∫2ˣ dx = 2ˣ/ln 2, so the area is (4 − 1)/ln 2 = 3/ln 2. The value 3 ln 2 multiplies by ln 2 instead of dividing, and 4/ln 2 forgets the lower limit 2⁰ = 1.

questions.s: The area under the curve y = 1/√x from x = 1 to x = 9 is
questions.e: Area = [2√x]₁⁹ = 6 − 2 = 4. The value 2 forgets the factor 2 in the antiderivative, giving √9 − √1.

questions.s: The area of the region enclosed between the parabola y = x² + 2 and the line y = 3x is
questions.e: x² + 2 = 3x gives x = 1 and x = 2, and the line is above the parabola between them, so the area is ∫₁² (3x − x² − 2) dx = (6 − 8/3 − 4) − (3/2 − 1/3 − 2) = −2/3 + 5/6 = 1/6. Subtracting in the wrong order gives −1/6, which cannot be an area.

questions.s: The area of the region enclosed between the parabola y = x² and the line y = 6 − x is
questions.e: x² = 6 − x gives x = −3 and x = 2, so the area is ∫₋₃² (6 − x − x²) dx = (12 − 2 − 8/3) − (−18 − 9/2 + 9) = 22/3 + 27/2 = 125/6. The value 22/3 integrates only from 0 to 2 and misses the part left of the y-axis.

questions.s: The area under the curve y = cos 2x from x = 0 to x = π/4 is
questions.e: Area = [sin 2x/2]₀^(π/4) = (sin(π/2))/2 = 1/2. The value 1 forgets to divide by 2, the coefficient of x.

questions.s: The area of the region bounded by y = x³, the x-axis and the lines x = 0 and x = 2 is
questions.e: Area = [x⁴/4]₀² = 16/4 = 4. The value 16 forgets to divide by 4, and 8 is just y(2) = 2³.

questions.s: The total area of the region between the curve y = x² − 1, the x-axis and the lines x = 0 and x = 2 is
questions.e: The curve is below the axis on [0, 1] and above it on [1, 2]. ∫₀¹ (1 − x²) dx = 2/3 and ∫₁² (x² − 1) dx = 4/3, so the total area is 2. The value 2/3 is the signed integral ∫₀² (x² − 1) dx, where the parts partly cancel.

questions.s: The general solution of the differential equation dy/dx = 2x is
questions.e: Integrating both sides with respect to x gives y = ∫2x dx = x² + c. The option y = 2x² + c forgets to divide by the new power 2.

questions.s: The general solution of dy/dx = y is
questions.e: Separating, dy/y = dx, so ln|y| = x + k and y = ceˣ. The option y = eˣ + c puts the constant in the wrong place: its derivative eˣ is not equal to y unless c = 0.

questions.s: The general solution of dy/dx = x/y is
questions.e: Separating, y dy = x dx, so y²/2 = x²/2 + k, that is y² − x² = c. The family x² + y² = c solves dy/dx = −x/y, which has the opposite sign.

questions.s: The solution curves of the differential equation dy/dx = −x/y are
questions.e: Separating, y dy = −x dx, so y²/2 = −x²/2 + k, which gives x² + y² = c, circles centred at the origin. Straight lines through the origin come from dy/dx = y/x instead.

questions.s: The general solution of dy/dx = y/x (x, y > 0) is
questions.e: Separating, dy/y = dx/x, so ln y = ln x + ln c and y = cx. The family xy = c solves dy/dx = −y/x.

questions.s: If dy/dx = 3x² and y = 2 when x = 0, then the value of y when x = 1 is
questions.e: y = x³ + c, and y(0) = 2 gives c = 2, so y(1) = 1 + 2 = 3. The value 5 adds the slope 3x² at x = 1 to the initial value instead of integrating.

questions.s: The solution of dy/dx = 2y that satisfies y(0) = 5 is
questions.e: dy/y = 2 dx gives ln y = 2x + k, so y = Ae^(2x); y(0) = 5 gives A = 5. The option e^(2x) + 4 fits y(0) = 5 but its derivative 2e^(2x) is not 2y.

questions.s: The general solution of dy/dx = e^(x − y) is
questions.e: Write e^(x − y) = eˣ/eʸ and separate: eʸ dy = eˣ dx, so eʸ = eˣ + c. The option y = x + c is only the special case c = 0 of this family, not the general solution.

questions.s: The general solution of dy/dx = 1 + y² is
questions.e: Separating, dy/(1 + y²) = dx, so tan⁻¹y = x + c and y = tan(x + c). The option tan x + c adds the constant outside, and its derivative sec²x = 1 + tan²x is not 1 + y² unless c = 0.

questions.s: If dy/dx = y² and y = 1 when x = 0, then the value of y at x = 1/2 is
questions.e: dy/y² = dx gives −1/y = x + c; y(0) = 1 gives c = −1, so 1/y = 1 − x and y = 1/(1 − x). At x = 1/2, y = 2. The value 1/2 stops at 1/y = 1/2 without inverting; e^(1/2) solves dy/dx = y instead.

questions.s: If dy/dx = sin x and y(0) = 1, then y(π) equals
questions.e: y = −cos x + c, and y(0) = −1 + c = 1 gives c = 2, so y(π) = −(−1) + 2 = 3. Using +cos x as the antiderivative gives c = 0 and y(π) = −1, a sign error.

questions.s: If dy/dx = xy and y(0) = 1, then y(2) equals
questions.e: dy/y = x dx gives ln y = x²/2 + c; y(0) = 1 gives c = 0, so y = e^(x²/2) and y(2) = e². The value e⁴ comes from forgetting to halve x², i.e. using y = e^(x²).

questions.s: A bacterial culture in a Lahore laboratory grows according to dP/dt = kP, where k is a positive constant. If the population doubles in 3 hours, the time it takes to become 8 times its initial size is
questions.e: The solution is P = P₀e^(kt), which multiplies by the same factor in equal times. Doubling every 3 hours, 8 = 2³ needs 3 doublings, i.e. 9 hours. The value 24 hours assumes linear growth (8 × 3).

questions.s: The curve satisfying dy/dx = (y + 1)/(x + 1) that passes through the point (0, 1) has, at x = 2, the value y equal to
questions.e: dy/(y + 1) = dx/(x + 1) gives ln(y + 1) = ln(x + 1) + ln c, so y + 1 = c(x + 1). At (0, 1), c = 2, so y = 2x + 1 and y(2) = 5. Taking y = c(x + 1) without the +1 on the left gives c = 1 and the wrong value 3.

questions.s: Which of the following differential equations is of the variables separable type?
questions.e: x²y is a product of a function of x and a function of y, so dy/y = x² dx separates the variables. A sum such as x + y or sin(x + y) cannot be written as f(x)g(y).

questions.s: If dy/dx = y tan x and y(0) = 2, then y(π/3) equals
questions.e: dy/y = tan x dx gives ln y = −ln cos x + c, so y = A sec x; y(0) = 2 gives A = 2. Then y(π/3) = 2 × 2 = 4. The value 1 uses y = 2 cos x, a sign slip in ∫tan x dx = −ln cos x.

questions.s: If dy/dx = 1/x for x > 0 and y(1) = 2, then y(e³) equals
questions.e: y = ln x + c, and y(1) = 0 + c = 2, so y(e³) = 3 + 2 = 5. The value 3 forgets the constant found from the initial condition.

questions.s: The slope of a curve at any point (x, y) is 4x, and the curve passes through (1, 2). The value of y at x = 3 is
questions.e: dy/dx = 4x gives y = 2x² + c, and 2 = 2 + c gives c = 0, so y(3) = 18. The value 20 adds the y-coordinate 2 as the constant instead of solving for c.

questions.s: If dy/dx = −2y and y(0) = 3, then y(ln 2) equals
questions.e: y = 3e^(−2x), so y(ln 2) = 3e^(−2 ln 2) = 3 × 2⁻² = 3/4. Dropping the minus sign gives 3e^(2 ln 2) = 12, and dropping the 2 gives 3/2.

questions.s: A curve satisfies y dy/dx = 2x with y > 0 and passes through (1, 2). The value of y at x = 3 is
questions.e: y dy = 2x dx gives y²/2 = x² + c; at (1, 2), 2 = 1 + c so c = 1. Then y² = 2(9 + 1) = 20 and y = 2√5. Ignoring the constant (c = 0) gives y² = 18, i.e. 3√2.

questions.s: ∫ x⁵ dx is equal to
questions.e: By the power rule ∫ xⁿ dx = xⁿ⁺¹/(n + 1) + c, so with n = 5 the result is x⁶/6 + c. The option 5x⁴ + c is the derivative of x⁵, not its antiderivative, and x⁶ + c forgets to divide by the new power 6.

questions.s: ∫ 1/x³ dx is equal to
questions.e: Write 1/x³ = x⁻³; then ∫ x⁻³ dx = x⁻²/(−2) + c = −1/(2x²) + c. Dropping the negative sign of the new power −2 gives 1/(2x²), and −3/x⁴ is the derivative of x⁻³ instead of its integral.

questions.s: ∫ √x dx is equal to
questions.e: √x = x^(1/2), so ∫ x^(1/2) dx = x^(3/2)/(3/2) + c = (2/3)x√x + c. Multiplying by 3/2 instead of dividing gives (3/2)x√x; 1/(2√x) is the derivative of √x and 2√x is the integral of 1/√x.

questions.s: ∫ e³ˣ dx is equal to
questions.e: Since d/dx(e³ˣ) = 3e³ˣ, we have ∫ e³ˣ dx = (1/3)e³ˣ + c. The answer 3e³ˣ multiplies by the inner derivative instead of dividing by it, and the power rule does not apply to an exponential with variable exponent.

questions.s: ∫ dx/(2x + 5) is equal to
questions.e: For a linear denominator, ∫ dx/(ax + b) = (1/a) ln|ax + b| + c; here a = 2, giving (1/2) ln|2x + 5| + c. Writing ln|2x + 5| alone ignores the factor 2 from the chain rule, which must be divided out.

questions.s: ∫ cos 4x dx is equal to
questions.e: d/dx(sin 4x) = 4 cos 4x, so ∫ cos 4x dx = (1/4) sin 4x + c. The negative options come from confusing this with the integral of sine, ∫ sin x dx = −cos x + c.

questions.s: ∫ sec x tan x dx is equal to
questions.e: Since d/dx(sec x) = sec x tan x, the antiderivative is sec x + c. The option tan x + c is the integral of sec²x, a different standard result.

questions.s: ∫ 2ˣ dx is equal to
questions.e: d/dx(aˣ) = aˣ ln a, so ∫ aˣ dx = aˣ/ln a + c; with a = 2 this is 2ˣ/ln 2 + c. The option 2ˣ ln 2 is the derivative of 2ˣ, and the power rule cannot be used because the variable is in the exponent.

questions.s: ∫ (x + 1/x)² dx, x ≠ 0, is equal to
questions.e: Expand first: (x + 1/x)² = x² + 2 + x⁻². Integrating term by term gives x³/3 + 2x + x⁻¹/(−1) = x³/3 + 2x − 1/x + c. The form (x + 1/x)³/3 wrongly treats the bracket like a single variable, and x³/3 − 1/x drops the middle term 2.

questions.s: ∫ cosec²(3x) dx is equal to
questions.e: d/dx(cot 3x) = −3 cosec²(3x), so ∫ cosec²(3x) dx = −(1/3) cot 3x + c. The positive option misses the minus sign in the derivative of cot, and −3 cot 3x multiplies by the inner derivative instead of dividing.

questions.s: ∫ (1 + x)/√x dx, x > 0, is equal to
questions.e: Split the fraction: (1 + x)/√x = x^(−1/2) + x^(1/2). Then ∫ x^(−1/2) dx = 2√x and ∫ x^(1/2) dx = (2/3)x√x, so the result is 2√x + (2/3)x√x + c. Writing (3/2)x√x multiplies by the new power instead of dividing by it.

questions.s: ∫ eˣ(1 + e⁻ˣ) dx is equal to
questions.e: Multiply out: eˣ(1 + e⁻ˣ) = eˣ + 1, and ∫ (eˣ + 1) dx = eˣ + x + c. The option eˣ + 1 + c forgets that the integral of the constant 1 is x, not 1.

questions.s: If d/dx[g(x)] = h(x), which of the following is correct?
questions.e: Integration reverses differentiation: if g′(x) = h(x), then g is an antiderivative of h and ∫ h(x) dx = g(x) + c. The option ∫ g(x) dx = h(x) + c runs the process backwards, since h is the derivative of g, not its integral; and ∫ g′(x) dx is g(x) + c, not h′(x).

questions.s: A function f satisfies f′(x) = 6x² − 4x and f(1) = 5. The value of f(2) is
questions.e: Integrating gives f(x) = 2x³ − 2x² + c, and f(1) = 2 − 2 + c = 5 gives c = 5. So f(2) = 16 − 8 + 5 = 13. The value 8 forgets the constant c, and 21 is f′(2) + 5, which mixes up f and f′.

questions.s: ∫ sin x/cos²x dx is equal to
questions.e: sin x/cos²x = (1/cos x)(sin x/cos x) = sec x tan x, whose integral is sec x + c. Alternatively, put t = cos x, dt = −sin x dx: ∫ −dt/t² = 1/t = sec x. A minus sign appears only if the sign of dt is handled twice.

questions.s: ∫ (eˣ + e⁻ˣ)² dx is equal to
questions.e: Expand: (eˣ + e⁻ˣ)² = e²ˣ + 2 + e⁻²ˣ. Integrating gives e²ˣ/2 + 2x − e⁻²ˣ/2 + c = (e²ˣ − e⁻²ˣ)/2 + 2x + c. The plus sign between the exponentials is wrong because ∫ e⁻²ˣ dx = −e⁻²ˣ/2, and the cube form treats the bracket as if its derivative were 1.

questions.s: ∫ dx/√(1 − x²), for −1 < x < 1, is equal to
questions.e: d/dx(sin⁻¹x) = 1/√(1 − x²), so the integral is sin⁻¹x + c. The derivative of cos⁻¹x is −1/√(1 − x²), so cos⁻¹x would need a minus sign, and tan⁻¹x belongs to 1/(1 + x²).

questions.s: ∫ dx/(1 + x²) is equal to
questions.e: d/dx(tan⁻¹x) = 1/(1 + x²), so the integral is tan⁻¹x + c. The logarithm forms would need x in the numerator (∫ x/(1 + x²) dx = (1/2) ln(1 + x²)), and cot⁻¹x has derivative −1/(1 + x²).

questions.s: ∫ (x³ − 1)/(x − 1) dx, x ≠ 1, is equal to
questions.e: Factorise: x³ − 1 = (x − 1)(x² + x + 1), so the integrand is x² + x + 1. Its integral is x³/3 + x²/2 + x + c. The option with − x²/2 uses the wrong factor x² − x + 1, which belongs to x³ + 1.

questions.s: ∫ eˡⁿ ˣ dx, x > 0, is equal to
questions.e: Since e and ln are inverse functions, eˡⁿ ˣ = x for x > 0, and ∫ x dx = x²/2 + c. The option x + c simply copies the simplified integrand instead of integrating it.

questions.s: ∫ 3²ˣ dx is equal to
questions.e: d/dx(3²ˣ) = 3²ˣ · ln 3 · 2, so ∫ 3²ˣ dx = 3²ˣ/(2 ln 3) + c (equivalently 9ˣ/ln 9). The option 3²ˣ/ln 3 forgets the factor 2 from the exponent 2x, and 2·3²ˣ ln 3 is the derivative.

questions.s: ∫ dx/(x² + 9) is equal to
questions.e: The standard result is ∫ dx/(x² + a²) = (1/a) tan⁻¹(x/a) + c. With a = 3 this gives (1/3) tan⁻¹(x/3) + c. Using a = 9 instead of a² = 9 gives the wrong (1/9) tan⁻¹(x/9).

questions.s: ∫ dx/√(16 − x²), for −4 < x < 4, is equal to
questions.e: ∫ dx/√(a² − x²) = sin⁻¹(x/a) + c, with no 1/a factor. Here a = 4, so the result is sin⁻¹(x/4) + c. The factor 1/4 is wrongly borrowed from the tan⁻¹ formula, and x/16 uses a² instead of a.

questions.s: ∫ dx/(4x² + 25) is equal to
questions.e: Write 4x² + 25 = 4(x² + 25/4), so the integral is (1/4) · (1/(5/2)) tan⁻¹(x/(5/2)) = (1/4)(2/5) tan⁻¹(2x/5) = (1/10) tan⁻¹(2x/5) + c. Check: the derivative is (1/10)(2/5)/(1 + 4x²/25) = 1/(25 + 4x²). Forgetting the factor 1/4 taken out of the denominator, or the 1/2 from the inner 2x, gives (1/5).

questions.s: ∫ (2 − 3 sin x + 4/x) dx, x > 0, is equal to
questions.e: Integrate term by term: ∫ 2 dx = 2x, ∫ −3 sin x dx = −3(−cos x) = 3 cos x, and ∫ 4/x dx = 4 ln x. So the result is 2x + 3 cos x + 4 ln x + c. The option with − 3 cos x forgets that ∫ sin x dx = −cos x, and −4/x² is the derivative of 4/x.

questions.s: ∫ 2x(x² + 1)⁴ dx is equal to
questions.e: Put t = x² + 1, so dt = 2x dx and the integral becomes ∫ t⁴ dt = t⁵/5 + c = (x² + 1)⁵/5 + c. Dividing by 10 counts the factor 2 twice: it has already been absorbed into dt.

questions.s: ∫ 2x/(x² + 3) dx is equal to
questions.e: The numerator 2x is exactly the derivative of the denominator x² + 3, and ∫ f′(x)/f(x) dx = ln|f(x)| + c, so the answer is ln(x² + 3) + c. The tan⁻¹ form belongs to a constant numerator, as in ∫ dx/(x² + 3).

questions.s: ∫ cot x dx, for 0 < x < π, is equal to
questions.e: cot x = cos x/sin x, and cos x is the derivative of sin x, so ∫ cot x dx = ln|sin x| + c. The option −cosec²x is the derivative of cot x, not its integral.

questions.s: ∫ x√(x² + 4) dx is equal to
questions.e: Put t = x² + 4, dt = 2x dx, so x dx = dt/2 and the integral is (1/2)∫ t^(1/2) dt = (1/2)(2/3)t^(3/2) = (1/3)(x² + 4)√(x² + 4) + c. The option (2/3) forgets the factor 1/2 from x dx = dt/2.

questions.s: ∫ eˢⁱⁿ ˣ cos x dx is equal to
questions.e: Put t = sin x, dt = cos x dx, so the integral is ∫ eᵗ dt = eᵗ + c = eˢⁱⁿ ˣ + c. A minus sign would only appear if the exponent were cos x, whose derivative is −sin x.

questions.s: ∫ (ln x)/x dx, x > 0, is equal to
questions.e: Put t = ln x, dt = dx/x, so the integral is ∫ t dt = t²/2 + c = (ln x)²/2 + c. The option ln|ln x| is the integral of 1/(x ln x), where ln x is in the denominator, and (1/2) ln(x²) simply equals ln x.

questions.s: ∫ sin³x cos x dx is equal to
questions.e: Put t = sin x, dt = cos x dx: ∫ t³ dt = t⁴/4 + c = sin⁴x/4 + c. The negative sign would arise only with t = cos x, which needs a sin x factor left over, and leaving cos x in the answer means the substitution was not finished.

questions.s: ∫ eˣ/(eˣ + 1) dx is equal to
questions.e: The numerator eˣ is the derivative of eˣ + 1, so the integral is ln(eˣ + 1) + c (no modulus needed since eˣ + 1 > 0). The form x − ln(eˣ + 1) is the integral of 1/(eˣ + 1), a different integrand.

questions.s: ∫ x/(x² + 1)² dx is equal to
questions.e: Put t = x² + 1, x dx = dt/2: (1/2)∫ t⁻² dt = (1/2)(−t⁻¹) = −1/(2(x² + 1)) + c. Dropping the sign of t⁻¹/(−1) gives the positive option, and −1/(x² + 1) forgets the factor 1/2.

questions.s: ∫ tan x dx, for −π/2 < x < π/2, is equal to
questions.e: tan x = sin x/cos x = −(−sin x)/cos x, so ∫ tan x dx = −ln|cos x| + c = ln|sec x| + c. The option ln|cos x| misses this minus sign, and sec²x is the derivative of tan x.

questions.s: ∫ (x + 1)/(x² + 2x + 5) dx is equal to
questions.e: The derivative of x² + 2x + 5 is 2x + 2 = 2(x + 1), so the numerator is half of it: the integral is (1/2) ln(x² + 2x + 5) + c (the quadratic is always positive). Missing the factor 1/2 gives ln(x² + 2x + 5), and the tan⁻¹ form needs a constant numerator.

questions.s: ∫ dx/(x ln x), x > 1, is equal to
questions.e: Put t = ln x, dt = dx/x: the integral becomes ∫ dt/t = ln|t| + c = ln|ln x| + c. The option (ln x)²/2 is the integral of (ln x)/x, where ln x is in the numerator.

questions.s: ∫ (3x − 2)⁷ dx is equal to
questions.e: For a linear inside, ∫ (ax + b)ⁿ dx = (ax + b)ⁿ⁺¹/(a(n + 1)) + c. With a = 3 and n = 7, the divisor is 3 × 8 = 24. The option /8 forgets to divide by a = 3, and /21 uses the old power 7.

questions.s: ∫ sec²x/(1 + tan x) dx is equal to
questions.e: Put t = 1 + tan x, dt = sec²x dx, so the integral is ∫ dt/t = ln|1 + tan x| + c. The option (1 + tan x)²/2 would come from 1 + tan x being in the numerator, and ln|sec x + tan x| is the integral of sec x.

questions.s: ∫ x/√(1 − x⁴) dx, for −1 < x < 1, is equal to
questions.e: Put t = x², dt = 2x dx; since x⁴ = t², the integral is (1/2)∫ dt/√(1 − t²) = (1/2) sin⁻¹t + c = (1/2) sin⁻¹(x²) + c. The option sin⁻¹(x²) forgets the factor 1/2 from x dx = dt/2.

questions.s: ∫ eˣ/(1 + e²ˣ) dx is equal to
questions.e: Put t = eˣ, dt = eˣ dx; then e²ˣ = t² and the integral is ∫ dt/(1 + t²) = tan⁻¹t + c = tan⁻¹(eˣ) + c. The logarithm forms would need the derivative of 1 + e²ˣ, which is 2e²ˣ, in the numerator.

questions.s: ∫ cos(ln x)/x dx, x > 0, is equal to
questions.e: Put t = ln x, dt = dx/x, so the integral is ∫ cos t dt = sin t + c = sin(ln x) + c. The minus sign belongs to ∫ sin t dt, and keeping a 1/x in the answer means the substitution was left half done.

questions.s: Writing exp(u) for eᵘ, ∫ x² exp(x³) dx is equal to
questions.e: Put t = x³, dt = 3x² dx, so x² dx = dt/3 and the integral is (1/3)∫ eᵗ dt = (1/3) exp(x³) + c. Multiplying by 3 instead of dividing gives 3 exp(x³), whose derivative is 9x² exp(x³).

questions.s: ∫ sin 2x/(1 + cos²x) dx is equal to
questions.e: Put t = 1 + cos²x; then dt = 2 cos x(−sin x) dx = −sin 2x dx. The integral becomes −∫ dt/t = −ln(1 + cos²x) + c. The positive option misses the minus from the derivative of cos x, and −1/2 wrongly halves a factor that sin 2x = 2 sin x cos x already supplies.

questions.s: ∫ dx/(x + 1)², x ≠ −1, is equal to
questions.e: ∫ (x + 1)⁻² dx = (x + 1)⁻¹/(−1) + c = −1/(x + 1) + c. The logarithm is only for the power −1, and −2/(x + 1)³ is the derivative of (x + 1)⁻², not its integral.

questions.s: ∫ dx/(x² + 4x + 13) is equal to
questions.e: Complete the square: x² + 4x + 13 = (x + 2)² + 9 = (x + 2)² + 3². Then ∫ dx/((x + 2)² + 3²) = (1/3) tan⁻¹((x + 2)/3) + c. Writing (x − 2) is a sign slip in completing the square, and leaving out 1/3 forgets the 1/a factor of the formula.

questions.s: ∫ dx/√(5 − 4x − x²), for −5 < x < 1, is equal to
questions.e: Complete the square: 5 − 4x − x² = 9 − (x² + 4x + 4) = 3² − (x + 2)². So the integral is sin⁻¹((x + 2)/3) + c. The sin⁻¹ formula has no 1/a factor in front, so the 1/3 option is wrong, and dividing by 9 uses a² instead of a.

questions.s: ∫ x(x − 1)⁵ dx is equal to
questions.e: Put u = x − 1, so x = u + 1 and ∫ (u + 1)u⁵ du = u⁷/7 + u⁶/6 + c = (x − 1)⁷/7 + (x − 1)⁶/6 + c. Check: the derivative is (x − 1)⁶ + (x − 1)⁵ = (x − 1)⁵ · x. Integrating each factor separately, as in x²(x − 1)⁶/12, is not valid for a product.

questions.s: To evaluate ∫ x cos(x²) dx, the most suitable substitution is
questions.e: With t = x², dt = 2x dx, so x dx = dt/2 and the integral becomes (1/2)∫ cos t dt = (1/2) sin(x²) + c. Choosing t = cos(x²) leaves a sin(x²) factor that is not in the integrand.

questions.s: ∫ (1 + cos x)/(x + sin x) dx is equal to
questions.e: The numerator 1 + cos x is the derivative of the denominator x + sin x, so the integral is ln|x + sin x| + c. Taking the log of the numerator, ln|1 + cos x|, reverses the roles of the two parts.

questions.s: ∫ xeˣ dx is equal to
questions.e: By parts with u = x, dv = eˣ dx: ∫ xeˣ dx = xeˣ − ∫ eˣ dx = xeˣ − eˣ + c = eˣ(x − 1) + c. The option eˣ(x + 1) has a sign error; its derivative is eˣ(x + 2), not xeˣ.

questions.s: ∫ x cos x dx is equal to
o: x sin x + cos x + c
x sin x − cos x + c
questions.e: Take u = x, dv = cos x dx, so v = sin x: ∫ x cos x dx = x sin x − ∫ sin x dx = x sin x + cos x + c. The option x sin x − cos x forgets that −∫ sin x dx = +cos x, and −x cos x + sin x is the integral of x sin x.

questions.s: ∫ ln x dx, x > 0, is equal to
questions.e: Write ln x as 1 · ln x and take u = ln x, dv = dx: ∫ ln x dx = x ln x − ∫ x · (1/x) dx = x ln x − x + c. The option 1/x is the derivative of ln x, and x ln x alone has derivative ln x + 1.

questions.s: ∫ x ln x dx, x > 0, is equal to
questions.e: Take u = ln x, dv = x dx, v = x²/2: the integral is (x²/2) ln x − ∫ (x²/2)(1/x) dx = (x²/2) ln x − ∫ x/2 dx = (x²/2) ln x − x²/4 + c. Writing − x²/2 forgets to integrate x/2, which gives x²/4.

questions.s: ∫ x sin 2x dx is equal to
questions.e: Take u = x, dv = sin 2x dx, so v = −(1/2) cos 2x. Then the integral is −(x/2) cos 2x + (1/2)∫ cos 2x dx = −(x/2) cos 2x + (1/4) sin 2x + c. The last option multiplies by 2 where it should divide when integrating sin 2x and cos 2x.

questions.s: When ∫ x³ ln x dx is found by parts using ∫ u dv = uv − ∫ v du, the better choice for u is
questions.e: Choose u = ln x, because its derivative 1/x is simpler and dv = x³ dx is easy to integrate; then v = x⁴/4 and ∫ v du = ∫ x³/4 dx. Choosing u = x³ would need dv = ln x dx, whose integral x ln x − x makes the new integral harder.

questions.s: ∫ x²eˣ dx is equal to
questions.e: Parts twice: ∫ x²eˣ dx = x²eˣ − 2∫ xeˣ dx = x²eˣ − 2(xeˣ − eˣ) + c = eˣ(x² − 2x + 2) + c. Check: the derivative is eˣ(x² − 2x + 2) + eˣ(2x − 2) = x²eˣ. The option with − 2 gets the sign of the second step wrong.

questions.s: ∫ eˣ(sin x + cos x) dx is equal to
questions.e: Use ∫ eˣ[f(x) + f′(x)] dx = eˣ f(x) + c. Here f(x) = sin x and f′(x) = cos x, so the result is eˣ sin x + c. Check: d/dx(eˣ sin x) = eˣ sin x + eˣ cos x. The option eˣ cos x differentiates to eˣ(cos x − sin x).

questions.s: ∫ eˣ(1/x − 1/x²) dx, x > 0, is equal to
questions.e: With f(x) = 1/x, f′(x) = −1/x², the integrand is eˣ[f(x) + f′(x)], so the integral is eˣ f(x) + c = eˣ/x + c. The option eˣ ln x treats 1/x as f′(x) instead of f(x); its derivative is eˣ(ln x + 1/x).

questions.s: ∫ tan⁻¹x dx is equal to
questions.e: Take u = tan⁻¹x, dv = dx: ∫ tan⁻¹x dx = x tan⁻¹x − ∫ x/(1 + x²) dx = x tan⁻¹x − (1/2) ln(1 + x²) + c. Forgetting the factor 1/2 in ∫ x/(1 + x²) dx gives − ln(1 + x²), and 1/(1 + x²) is the derivative of tan⁻¹x.

questions.s: ∫ sin⁻¹x dx, for −1 < x < 1, is equal to
questions.e: By parts, ∫ sin⁻¹x dx = x sin⁻¹x − ∫ x/√(1 − x²) dx. Since d/dx √(1 − x²) = −x/√(1 − x²), the remaining integral is −√(1 − x²), giving x sin⁻¹x + √(1 − x²) + c. The minus option misses this sign.

questions.s: ∫ eˣ sin x dx is equal to
questions.e: Let I = ∫ eˣ sin x dx. Parts twice gives I = eˣ sin x − eˣ cos x − I, so 2I = eˣ(sin x − cos x) and I = (eˣ/2)(sin x − cos x) + c. Check: the derivative is (eˣ/2)(sin x − cos x + cos x + sin x) = eˣ sin x. Forgetting to divide by 2 gives eˣ(sin x − cos x).

questions.s: ∫ xe⁻ˣ dx is equal to
questions.e: Take u = x, dv = e⁻ˣ dx, v = −e⁻ˣ: the integral is −xe⁻ˣ + ∫ e⁻ˣ dx = −xe⁻ˣ − e⁻ˣ + c = −e⁻ˣ(x + 1) + c. Check: the derivative is e⁻ˣ(x + 1) − e⁻ˣ = xe⁻ˣ. The option −e⁻ˣ(x − 1) mishandles the sign of ∫ e⁻ˣ dx = −e⁻ˣ.

questions.s: ∫ (ln x)² dx, x > 0, is equal to
questions.e: With u = (ln x)², dv = dx: ∫ (ln x)² dx = x(ln x)² − 2∫ ln x dx = x(ln x)² − 2(x ln x − x) + c = x(ln x)² − 2x ln x + 2x + c. The option − 2x forgets that −2 × (−x) = +2x, and (ln x)³/3 would be the integral of (ln x)²/x.

questions.s: ∫ (ln x)/x² dx, x > 0, is equal to
questions.e: Take u = ln x, dv = x⁻² dx, v = −1/x: the integral is −(ln x)/x + ∫ (1/x)(1/x) dx = −(ln x)/x − 1/x + c = −(1 + ln x)/x + c. The option −(ln x)/x stops after the first term and forgets the remaining integral of 1/x².

questions.s: ∫ eˣ(x + 1) dx is equal to
questions.e: Here f(x) = x and f′(x) = 1, so the integrand is eˣ[f(x) + f′(x)] and the integral is xeˣ + c. Check: d/dx(xeˣ) = eˣ + xeˣ = eˣ(x + 1). The option (x + 1)eˣ has derivative (x + 2)eˣ.

questions.s: ∫ x sec²x dx is equal to
o: x tan x − ln|cos x| + c
x tan x + ln|cos x| + c
questions.e: Take u = x, dv = sec²x dx, v = tan x: the integral is x tan x − ∫ tan x dx = x tan x − ln|sec x| + c = x tan x + ln|cos x| + c. The option − ln|cos x| uses ∫ tan x dx = ln|cos x|, which has the wrong sign.

questions.s: Writing exp(u) for eᵘ, ∫ x³ exp(x²) dx is equal to
questions.e: Put t = x², dt = 2x dx, so x³ dx = (1/2) t dt and the integral is (1/2)∫ teᵗ dt. By parts ∫ teᵗ dt = eᵗ(t − 1), giving (1/2) exp(x²)(x² − 1) + c. The option without 1/2 forgets x dx = dt/2.

questions.s: ∫ x² sin x dx is equal to
o: −x² cos x + 2x sin x + 2 cos x + c
−x² cos x + 2x sin x − 2 cos x + c
x² cos x − 2x sin x − 2 cos x + c
−x² cos x − 2x sin x + 2 cos x + c
questions.e: First, ∫ x² sin x dx = −x² cos x + 2∫ x cos x dx, and ∫ x cos x dx = x sin x + cos x. So the result is −x² cos x + 2x sin x + 2 cos x + c. Check: the derivative is 2x(−cos x) + x² sin x + 2 sin x + 2x cos x − 2 sin x = x² sin x. The − 2 cos x option makes a sign slip in the second step.

questions.s: ∫ ln(x + 1) dx, x > −1, is equal to
questions.e: Put t = x + 1: ∫ ln t dt = t ln t − t + c = (x + 1) ln(x + 1) − (x + 1) + c, and the constant −1 joins c, giving (x + 1) ln(x + 1) − x + c. The option x ln(x + 1) − x copies the result for ln x without adjusting for x + 1; its derivative is not ln(x + 1).

questions.s: ∫ sin²x dx is equal to
questions.e: Use sin²x = (1 − cos 2x)/2: ∫ sin²x dx = x/2 − (1/2)(sin 2x)/2 = x/2 − (sin 2x)/4 + c. The plus sign belongs to ∫ cos²x dx, and (sin³x)/3 wrongly applies the power rule to sin x without the factor cos x.

questions.s: ∫ tan²x dx is equal to
questions.e: Use tan²x = sec²x − 1, so ∫ tan²x dx = tan x − x + c. The option tan x + x comes from writing tan²x = sec²x + 1, and the power rule does not apply because sec²x is not present as a factor.

questions.s: ∫ sin 3x cos x dx is equal to
questions.e: Use 2 sin A cos B = sin(A + B) + sin(A − B): sin 3x cos x = (1/2)(sin 4x + sin 2x). Integrating gives (1/2)(−(cos 4x)/4 − (cos 2x)/2) = −(cos 4x)/8 − (cos 2x)/4 + c. The option with /4 and /2 forgets the factor 1/2 from the identity.

questions.s: ∫ sec x dx is equal to
questions.e: Multiply and divide by sec x + tan x: the numerator sec²x + sec x tan x is the derivative of sec x + tan x, so ∫ sec x dx = ln|sec x + tan x| + c. ln|sec x| is the integral of tan x, and ln|cosec x − cot x| is the integral of cosec x.

questions.s: ∫ cos²(x/2) dx is equal to
questions.e: Use cos²θ = (1 + cos 2θ)/2 with θ = x/2: cos²(x/2) = (1 + cos x)/2. Integrating gives x/2 + (sin x)/2 + c. The option with (sin x)/4 applies the cos 2x pattern again, but here the angle 2θ is just x.

questions.s: ∫ dx/(x(x + 1)) is equal to
questions.e: Partial fractions give 1/(x(x + 1)) = 1/x − 1/(x + 1), so the integral is ln|x| − ln|x + 1| + c = ln|x/(x + 1)| + c. The option ln|(x + 1)/x| has the signs of the two fractions swapped, and 1/x − 1/(x + 1) is only the decomposition, not yet integrated.

questions.s: ∫ dx/(x² − 1), for x > 1, is equal to
questions.e: 1/(x² − 1) = (1/2)[1/(x − 1) − 1/(x + 1)], so the integral is (1/2)(ln|x − 1| − ln|x + 1|) = (1/2) ln|(x − 1)/(x + 1)| + c. The fraction inverted inside the log is the result for 1/(1 − x²), and ln|x² − 1| would need 2x in the numerator.

questions.s: ∫ dx/(9 − x²), for −3 < x < 3, is equal to
questions.e: 1/(9 − x²) = (1/6)[1/(3 − x) + 1/(3 + x)]. Integrating, (1/6)(−ln|3 − x| + ln|3 + x|) = (1/6) ln|(3 + x)/(3 − x)| + c. The factor is 1/(2a) = 1/6, not 1/3, and sin⁻¹(x/3) belongs to 1/√(9 − x²), which has a square root.

questions.s: ∫ (x + 5)/((x + 1)(x + 2)) dx is equal to
questions.e: Write (x + 5)/((x + 1)(x + 2)) = A/(x + 1) + B/(x + 2). Putting x = −1 gives A = 4/1 = 4, and x = −2 gives B = 3/(−1) = −3. So the integral is 4 ln|x + 1| − 3 ln|x + 2| + c. The option + 3 ln|x + 2| drops the negative sign of x + 1 at x = −2.

questions.s: The correct form of partial fractions for (2x + 3)/((x − 1)(x² + 4)) is
questions.e: A linear factor gets a constant numerator and an irreducible quadratic factor gets a linear numerator Bx + C. Since x² + 4 has no real factors, writing it as (x + 2)(x − 2) is wrong; that is x² − 4. A constant B over x² + 4 is not general enough.

questions.s: ∫ x/((x − 1)(x − 2)) dx is equal to
questions.e: x/((x − 1)(x − 2)) = A/(x − 1) + B/(x − 2) with A = 1/(1 − 2) = −1 and B = 2/(2 − 1) = 2. The integral is −ln|x − 1| + 2 ln|x − 2| = ln|(x − 2)²/(x − 1)| + c. Swapping A and B gives the option ln|(x − 1)²/(x − 2)|.

questions.s: ∫ dx/(x(x² + 1)), x > 0, is equal to
questions.e: Write 1/(x(x² + 1)) = A/x + (Bx + C)/(x² + 1); comparing coefficients gives A = 1, B = −1, C = 0. So the integral is ln x − ∫ x/(x² + 1) dx = ln x − (1/2) ln(x² + 1) + c. The option ln x − tan⁻¹x wrongly takes the second numerator as a constant.

questions.s: ∫ dx/(x²(x + 1)), x > 0, is equal to
questions.e: Write 1/(x²(x + 1)) = A/x + B/x² + C/(x + 1). Then x = 0 gives B = 1, x = −1 gives C = 1, and the x² coefficients give A + C = 0, so A = −1. Integrating: −ln x − 1/x + ln(x + 1) = ln|(x + 1)/x| − 1/x + c. The + 1/x option forgets that ∫ x⁻² dx = −1/x.

questions.s: ∫ (x² + 1)/(x² − 1) dx, for x > 1, is equal to
questions.e: Divide first: (x² + 1)/(x² − 1) = 1 + 2/(x² − 1), and 2/(x² − 1) = 1/(x − 1) − 1/(x + 1). The integral is x + ln|x − 1| − ln|x + 1| = x + ln|(x − 1)/(x + 1)| + c. The factor 2 cancels with the 1/2 of the standard result, so the option with 2 ln is wrong.

questions.s: ∫ (3x + 1)/(x² − 1) dx, for x > 1, is equal to
questions.e: Write (3x + 1)/((x − 1)(x + 1)) = A/(x − 1) + B/(x + 1). At x = 1, A = 4/2 = 2; at x = −1, B = (−2)/(−2) = 1. So the integral is 2 ln|x − 1| + ln|x + 1| + c. The option (3/2) ln|x² − 1| integrates only 3x/(x² − 1) and ignores the + 1 in the numerator.

questions.s: ∫ dx/((x − 2)(x − 3)), for x > 3, is equal to
questions.e: Partial fractions: 1/((x − 2)(x − 3)) = 1/(x − 3) − 1/(x − 2), since at x = 3 the coefficient is 1/(3 − 2) = 1 and at x = 2 it is 1/(2 − 3) = −1. Integrating gives ln|(x − 3)/(x − 2)| + c. The factor 1/2 is wrongly copied from the formula for 1/(x² − a²) with a = 1.

questions.s: ∫ 2x/((x + 1)(x² + 1)) dx, x > −1, is equal to
questions.e: Write 2x/((x + 1)(x² + 1)) = A/(x + 1) + (Bx + C)/(x² + 1). At x = −1, A = −2/2 = −1; the x² coefficients give A + B = 0, so B = 1, and the constants give A + C = 0, so C = 1. Then ∫ (x + 1)/(x² + 1) dx = (1/2) ln(x² + 1) + tan⁻¹x, and the total is −ln(x + 1) + (1/2) ln(x² + 1) + tan⁻¹x + c. Dropping the 1/2 in front of ln(x² + 1) is the most common slip.

questions.s: ∫ (x − 1)/(x + 1) dx, x > −1, is equal to
questions.e: Rewrite (x − 1)/(x + 1) = (x + 1 − 2)/(x + 1) = 1 − 2/(x + 1), whose integral is x − 2 ln(x + 1) + c. The option x + 2 ln(x + 1) has a sign slip in the split, and (x − 1) ln(x + 1) wrongly treats the numerator as a constant.

questions.s: ∫ dx/(eˣ + 1) is equal to
questions.e: Write 1/(eˣ + 1) = (eˣ + 1 − eˣ)/(eˣ + 1) = 1 − eˣ/(eˣ + 1). Integrating gives x − ln(eˣ + 1) + c. The option ln(eˣ + 1) is the integral of eˣ/(eˣ + 1), which has eˣ in the numerator.

questions.s: ∫ x²/((x − 1)(x + 2)) dx, for x > 1, is equal to
questions.e: The fraction is improper, so divide: x²/(x² + x − 2) = 1 + (2 − x)/((x − 1)(x + 2)). For the remainder, x = 1 gives 1/3 and x = −2 gives 4/(−3) = −4/3. So the integral is x + (1/3) ln|x − 1| − (4/3) ln|x + 2| + c. Skipping the division loses the x term.

questions.s: ∫ cos x/((1 + sin x)(2 + sin x)) dx, for −π/2 < x < π/2, is equal to
o: ln|(2 + sin x)/(1 + sin x)| + c
ln|(1 + sin x)/(2 + sin x)| + c
ln|(1 + sin x)(2 + sin x)| + c
questions.e: Put t = sin x, dt = cos x dx: the integral is ∫ dt/((1 + t)(2 + t)) = ∫ [1/(1 + t) − 1/(2 + t)] dt = ln|(1 + t)/(2 + t)| + c = ln|(1 + sin x)/(2 + sin x)| + c. Inverting the fraction swaps the signs of the partial fractions.

questions.s: ∫ (x + 3)/(x² + 2x) dx, x > 0, is equal to
questions.e: Factorise x² + 2x = x(x + 2) and write (x + 3)/(x(x + 2)) = A/x + B/(x + 2). At x = 0, A = 3/2; at x = −2, B = 1/(−2) = −1/2. So the integral is (3/2) ln x − (1/2) ln(x + 2) + c. The option 3 ln x − ln(x + 2) forgets to divide by the other factor's value, 2 and −2.

questions.s: ∫ (sin x + cos x)² dx is equal to
questions.e: Expand: (sin x + cos x)² = sin²x + cos²x + 2 sin x cos x = 1 + sin 2x. Integrating gives x − (cos 2x)/2 + c. The cube form ignores the chain rule, and x − cos 2x forgets to divide by 2 when integrating sin 2x.

questions.s: ∫ cos³x dx is equal to
questions.e: Write cos³x = (1 − sin²x) cos x and put t = sin x: ∫ (1 − t²) dt = t − t³/3 = sin x − (sin³x)/3 + c. The option (cos⁴x)/4 applies the power rule without the needed factor −sin x.

questions.s: ∫ cosec x cot x dx is equal to
questions.e: d/dx(cosec x) = −cosec x cot x, so ∫ cosec x cot x dx = −cosec x + c. The option cosec x misses the minus sign, and −cot x is the integral of cosec²x.

questions.s: ∫ dx/(1 + cos x), for −π < x < π, is equal to
questions.e: Use 1 + cos x = 2 cos²(x/2): the integrand is (1/2) sec²(x/2), and ∫ sec²(x/2) dx = 2 tan(x/2), so the result is (1/2)(2) tan(x/2) = tan(x/2) + c. The option (1/2) tan(x/2) forgets the factor 2 from the inner x/2.

questions.s: ∫ cos 2x/(cos x + sin x) dx is equal to
questions.e: cos 2x = cos²x − sin²x = (cos x − sin x)(cos x + sin x), so the integrand simplifies to cos x − sin x. Its integral is sin x + cos x + c. The option cos x − sin x just copies the simplified integrand without integrating it.

questions.s: ∫ sin 5x sin 3x dx is equal to
questions.e: Use 2 sin A sin B = cos(A − B) − cos(A + B): sin 5x sin 3x = (1/2)(cos 2x − cos 8x). Integrating gives (1/2)((sin 2x)/2 − (sin 8x)/8) = (sin 2x)/4 − (sin 8x)/16 + c. The option (sin 2x)/2 − (sin 8x)/8 forgets the factor 1/2 of the identity.

questions.s: ∫ (1 + tan²x) dx is equal to
questions.e: Since 1 + tan²x = sec²x, the integral is ∫ sec²x dx = tan x + c. The option x + (tan³x)/3 integrates tan²x as if it were a power of x, and sec x + c is the integral of sec x tan x.

questions.s: ∫ dx/(sin²x cos²x) is equal to
questions.e: Write 1 = sin²x + cos²x, so 1/(sin²x cos²x) = 1/cos²x + 1/sin²x = sec²x + cosec²x. Integrating gives tan x − cot x + c, because ∫ cosec²x dx = −cot x. The option tan x + cot x misses this minus sign.

questions.s: ∫x⁴ dx equals
questions.e: Use ∫xⁿ dx = xⁿ⁺¹/(n + 1) + c with n = 4, giving x⁵/5 + c. The option 4x³ is the derivative of x⁴, not its integral.

questions.s: ∫cos 3x dx equals
questions.e: Since d/dx(sin 3x) = 3 cos 3x, we need (1/3) sin 3x + c. The option 3 sin 3x multiplies by the inner derivative instead of dividing by it.

questions.s: For x > 0, ∫(2/x) dx equals
questions.e: The constant 2 comes outside and ∫(1/x) dx = ln x, giving 2 ln x + c. The option ln 2x + c equals ln x + ln 2 + c, whose derivative is only 1/x.

questions.s: ∫e^(5x) dx equals
questions.e: d/dx(e^(5x)) = 5e^(5x), so ∫e^(5x) dx = e^(5x)/5 + c. The option e^(6x)/6 wrongly applies the power rule to the exponent.

questions.s: ∫sec²(2x) dx equals
questions.e: d/dx(tan 2x) = 2 sec²(2x), so ∫sec²(2x) dx = ½ tan 2x + c. The option 2 tan 2x multiplies by the inner derivative instead of dividing.

questions.s: ∫2x(x² + 1)³ dx equals
questions.e: Put u = x² + 1, du = 2x dx: ∫u³ du = u⁴/4 + c = (x² + 1)⁴/4 + c. The option with an extra x² factor integrates the two factors separately, which is not allowed.

questions.s: ∫(cos x/sin x) dx equals
questions.e: The numerator cos x is the derivative of the denominator sin x, so the integral is ln|sin x| + c. The option −cosec²x is the derivative of cot x, not its integral.

questions.s: ∫x eˣ dx equals
questions.e: By parts with u = x, dv = eˣ dx: x eˣ − ∫eˣ dx = eˣ(x − 1) + c. The option eˣ(x + 1) has the sign of the second term wrong; its derivative is eˣ(x + 2).

questions.s: For x > 0, ∫ln x dx equals
questions.e: By parts with u = ln x, dv = dx: x ln x − ∫x·(1/x) dx = x ln x − x + c. The option 1/x + c is the derivative of ln x, not its integral.

questions.s: ∫x cos x dx equals
o: x sin x − cos x + c
x sin x + cos x + c
questions.e: By parts with u = x, dv = cos x dx: x sin x − ∫sin x dx = x sin x + cos x + c. Writing − cos x forgets that ∫sin x dx = −cos x, so subtracting it gives + cos x.

questions.s: ∫1/(x² − 1) dx equals
questions.e: Partial fractions: 1/(x² − 1) = ½[1/(x − 1) − 1/(x + 1)], which integrates to ½ ln|(x − 1)/(x + 1)| + c. The fraction (x + 1)/(x − 1) reverses the signs of the two parts; tan⁻¹x belongs to 1/(1 + x²).

questions.s: ∫1/(x(x + 1)) dx equals
questions.e: 1/(x(x + 1)) = 1/x − 1/(x + 1), so the integral is ln|x| − ln|x + 1| + c = ln|x/(x + 1)| + c. The option ln|x(x + 1)| adds the two logarithms instead of subtracting.

questions.s: ∫1/√(4 − x²) dx equals
questions.e: Use ∫1/√(a² − x²) dx = sin⁻¹(x/a) + c with a = 2. Unlike the tan⁻¹ form, there is no factor 1/a in front, so ½ sin⁻¹(x/2) is wrong.

questions.s: ∫1/(9 + x²) dx equals
questions.e: Use ∫1/(a² + x²) dx = (1/a) tan⁻¹(x/a) + c with a = 3. Leaving out the factor 1/3 gives a derivative three times too large.

questions.s: ∫(3x² − 2x) dx equals
questions.e: Integrate term by term: ∫3x² dx = x³ and ∫2x dx = x², giving x³ − x² + c. The option 6x − 2 differentiates instead of integrating.

questions.s: The value of ∫₀¹ 4x³ dx is
questions.e: [x⁴]₀¹ = 1 − 0 = 1. The value 12 is the derivative 12x² at x = 1, not the integral.

questions.s: The value of ∫₁² (6x² + 2) dx is
questions.e: [2x³ + 2x]₁² = (16 + 4) − (2 + 2) = 16. The value 20 uses only the upper limit and forgets to subtract the value at x = 1.

questions.s: The value of ∫₀^(π/2) sin x cos²x dx is
questions.e: Put u = cos x, du = −sin x dx: the integral is [−cos³x/3]₀^(π/2) = 0 + 1/3 = 1/3. Losing the minus sign from du gives −1/3, impossible since the integrand is positive.

questions.s: The value of ∫₋₂² (x³ + 2) dx is
questions.e: x³ is odd, so it integrates to 0 over [−2, 2]; the constant gives 2 × 4 = 8. The value 0 wrongly treats the whole integrand as odd.

questions.s: The value of ∫₀¹ x e^(x²) dx is
questions.e: Put u = x², du = 2x dx: ½∫₀¹ eᵘ du = (e − 1)/2. The value e − 1 forgets the ½, and e/2 forgets that the lower limit gives e⁰ = 1.

questions.s: The area of the region bounded by y = 3x², the x-axis and the lines x = 0 and x = 2 is
questions.e: Area = [x³]₀² = 8. The value 24 forgets to divide 3x³ by 3, and 12 is the slope 6x at x = 2.

questions.s: The area of the region enclosed between the parabola y = x² and the line y = 2x is
questions.e: They meet at x = 0 and x = 2, and 2x ≥ x² there, so the area is ∫₀² (2x − x²) dx = 4 − 8/3 = 4/3. The value 4 is the area under the line alone, and 8/3 the area under the parabola alone.

questions.s: The area under the curve y = e^(−x) from x = 0 to x = ln 2 is
questions.e: Area = [−e^(−x)]₀^(ln 2) = −1/2 + 1 = 1/2. Writing the antiderivative as +e^(−x) gives 1/2 − 1 = −1/2, which cannot be an area.

questions.s: The area of the region enclosed between the parabola y = 4 − x² and the line y = x + 2 is
questions.e: 4 − x² = x + 2 gives x² + x − 2 = 0, so x = −2 or 1. Area = ∫₋₂¹ (2 − x − x²) dx = (2 − 1/2 − 1/3) − (−4 − 2 + 8/3) = 7/6 + 10/3 = 9/2. The value 7/6 integrates only from 0 to 1.

questions.s: The general solution of dy/dx = 4x³ is
questions.e: Integrating, y = ∫4x³ dx = x⁴ + c. The option 12x² + c differentiates the right side instead of integrating it.

questions.s: The solution of dy/dx = −y that satisfies y(0) = 4 is
questions.e: dy/y = −dx gives ln y = −x + k, so y = Ae^(−x); y(0) = 4 gives A = 4. The option e^(−x) + 3 also gives 4 at x = 0, but its derivative −e^(−x) is not −y.

questions.s: The general solution of dy/dx = x²/y² is
questions.e: Separating, y² dy = x² dx, so y³/3 = x³/3 + k, i.e. y³ = x³ + c. The option y³ + x³ = c has the wrong sign; it solves dy/dx = −x²/y².

questions.s: If y dy/dx = 1, y > 0 and y = 1 when x = 0, then the value of y at x = 4 is
questions.e: y dy = dx gives y²/2 = x + c; y(0) = 1 gives c = 1/2, so y² = 2x + 1 = 9 and y = 3. Forgetting the ½ in y²/2 gives y² = x + 1 and the wrong value √5.

questions.s: ∫tan x dx equals
questions.e: tan x = sin x/cos x, and the numerator is minus the derivative of cos x, so ∫tan x dx = −ln|cos x| + c = ln|sec x| + c. The option sec²x is the derivative of tan x, not its integral.

questions.s: ∫eˣ(sin x + cos x) dx equals
questions.e: Use ∫eˣ[f(x) + f′(x)] dx = eˣ f(x) + c with f(x) = sin x, f′(x) = cos x, giving eˣ sin x + c. Check: d/dx(eˣ cos x) = eˣ(cos x − sin x), which is not the integrand.

questions.s: The distance between the points (−2, 3) and (4, −5) is
questions.e: Δx = 4 − (−2) = 6 and Δy = −5 − 3 = −8, so d = √(36 + 64) = √100 = 10. Adding 6 + 8 = 14 forgets the Pythagoras step, and 2√17 comes from writing Δx as 4 − 2 instead of 4 + 2.

questions.s: The midpoint of the segment joining (3, −7) and (−5, 1) is
questions.e: Midpoint = ((3 + (−5))/2, (−7 + 1)/2) = (−2/2, −6/2) = (−1, −3). The option (−2, −6) adds the coordinates but forgets to halve them, and (4, −4) halves the differences instead of the sums.

questions.s: If the distance between the points (k, 2) and (3, −2) is 5 units, then k is
questions.e: (k − 3)² + (2 + 2)² = 25 gives (k − 3)² = 9, so k − 3 = ±3 and k = 6 or 0. The pair −6 or 0 comes from writing (k + 3)² by a sign slip; 3 or −3 is only the value of k − 3, not k.

questions.s: The point on the x-axis that is equidistant from A(1, 4) and B(5, 2) is
questions.e: Let P = (x, 0). Then (x − 1)² + 16 = (x − 5)² + 4, so x² − 2x + 17 = x² − 10x + 29, giving 8x = 12 and x = 3/2. (3, 0) is the foot of the midpoint of AB dropped to the x-axis, which is not equidistant because AB is not vertical.

questions.s: The points A(1, 1), B(4, 5) and C(8, 2) are the vertices of a triangle that is
questions.e: AB = √(9 + 16) = 5, BC = √(16 + 9) = 5 and AC = √(49 + 1) = √50. Two sides are equal and AB² + BC² = 25 + 25 = 50 = AC², so the right angle is at B and the triangle is right-angled isosceles. It is not equilateral because AC ≠ 5.

questions.s: The point that divides the join of A(2, −3) and B(8, 9) internally in the ratio 1 : 2 is
questions.e: With m : n = 1 : 2, x = (1·8 + 2·2)/3 = 12/3 = 4 and y = (1·9 + 2·(−3))/3 = 3/3 = 1, so the point is (4, 1). (6, 5) uses the ratio 2 : 1 (weights swapped), and (5, 3) is just the midpoint.

questions.s: The point that divides the join of A(1, 2) and B(4, 5) externally in the ratio 2 : 1 is
questions.e: External division: x = (2·4 − 1·1)/(2 − 1) = 7 and y = (2·5 − 1·2)/(2 − 1) = 8, giving (7, 8). (3, 4) is the internal 2 : 1 point, and (−2, −1) is the external point for the ratio 1 : 2.

questions.s: The x-axis divides the segment joining (2, −4) and (5, 6) in the ratio
questions.e: Let the ratio be k : 1. The dividing point has y = (6k − 4)/(k + 1) = 0, so k = 2/3, a positive value, meaning 2 : 3 internally. The ratio 3 : 2 swaps the order; it would be correct only if measured from (5, 6).

questions.s: The centroid of the triangle with vertices (2, 5), (−4, 1) and (5, −3) is
questions.e: Centroid = ((2 − 4 + 5)/3, (5 + 1 − 3)/3) = (3/3, 3/3) = (1, 1). (3, 3) is the sum of the coordinates without dividing by 3, and (3/2, 3/2) divides by 2 as for a midpoint.

questions.s: ABCD is a parallelogram with A(1, 2), B(4, 3) and C(6, 6). The vertex D is
questions.e: The diagonals AC and BD bisect each other, so A + C = B + D and D = (1 + 6 − 4, 2 + 6 − 3) = (3, 5). (9, 7) is B + C − A, which gives the fourth vertex of parallelogram ABDC instead, and (7/2, 4) is only the midpoint of AC.

questions.s: The circumcentre of the triangle with vertices (0, 0), (6, 0) and (0, 8) is
questions.e: The angle at the origin is 90°, so the circumcentre is the midpoint of the hypotenuse joining (6, 0) and (0, 8), which is (3, 4); the circumradius is 5. (2, 8/3) is the centroid, (2, 2) is the incentre (r = (6 + 8 − 10)/2 = 2), and (0, 0) is the orthocentre.

questions.s: The slope of the line through (−1, 4) and (3, −4) is
questions.e: m = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁) = (−4 − 4)/(3 + 1) = −8/4 = −2. The value −1/2 comes from dividing Δx by Δy, and 2 drops the sign of the rise.

questions.s: A line makes an angle of 135° with the positive direction of the x-axis. Its slope is
questions.e: Slope = tan 135° = tan(180° − 45°) = −tan 45° = −1. The value 1 forgets that tangent is negative in the second quadrant; −√3 and −1/√3 are tan 120° and tan 150°.

questions.s: If the points (1, k), (3, 5) and (5, 9) are collinear, then k equals
questions.e: The slope from (3, 5) to (5, 9) is 4/2 = 2. For collinearity the slope from (1, k) to (3, 5) must also be 2: (5 − k)/2 = 2, so k = 1. Taking k = 2 confuses the slope with the required coordinate.

questions.s: The inclination of the line passing through (1, 2) and (4, 2 + √3) is
questions.e: m = √3/(4 − 1) = √3/3 = 1/√3, and tan α = 1/√3 gives α = 30°. Choosing 60° treats the rise √3 alone as the slope, forgetting to divide by the run 3.
